lessons.title: The final Keyword
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 14 · Lesson 15 of 15 · final Reference Deep Dive: The final Keyword in Java ~35 minutes · ties to mission 1. Why Does Java Have final? In software engineering, managing state mutation is one of the most significant sources of complexity and bugs. By default, Java variables, methods, and classes are mutable and open to extension. However, unrestrained modification violates key design principles such as encapsulation, predictability, and safety. Java introduced the final keyword to declare non-modifiable intent at the language level. By enforcing constraints at compile-time, final protects structural design invariants, guarantees thread safety, and provides the JVM compiler with hints for low-level performance optimizations. Key Principle: The final keyword enforces immutability of references, prevents inheritance hijacking, and preserves design contracts across API boundaries. 2. The Four Applications of final The final keyword is context-sensitive. Its behavior is determined by where it is applied in the codebase: A. final Variables When applied to a variable, final guarantees that the variable can be assigned a value exactly once . Any attempt to reassign it triggers a compiler error. Primitives: The actual value stored in the variable cannot change. References: The memory address pointing to the heap object cannot change, meaning the variable cannot be reassigned to a different object. final int threshold = 100; // threshold = 200; // COMPILER ERROR: Cannot assign a value to final variable 'threshold' final List items = new ArrayList < >(); // items = new ArrayList < >(); // COMPILER ERROR: Cannot reassign final reference 'items' items.add("New Element"); // ALLOWED: Object mutation is permitted! B. final Methods A method marked as final cannot be overridden or hidden by subclasses. This is used to lock down critical internal behavior that must not be customized. public class SecureChannel { public final void authenticate() { // Core security logic that subclasses must not alter } } C. final Classes A class marked as final cannot be extended. This prevents subclassing, effectively closing the class to polymorphic variation. Famous examples include java.lang.String , java.lang.System , and all wrapper classes like Integer and Double . public final class ConfigurationManager { // Cannot be extended or subclassed } // class LocalManager extends ConfigurationManager {} // COMPILER ERROR: Cannot inherit from final 'ConfigurationManager' D. final Parameters Declaring method parameters as final prevents them from being reassigned within the method body. This reduces programmer error by maintaining pure input variables. public void process(final int id) { // id = 20; // COMPILER ERROR: Cannot assign a value to final variable 'id' } 3. Reference Invariance vs. Object Immutability One of the most common design misconceptions in Java is confusing a final reference with an immutable object . final Reference: Binds the reference pointer. The variable can never point to a different heap location. It does not restrict state changes inside the referenced object. Immutable Object: Ensures that the object's state cannot be modified after construction. This requires all fields to be private/final and returning copy values rather than internal mutable references. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ JVM HEAP │ │ │ │ final List list ───► [ ArrayList Object ] │ │ (Reference address fixed) │ │ │ │ Internal array │ │ │ can still grow! │ │ └────────────────────┘ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ To enforce absolute immutability, we must combine final references with unmodifiable structures: // Reference is final, but list is mutable final List mutableList = new ArrayList < >(); mutableList.add("Data"); // Works // Reference is final, and list object is unmodifiable final List immutableList = List.of("One", "Two"); // immutableList.add("Three"); // Throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime 4. Blank final Variables & Constructor Initialization A final instance variable that is not initialized at its declaration is called a blank final variable . It must be initialized in every constructor (or instance initializer block) of the class, ensuring the object is fully initialized before construction completes. public class Customer { private final String ssn; // Blank final private final int age; // Blank final // Instance Initializer Block { this.age = 18; // Valid initialization } public Customer(String ssn) { this.ssn = ssn; // Valid initialization } public Customer() { // COMPILER ERROR: Variable 'ssn' might not have been initialized } } The compiler performs definite assignment analysis . It traces every execution path of every constructor to prove that a blank final is assigned exactly once. If any branch leaves a final field unassigned, compilation fails. 5. Comparison: final vs. static vs. static final These modifiers control distinct aspects of class members and must not be confused: Modifier Combination Memory / Instance Scope Re-assignment Rule final (non-static) Bound to instance heap. Every object can store a different constant value. Initialized once per instance. Cannot be updated. static (non-final) Bound to Class object on Heap. Shared across all class instances. Can be updated repeatedly by any thread at runtime (thread-unsafe). static final Class-level constant. One instance exists in the heap metadata. Initialized once at class load. Read-only constant. 6. Compile-Time Constants (CTC) & Constant Inlining A variable is considered a compile-time constant if it satisfies all of these criteria: It is declared as final . Its type is either a primitive type or java.lang.String . It is initialized with a constant expression (resolved at compile-time). public class Limits { public static final int MAX_USERS = 500; // Compile-time constant public static final String TITLE = "Admin"; // Compile-time constant public static final double RANDOM_VAL = Math.random(); // NOT a CTC (evaluated at runtime) } The Inlining Mechanism When another class references a compile-time constant, the compiler does not emit a field lookup bytecode instruction. Instead, it reads the constant value from the defining class and inlines (embeds) the literal value directly into the referencing class's compiled bytecode. // Source Code if (userCount > Limits.MAX_USERS) { ... } // Compiled Bytecode representation (inlined literal 500) if (userCount > 500) { ... } Warning (The Constant Inlining Pitfall): If you update a compile-time constant in Limits.class but do not recompile the calling classes, the calling classes will continue using the old, inlined literal value. Always perform a clean build when constants change! 7. Why is String Immutable and final in Java? Java's java.lang.String class is declared public final class String . This was a critical design choice made for several architectural reasons: Security: Parameters like database URLs, file paths, and network ports are passed as Strings. If String were mutable, or could be subclassed, malicious code could bypass security checks by altering the String value after the check completed (Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use security vulnerability). String Pool: Java optimizes memory by sharing String literal instances (e.g. "abc" ). Sharing is only safe if the String cannot be modified by any referrer. Thread Safety: Because String state cannot change, Strings are inherently thread-safe and can be shared concurrently across threads without synchronization. HashCode Caching: Strings are widely used as keys in HashMaps. String caches its hash value upon creation. If String were mutable, modifications would change its hash code, losing the object within collections. 8. JVM Optimizations: final and the JIT Compiler By declaring classes, methods, or variables as final , you write safe code and supply critical static analysis hints to the Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler. This enables optimizations: A. Devirtualization By default, Java resolves method calls at runtime using a virtual method table (vtable) because methods can be overridden (dynamic dispatch). This carries a performance lookup overhead. If a class or method is marked final , the JIT knows it cannot be overridden. It bypassed virtual lookup entirely, transforming the call into a direct instruction. This is called devirtualization . B. Method Inlining Once a method call is devirtualized, the JIT can replace the method call instruction with the actual body of the target method. This removes the overhead of pushing and popping stack frames. Methods that are final are primary candidates for JIT inlining. C. Constant Folding If a field is marked final , the compiler and JIT can safely execute arithmetic operations on it at compile-time (constant folding). For instance, final int days = 7; int hours = days * 24; is optimized directly to the constant value 168 . Retrieval Practice What is the behavior of a final reference variable initialized with a mutable ArrayList instance? The list contents cannot mutate and reference cannot point to other objects. The list contents can mutate but reference cannot point to other objects. The list contents cannot mutate but reference can point to other objects. The list contents can mutate and reference can point to other objects. What happens if a compile-time constant is changed but dependent client code is not recompiled? The runtime loader detects discrepancy and throws NoSuchFieldException. The dependent client code uses the outdated compile-time value. The JVM re-inlines constant values during runtime class validation. The client code fails validation throwing ExceptionInInitializerError. 9. How final Influences Framework and API Design Modern framework design embraces immutability and final definitions to prevent runtime surprises: Spring Boot Constructor Injection Older Spring applications used mutable field injection ( @Autowired private Service service; ). Modern Spring Boot guidelines advocate for constructor injection using final fields. This guarantees that dependency variables cannot be null, prevents post-initialization mutation, and allows objects to be initialized in test environments without starting a Spring Context container. @Service public class OrderService { private final PaymentClient paymentClient; // Guarantees dependency is never null public OrderService(PaymentClient paymentClient) { this.paymentClient = paymentClient; } } Java Records (Java 14+) The introduction of record in Java formalizes data carrier immutability. A Record is compiled as a final class, and all its fields are implicitly declared private and final. 10. 5 Coding Exercises Exercise 1: Thread-Safe Immutable Configuration Create an immutable database configuration class holding configuration properties, preventing mutation and subclassing. public final class DbConfig { private final String url; private final String username; private final String password; public DbConfig(String url, String username, String password) { this.url = url; this.username = username; this.password = password; } public String getUrl() { return url; } public String getUsername() { return username; } public String getPassword() { return password; } } Exercise 2: Defensive Copying to Ensure Immutability Implement a class that contains a final reference to a Date field, ensuring that external modifications to the passed Date do not affect the internal state of the class. import java.util.Date; public final class Appointment { private final Date scheduledTime; public Appointment(Date scheduledTime) { // Defensive copy prevents caller from modifying the date object later this.scheduledTime = new Date(scheduledTime.getTime()); } public Date getScheduledTime() { // Return a copy to prevent external mutation of internal state return new Date(scheduledTime.getTime()); } } Exercise 3: Custom Blank Final Constructor Chaining Implement a class containing multiple constructors that initialize a final field, verifying compiler definite assignment rules. public class Token { private final String value; public Token() { this("DEFAULT_TOKEN"); // Delegate to parameterized constructor } public Token(String value) { this.value = value; // Single point of final assignment } } Exercise 4: Spring Bean Constructor Injection Define a Spring component with two required dependencies declared as final fields, avoiding fields re-assignment. import org.springframework.stereotype.Component; @Component public class ReportGenerator { private final DatabaseService dbService; private final EmailService emailService; // Spring autowires this constructor automatically when it is the sole constructor public ReportGenerator(DatabaseService dbService, EmailService emailService) { this.dbService = dbService; this.emailService = emailService; } } Exercise 5: Constant-Inlining Bytecode Verification Analyze how the JVM compiles static final primitive variables vs runtime evaluated static final variables. public class OptimizationTest { public static final int CONSTANT_VAL = 100; // CTC public static final double DYNAMIC_VAL = Math.sin(1.0); // Runtime evaluated public void execute() { System.out.println(CONSTANT_VAL); // Inlined as bytecode operand bipush 100 System.out.println(DYNAMIC_VAL); // Compiled as static field access instruction getstatic } } 11. 5 Tricky Interview Questions T1: Can you declare a final variable inside a method without initializing it? Yes. You can declare a final local variable without initialization. It only must be assigned a value exactly once before it is first read in the method body. If it is never read, it does not need initialization. T2: Can an abstract class declare final methods? Yes. An abstract class can define concrete final methods. This allows the abstract class to specify skeletal algorithms (Template Method design pattern) that subclasses can use but cannot modify or override. T3: Can we override a private final method in a subclass? No. While you can write a method with the same signature in the subclass, you are not overriding it. Private methods are invisible to subclasses, so the subclass method is treated as a completely new method. The final modifier here is redundant but allowed. T4: How does final influence Garbage Collection (GC) behavior? The final keyword itself does not alter GC garbage collector rules. However, classes containing final fields can be garbage collected faster if they are immutable, because immutable objects do not form circular references to newer objects, improving generational GC efficiency. T5: Can you change the value of a static final field reflectively? In older Java versions, you could reflectively modify a static final field by clearing the "final" modifier flag in the Field class. In modern JDKs (Java 12+), the JVM blocks reflective modification of static final fields, throwing an IllegalAccessException to protect the integrity of constant inlining optimizations. Common Misconceptions "All final fields must be initialized at declaration": False. They can be left as blank finals and initialized in instance initializer blocks or constructors. "Marking an object final makes it thread-safe": False. Only the reference is final. If the underlying object is mutable (like a HashMap), concurrent modifications remain thread-unsafe. "final classes are faster because they don't use dynamic dispatch": Mostly false. Modern JVMs perform speculative devirtualization and profiling anyway. final helps, but don't use it prematurely as a performance silver bullet. Primary Sources & Reading Review JLS Chapter 4: Section 4.12.4 (final Variables) . Read Effective Java (3rd Edition) by Joshua Bloch: Item 17 ("Minimize mutability"). Have a question about implementing immutability in your current API design? Describe your domain class structure below, and let's design its immutable representation!

lessons.title: What Is a Functional Interface?
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · Lesson 1 of ? · Rules reference What Is a Functional Interface? ~5 minutes · ties to mission The problem it solves Before Java 8, passing behaviour meant anonymous inner classes: button.addActionListener(new ActionListener() { public void actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) { System.out.println("clicked"); } }); Verbose. The interface had one method to implement — the compiler already knew which one. Lambdas exploit that fact. Background: Oracle — Lambda Expressions tutorial The definition Functional interface An interface with exactly one abstract method. It is the target type for a lambda or method reference. Default and static methods don't count toward the one-method limit. Neither do Object overrides like equals . Source: @FunctionalInterface javadoc See it work @FunctionalInterface interface Greeter { String greet(String name); // the one abstract method default void shout(String name) { System.out.println(greet(name).toUpperCase()); } } // Lambda supplies the one method: Greeter casual = name -> "hey, " + name; System.out.println(casual.greet("Riyaz")); // hey, Riyaz Practice — spot the functional interface Which interface can be implemented with a lambda? Pick the functional interface: Two methods, both abstract One abstract, one default Three abstract methods total One abstract equals method Primary reading Read the first two sections of the Oracle Lambda Expressions tutorial — stop after "Approach 5". That is the authoritative story of why functional interfaces exist. What's next Lesson 2 — Lambda Expressions : syntax, expression vs block bodies, and target typing. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — paste a code snippet or describe what confused you.

lessons.title: Lambda Expressions
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 1 · Syntax reference Lambda Expressions ~7 minutes · builds on functional interfaces What a lambda is A lambda expression is a compact way to supply the single abstract method of a functional interface — without naming the method or the class. // Anonymous inner class (5+ lines) Comparator<String> byLen = new Comparator<String>() { public int compare(String a, String b) { return a.length() - b.length(); } }; // Lambda (1 line) Comparator<String> byLen = (a, b) -> a.length() - b.length(); Source: Oracle — Lambda Quick Start Syntax — three parts (parameters) -> body Argument list · arrow token · expression or block Parameters Zero: () -> 42 One (type inferred): x -> x * 2 — parentheses optional One (typed): (int x) -> x * 2 Many: (a, b) -> a + b — parentheses required Types are usually inferred from context ( target typing ). If you type one parameter, type them all. Source: Oracle — Syntax of Lambda Expressions Body — expression vs block // Expression body — result is returned automatically Function<Integer, Integer> square = n -> n * n; // Block body — use return for non-void results Function<Integer, Integer> square = n -> { int result = n * n; return result; }; // Void — single statement needs no braces Consumer<String> print = s -> System.out.println(s); A block body that must produce a value needs an explicit return on every path. A block with only s.isEmpty() does not return a boolean — it just calls the method and discards the result. Target typing Lambdas have no standalone type. The compiler checks them against the expected functional interface: Predicate<String> isBlank = s -> s.isBlank(); // ^ target type tells compiler: test(String) -> boolean That is why a lambda alone — s -> s.isEmpty() — does not compile. It needs a target. Practice — pick the valid lambda Target type: Predicate<String> (method boolean test(String) ). Which lambda is valid? one param, expression returns value one param, return without braces block body, return is missing two params, no parens at all Reveal the code behind each option // correct: s -> s.isEmpty() // wrong: s -> return s.isEmpty(); // wrong: (s) -> { s.isEmpty(); } // wrong: s, t -> s.isEmpty() Retrieval — rewrite from memory Without looking above, write a lambda that implements Runnable and prints "start" . Then check: () -> System.out.println("start") Cover the answer, try yourself first — that effort is what builds retention. Primary reading Read Oracle — Syntax of Lambda Expressions and Target Typing . Stop before method references. What's next Lesson 3 — Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — paste your lambda and the compiler error, if you have one.

lessons.title: Predicate, Function, Consumer, & Supplier
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 2 · Four-core reference Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier ~8 minutes · the four shapes you'll use most One sentence each Java ships 43 functional interfaces in java.util.function . Four cover almost everything: Interface Shape Method Predicate<T> T → boolean test Function<T,R> T → R apply Consumer<T> T → void accept Supplier<T> () → T get Source: Oracle — java.util.function Predicate — test, don't transform Answers: "Should I keep this?" Predicate<Integer> isEven = n -> n % 2 == 0; List.of(1, 2, 3, 4).stream() .filter(isEven) // filter expects Predicate .forEach(System.out::println); // 2, 4 filter drops elements where test returns false . Function — transform Answers: "What does this become?" Function<String, Integer> length = String::length; List.of("hi", "hello").stream() .map(length) // map expects Function .forEach(System.out::println); // 2, 5 Input type T and output type R can differ — that's the point of the second type parameter. Consumer — act, return nothing Answers: "Do something with this." Side effects live here — printing, logging, saving. Consumer<String> print = System.out::println; List.of("a", "b").forEach(print); // forEach expects Consumer Source: Consumer javadoc — "expected to operate via side-effects" Supplier — produce on demand Answers: "Give me a value." No input — lazy production. Supplier<String> id = () -> UUID.randomUUID().toString(); System.out.println(id.get()); // new UUID each call System.out.println(id.get()); Common pattern: defer expensive work until someone calls get() . See all four in one pipeline List<Integer> nums = List.of(10, 15, 20, 25); nums.stream() .filter(n -> n % 2 == 0) // Predicate — keep evens .map(n -> n * n) // Function — square .forEach(System.out::println); // Consumer — print (400) Practice — match interface to stream op list.stream().filter(???) — which interface must ??? be? Pick the required interface: accepts T, returns boolean value accepts T, returns transformed value accepts T, returns void after use accepts none, returns T on call Retrieval — fill in the blanks Cover the answers. Write the interface for each: Validate an email string → Predicate<String> Parse a string to an integer → Function<String, Integer> Write a line to a file → Consumer<String> Read current timestamp → Supplier<Instant> Try before peeking. Effortful recall beats re-reading. Rule of thumb Before writing a custom interface Check if Predicate , Function , Consumer , or Supplier already fits. Effective Java Item 44: favor standard functional interfaces. Effective Java Item 44 summary Primary reading Skim the interface list in the java.util.function package . Click into Predicate and Function — note the default methods for composing behaviour. What's next Lesson 4: method references — when your lambda only calls one existing method ( String::length , System.out::println ). Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — try writing a pipeline and paste your code.

lessons.title: HashMap Internals: Buckets & put()
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← prior track · Internals reference HashMap: Buckets and put() ~10 minutes · mission · first of HashMap series Not magic — an array of buckets A HashMap is a hash table : an array called table , each slot a bucket . Each bucket holds zero or more key-value entries. table (capacity 8): [0] null [1] null [2] (hash|keyA|valA|next) → (hash|keyD|valD|null) ← collision chain [3] null [4] (hash|keyB|valB|null) ... Each entry is a Node : cached hash , key , value , and next pointer for collisions. Source: Oracle HashMap javadoc Step 1 — spread the hash Java doesn't use key.hashCode() raw. It spreads high bits into low bits so poor hashCode() implementations still distribute: int h = key.hashCode(); int hash = h ^ (h >>> 16); Step 2 — pick a bucket index Capacity is always a power of 2 (default 16). Index uses bitwise AND — fast modulo: int index = (capacity - 1) & hash; // capacity 16 → index = hash & 15 → always 0..15 Step 3 — put() at that bucket Three outcomes when you call map.put(key, value) : Case What happens Bucket empty Create a Node , store at table[index] Same key hash matches and key.equals() → replace value Different key, same index Collision — link new node via next (tail of chain) map.put("Alice", 1); // bucket 5 empty → Node stored map.put("Bob", 2); // bucket 2 empty → Node stored map.put("Carol", 3); // bucket 5 again → chain: Alice → Carol Collisions are normal — two different keys can land in the same bucket. The map walks the chain with equals to find the right one. get() is the mirror V get(K key) { int index = (capacity - 1) & spreadHash(key); for (Node n = table[index]; n != null; n = n.next) if (n.hash == hash && key.equals(n.key)) return n.value; return null; } Check hash first (fast), then equals (correct). Practice — what happens on put? Bucket at index 3 already has one entry for key "X" . You call put("Y", 99) and "Y".hashCode() maps to index 3, but "Y".equals("X") is false. What does HashMap do next? replace the old value at index three append new node to chain at three throw exception for duplicate index skip put and leave map unchanged Retrieval — explain in one sentence Cover the answer. Why does HashMap store hash inside each Node instead of calling key.hashCode() on every comparison? Reveal During resize, keys are re-indexed — cached hash avoids recomputing. On lookup, comparing cached hash before equals skips expensive equality checks when hashes differ. Primary reading Read the Implementation Notes section of the HashMap javadoc — capacity, load factor, and rehashing. Then skim Baeldung — HashMap Under the Hood sections 1–6. What's next Lesson 5 — Resize & load factor · Lesson 6: treeification. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — draw a bucket diagram or paste a put/get scenario.

lessons.title: HashMap Internals: Resize & Load Factor
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 4 · Resize reference Resize and Load Factor ~8 minutes · builds on buckets & put() Why resize exists As entries accumulate, buckets get crowded — collision chains grow and get / put slow down. HashMap grows the table array to spread entries across more buckets. Source: Oracle HashMap — Implementation Notes Load factor Load factor How full the table is allowed to get before doubling. Default 0.75f — a time/space tradeoff chosen by the JDK authors. threshold = capacity × loadFactor // defaults: capacity 16, load factor 0.75 threshold = 16 × 0.75 = 12 Higher load factor → fewer empty buckets, less memory, longer chains. Lower load factor → more buckets, more memory, shorter chains. Baeldung — HashMap Load Factor When resize fires After every successful put , HashMap checks: if (++size > threshold) resize(); // double capacity, rehash every entry With defaults: entries 1–12 fit without resize. The 13th insert makes size = 13 > 12 → resize to capacity 32, new threshold 24. Event capacity threshold new HashMap() 16 12 13th entry added 32 24 25th entry added 64 48 What resize actually does Allocate new array with double the capacity For each entry in the old table, recompute index — mask changed from 15 to 31 Move entries into new buckets (chains may split across two indices) Before resize (capacity 4, mask 011): index 2: A → C → null After resize (capacity 8, mask 1111): index 2: A → null (stayed — extra bit was 0) index 6: C → null (moved — extra bit was 1) Each entry either stays or moves to oldIndex + oldCapacity . Cached hash in each Node avoids recomputing hashCode() during this walk. Cost of resize Resize is O(n) — every entry is revisited. Frequent resizes on a growing map cause latency spikes. If you know the final size upfront, set initial capacity to avoid them: // Java 19+: sized for ~100 entries without resize Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>(100); // Older pattern: capacity = expectedSize / 0.75 + 1 int cap = (int) (expectedSize / 0.75f) + 1; new HashMap<>(cap); Oracle: "If the initial capacity is greater than the maximum number of entries divided by the load factor, no rehash operations will ever occur." Practice — when does resize happen? Default HashMap : capacity 16, load factor 0.75. Which insert triggers the first resize? the eighth distinct key-value pair the twelfth distinct key-value pair the thirteenth distinct key-value pair the sixteenth distinct key-value pair Retrieval — calculate threshold Cover the answer. A map is created with new HashMap<>(32, 0.5f) . What is the threshold? Reveal 32 × 0.5 = 16 . Resize when the 17th entry is added ( size > 16 ). Primary reading Read Baeldung — HashMap Load Factor in full. Re-read the capacity/load-factor paragraph in the HashMap javadoc . What's next Lesson 6 — Treeification : when collision chains become red-black trees (Java 8+). Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — try calculating threshold for a custom constructor.

lessons.title: HashMap Internals: Treeify Threshold
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 5 · Treeification reference Treeification ~7 minutes · builds on resize & load factor The problem: O(n) worst-case In standard hash tables, if many keys hash to the same bucket (due to poor hashCode() or an intentional hash collision attack), search times degrade from O(1) to O(n) . In Java 8, the JDK developers addressed this by introducing treeification . Source: Oracle HashMap — Implementation Notes Red-Black Trees When a bucket's collision chain grows too long, the linked list is converted into a self-balancing Red-Black Tree . Under high collisions, this changes lookup and insertion performance from O(n) to O(log n) . Instead of Node instances, the bucket uses TreeNode instances (which hold left , right , parent , and red properties). Linked List (O(n)): [Bucket 2] → A → B → C → D → E → F → G → H → I (9 nodes) Red-Black Tree (O(log n)): [Bucket 2] → E / \ B G / \ / \ A C F H \ \ D I The two conditions for treeification A bucket does not instantly treeify just because it has collisions. Two thresholds must be met: Treeify Threshold ( TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 ): A linked list chain must grow to length 8. When adding the 9th node (chain length becomes 9), treeification is triggered. Minimum Capacity ( MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64 ): The total capacity of the map must be at least 64. If the map is smaller than 64 (e.g. default capacity of 16), the HashMap will trigger a resize() instead of treeifying. Resizing splits the bucket and distributes nodes, which usually resolves the collision chain. Source: JDK 8+ HashMap.java source code ( treeifyBin method) Untreeification (The Hysteresis) If the number of entries in a treeified bucket decreases (due to removals or split buckets during resizing), the tree is converted back to a linked list. This happens when the count falls to UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6 . Why 6 and not 8? Having different thresholds (8 for treeifying, 6 for untreeifying) prevents thrashing — rapid, expensive conversions back and forth between a list and a tree if the bucket size fluctuates around 8. Practice — when does it treeify? Assume you create a new HashMap with default options (capacity 16) and insert 9 keys that all hash to the same bucket index. What is the result after inserting the 9th key? the map will resize and double its capacity the bucket will treeify into a search tree the map will throw a hash collision error the bucket will ignore the newly added node Retrieval — identify the thresholds Cover the answer. What are the default values for the treeify threshold, untreeify threshold, and minimum treeify capacity in Java's HashMap? Reveal TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8 , UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6 , and MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64 . Primary reading Read the Java 8+ HashMap Treeification explanation on Baeldung — HashMap Advanced (Section 6) . Then, review the implementation comments at the top of the JDK HashMap source code (search for TREEIFY_THRESHOLD ). What's next That completes the HashMap internals core track! You can explore custom key design, mutable keys, or ask your teacher for a summary of Map variations. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — try asking why Red-Black Trees are used instead of simpler AVL Trees or Binary Search Trees.

lessons.title: ArrayList Internals & Resizing
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 6 · ArrayList reference ArrayList Internals ~8 minutes · builds on resize & load factor The Backing Array Unlike a `LinkedList`, which represents elements as node chain links, Java's ArrayList stores elements inside a simple, contiguous backing array : Object[] elementData . Because primitive Java arrays have a fixed size, the ArrayList class manages the complexity of expanding this array dynamically behind the scenes as you insert elements. Source: Oracle ArrayList API Specifications Capacity vs Size To understand the mechanics, we must separate two fundamental properties of an ArrayList : Capacity: The physical length of the backing array ( elementData.length ). This is the maximum number of items the list can hold before allocating a new array. Size: The logical count of elements currently stored in the list by the user (accessed via size() ). The condition size < = capacity is always true. When size == capacity , the backing array is full, and the next insertion will trigger a growth phase. Interactive Simulator Use the simulator below to inspect the state of the backing array. Notice how adding elements changes Size , and watch what happens to the array's Capacity when it runs out of empty slots. Backing Array Length (Capacity) 4 List Size 0 Add to End (add(x)) Insert at Index 0 (add(0, x)) Delete at Index 0 (remove(0)) Random Access Index 2 (get(2)) Reset (Capacity = 4) Simulator initialized. Capacity is 4. Size is 0. Growth Strategy (1.5x Scaling) When you attempt to add an element to a full list, Java reallocates a larger array. The JDK calculates the new capacity using a bitwise shift right operation: int newCapacity = oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1); Since shifting right by 1 bit ( >> 1 ) is equivalent to integer division by 2, this means: newCapacity = oldCapacity + 0.5 * oldCapacity = 1.5 * oldCapacity . Once the new capacity is computed, Java allocates the new array and copies the old elements over via Arrays.copyOf() , which internally utilizes the extremely fast, native memory copying operation System.arraycopy() . Why Random Access is O(1) In computer memory, an array is stored as a contiguous block of bytes. Because every object reference in Java takes up the same fixed amount of space (typically 4 or 8 bytes), the JVM can compute the exact physical address of any element immediately without traversing the list: Address(index) = BaseAddress + index * ReferenceSize This single addition and multiplication allows the computer to look up the element at any arbitrary index in constant O(1) time, whether it is the first element, the middle element, or the last. Insertions and Deletions While indexing is fast, altering the size of the array has trade-offs: Inserting/Deleting at the end: This takes O(1) time. Resizing occurs only occasionally (at a geometric interval), so the cost of copies amortizes to a constant O(1) overall. Inserting/Deleting at arbitrary indices: This takes O(n) time. If you insert at index i , all elements from index i to size - 1 must be shifted one slot to the right. Deleting an element requires shifting everything to the left. Try this in the simulator above and watch the orange highlight shift step-by-step. Practice — Growth Mechanics Assume you initialize an ArrayList using the default constructor (which starts with an empty buffer and scales to capacity 10 on the first element). You add 10 items to fill the list. What is the capacity of the backing array immediately after you add the 11th item? fifteen (it grows the capacity by fifty percent) twenty (it doubles the capacity of the list) eleven (it expands the capacity by one slot) ten (it maintains the current capacity size limit) Retrieval Practice Cover the answer. What is the time complexity of looking up a value in an ArrayList if you do not know its index (e.g. searching for a value using contains(Object o) )? Reveal It is O(n) . Because you do not know the index, the list must iterate through the backing array one-by-one from index 0 until the matching element is found. Primary Reading Review the Oracle official documentation for the ArrayList class to review its performance guarantees, and read Baeldung's guide on ArrayList capacity management . What's next You can ask your teacher about the differences between ArrayList and LinkedList , or deep-dive into how System.arraycopy() works at the OS level. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — for example, ask how ArrayList handles element removals to avoid memory leaks (loitering references).

lessons.title: LinkedList Internals & Deque
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 7 · LinkedList reference LinkedList Internals ~9 minutes · builds on ArrayList internals The Node Structure Unlike ArrayList , which aggregates its objects inside a contiguous backing array, a LinkedList stores its elements inside individual, disjoint heap-allocated objects called nodes . In Java, java.util.LinkedList implements a doubly linked list . Each node is an instance of a private static nested class containing three fields: private static class Node<E> { E item; // The actual data element Node<E> next; // Reference to the next node in the list Node<E> prev; // Reference to the previous node in the list } The list itself maintains three basic references: int size , Node<E> first (pointing to the head), and Node<E> last (pointing to the tail). Source: Oracle LinkedList API Specifications Interactive Simulator Inspect the visual representation of nodes below. Each node is split into a prev reference, an item value, and a next reference. Pointers represent memory memory addresses (indicated as • or null ). First Node Pointer (first) node0 Last Node Pointer (last) node2 Size 3 Add to Start (addFirst(x)) Add to End (addLast(x)) Get Index 2 (get(2)) Insert after Index 0 (O(1) once known) Reset List (A ⟷ B ⟷ C) Simulator initialized. List size is 3. Why Random Access is O(n) Because nodes are allocated dynamically in separate segments of memory, they do not occupy a contiguous physical block. This means we cannot calculate a node's physical address directly from an index using simple arithmetic. To find the element at index i , the JVM must perform a list traversal starting at one end of the list and following the chain of pointers step-by-step: Node<E> x = first; for (int k = 0; k < index; k++) { x = x.next; } return x.item; Since the number of hops is proportional to the index value, lookup takes linear O(n) time. Bidirectional Optimization As a doubly linked list, Java optimizes this traversal. If the target index is in the second half of the list ( index > size / 2 ), it starts from the last pointer and walks backward using prev . While this cuts search steps in half, the worst-case complexity remains O(n) . O(1) Insertions (When Reference is Known) Adding an element to an ArrayList requires shifting subsequent items to the right to make room (taking O(n) time). A LinkedList never shifts items. If you already hold a direct reference to a node (say, target ), inserting a new node involves only re-linking four pointer fields: Create the new node: Node<E> newNode = new Node<>(target, element, target.next); Update the following node: target.next.prev = newNode; Update the target node: target.next = newNode; Because this re-linking relies on a fixed number of variable updates, it takes constant O(1) time. (Note: Locating the node by index first still requires an O(n) search, but the insertion operation itself is O(1) once you are at that node). Doubly Linked List Trade-Offs The extra pointers in a doubly linked list add both advantages and costs: Pros: Efficient traversal in both directions, simple insertion and deletion at both ends ( first and last ) in O(1) time, which makes it ideal for implementing double-ended queues (Deques). Cons: High memory overhead. Every node must store two object pointers ( prev and next references) in addition to the element reference. In a 64-bit JVM, this pointer metadata can easily consume more memory than the actual payload data. Practice — Bidirectional Traversal Java's LinkedList.get(index) method optimizes lookups by splitting the list in half. In a doubly linked list, how does the index lookup method get(i) optimize traversal? it starts searching from the closest list end point it searches from both list ends using separate threads it caches node memory pointers to skip traversal steps it uses binary search algorithms to locate target nodes Retrieval Practice Cover the answer. If you are adding elements exclusively to the end of a list using add(E element) , which structure is generally faster and uses less memory: ArrayList or LinkedList ? Reveal ArrayList is generally faster and uses significantly less memory. An ArrayList packs references contiguously without node wrappers, reducing metadata overhead. Adding to the end is an amortized O(1) operation, which runs extremely fast due to sequential memory access patterns, whereas LinkedList must allocate a new node object on every single insertion. Primary Reading Read the official OpenJDK implementation details in the LinkedList.java source code (specifically focus on the linkBefore , unlink , and node(int index) methods). What's next Lesson 9 — HashSet Internals · Learn how Java prevents duplicate elements using a backing HashMap. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — for example, ask how Java's garbage collector cleans up unlinked nodes to avoid memory leaks.

lessons.title: HashSet Internals & HashMap Backing
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 8 · HashSet reference HashSet Internals ~10 minutes · builds on HashMap internals The Backing HashMap In Java, a HashSet does not implement hashing logic or collision buckets from scratch. Instead, it is a simple wrapper around a HashMap . When you instantiate a HashSet , it secretly allocates an internal HashMap instance: public HashSet() { map = new HashMap<>(); } Every element you add to a HashSet is stored as a key in this backing map. Because a map requires both keys and values, the set uses a single static sentinel dummy object called PRESENT as the value for every entry: private static final Object PRESENT = new Object(); Source: Oracle HashSet Specifications How Duplicates are Rejected A key property of a Set is that it cannot contain duplicate elements. This rule is naturally enforced by the backing map's key uniqueness guarantee. When you call hashSet.add(element) , it delegates directly to map.put(element, PRESENT) : public boolean add(E e) { return map.put(e, PRESENT) == null; } Recall the behavior of HashMap.put(K key, V value) : If the key is new : The map stores it, returns null . The set checks null == null and returns true (item added). If the key is a duplicate : The map replaces the old value with PRESENT (which changes nothing) and returns the previous value (which is PRESENT ). The set checks PRESENT == null , which evaluates to false (item rejected). Interactive HashSet Simulator Add strings to the HashSet below. Watch how the backing HashMap computes their hash values, finds their bucket slots, traverses collision chains, and returns either null or PRESENT to accept or reject the element. HashMap Capacity 8 HashMap Size 0 HashSet Size 0 Add "Apple" Add "Banana" Add "Cherry" Add "Apple" (Duplicate) Add Custom Reset Map Simulator initialized. Backing HashMap table allocated (8 slots). Role of equals() and hashCode() To identify if a key is a duplicate, the backing HashMap needs a way to locate and compare objects. It does this in two steps using the element's hashCode() and equals() methods: Locate the bucket : It hashes the element and finds the bucket slot index. Compare key references : If the bucket already contains nodes, the map walks the chain, checking if (node.hash == hash && (node.key == key || key.equals(node.key))) . Because of this, if you store custom objects in a HashSet , you must override both hashCode() and equals() . If you override only one, or fail to override them consistently, the set will either allow duplicate entries or fail to locate elements during lookup. Time Complexities Because all operations delegate directly to the backing HashMap , they share its performance characteristics: add() , remove() , contains() : Average case: O(1) . If hash codes are well-distributed, elements map to distinct buckets with short chains, requiring constant-time lookups. Worst case: O(log n) (Java 8+) / O(n) (Java 7-). Under severe hash collisions where all elements hash to the same bucket index, the chain grows linear in size. In Java 8+, the bucket treeifies into a Red-Black Tree, capping search time to logarithmic complexity. Practice — Duplicate Rejection Test your understanding of the return value check that determines if an element was already in the set. What does the backing Map return when adding a duplicate key? A sentinel PRESENT object A null reference pointer A new key element object A map size integer value Practice — Bucket Treeification Recall the performance limit of hash collections under collisions. What is the worst-case time complexity of HashSet.contains() in Java 8+ if keys have identical hash codes? O(log n) O(1) O(n) O(n^2) Retrieval Practice Cover the answer. Why is the dummy value PRESENT defined as a static member ( private static final Object PRESENT = new Object(); ) instead of creating a new Object instance inside each HashSet or for each element? Reveal To conserve memory. Since the backing HashMap requires a value for every node, creating a new dummy object instance per element would waste heaps of memory. Defining PRESENT as a static member creates exactly one instance of Object in heap memory, shared across all keys and all instances of HashSet in the application. Primary reading Review the official JDK source implementation in the HashSet.java source code (focus on the constructors, and the add and contains methods). What's next Lesson 10 — TreeSet Internals · Learn how Java stores unique elements in sorted order using a Red-Black Tree. Stuck on anything? lessons.title: TreeSet Internals & Red-Black Tree
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 9 · TreeSet reference TreeSet Internals ~11 minutes · builds on HashSet internals The Backing TreeMap Like HashSet , a TreeSet does not implement its core data structures from scratch. It is a wrapper delegating all elements to a backing TreeMap instance as keys, with the sentinel object PRESENT as values: public class TreeSet<E> extends AbstractSet<E> implements NavigableSet<E> { private transient NavigableMap<E,Object> m; private static final Object PRESENT = new Object(); public TreeSet() { this(new TreeMap<>()); } } Under the hood, a TreeMap is implemented as a Red-Black Tree : a self-balancing binary search tree. Each node contains a key, a value, and links to left, right, and parent nodes, plus a boolean flag representing its color (Red or Black). Source: Oracle TreeSet API Specifications Self-Balancing Binary Search Trees In a standard binary search tree, search time depends on node layout. If keys are added in sorted order (e.g. 10, 20, 30), the tree degenerates into a straight linked list, degrading search performance to linear O(n) time. A Red-Black Tree enforces structural rules (such as maintaining black height balance and avoiding adjacent red nodes) that trigger tree rotations on insertion. This guarantees that the tree height remains bounded by approximately 2 log(n + 1) . As a result, lookups, insertions, and deletions are guaranteed to scale at logarithmic O(log n) time. Interactive TreeSet BST Simulator Insert values to build a Binary Search Tree. Observe how the insertion logic traverses from the root node downward: comparing values, deciding to branch left (smaller) or right (larger), and rejecting duplicates if a comparison yields exactly zero. Tree Depth Limit 4 Levels TreeSet Size 0 Insert 20 Insert 40 Insert 60 Insert 80 Insert 50 (Duplicate) Insert Custom Reset to [50, 30, 70] Simulator initialized. Pre-populated root node (50) and children (30, 70). Role of Ordering: Comparable vs. Comparator Because elements must be sorted, a TreeSet requires a way to compare them. It utilizes one of two interfaces: Comparable (Natural Ordering) : The element's class implements java.lang.Comparable and overrides compareTo(E other) . Standard classes like String , Integer , and Date implement this by default. Comparator (Custom Ordering) : You pass a custom java.util.Comparator implementation to the TreeSet constructor, defining comparison rules externally (e.g. comparing Strings by length instead of alphabetical order). Gotcha: Comparison vs. equals() A HashSet checks if an item is a duplicate using equals() . A TreeSet ignores equals() entirely during insertion; duplicate check is strictly based on the comparison result. If compareTo(x) == 0 (or compare(a, b) == 0 ), the element is rejected as a duplicate, even if equals() returned false! Practice — Duplicate Condition Test your understanding of the TreeSet contract for duplicate checks. What determines if two objects are duplicates in a TreeSet? compareTo() results in zero equals() returns true value hashCode() outputs are same identity comparison is match Practice — Interface Violations What happens if you violate the collection invariants during initialization? What occurs if you add elements to a TreeSet that do not implement Comparable and no Comparator is provided? A ClassCastException is thrown A NullPointerException occurs The element is added normally The set silently rejects values Retrieval Practice Cover the answer. If you need a collection that stores unique values and you only need lookup, insertion, and deletion operations, which collection should you select: HashSet or TreeSet ? Reveal You should select HashSet . HashSet operates in average constant O(1) time for lookup, insertion, and deletion, which is faster than the logarithmic O(log n) performance of TreeSet . You should only choose TreeSet if you specifically need elements to be sorted or require range operations (like extracting sub-sets). Primary reading Inspect the official source implementation in the TreeSet.java source code (focus on constructor initializations and the add method). What's next Lesson 11 — PriorityQueue Internals · Learn how Java processes element priorities using a backing Binary Heap inside a contiguous array. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — for example, ask how Red-Black Tree rotation mechanisms balance parent-child heights.

lessons.title: PriorityQueue Internals & Binary Heap
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 10 · PriorityQueue reference PriorityQueue Internals ~12 minutes · builds on ArrayList internals The Backing Array (Binary Heap) In Java, a PriorityQueue is structured under the hood as a binary heap . A binary heap is a complete binary tree (all levels are filled completely, except possibly the bottom level, which is filled from left to right). Because the tree is guaranteed to be complete, it can be packed into a flat, contiguous primitive array (represented as Object[] queue ) without the need for left/right node reference pointers. This merges the structural speed of tree hierarchies with the memory efficiency of contiguous arrays. Source: Oracle PriorityQueue API Specifications Mapping Trees to Array Indexes By filling tree nodes level-by-level, we establish a mathematical link between tree parent-child relations and array indices. For any element located at index i in the zero-indexed array: Left child index is calculated as: 2 * i + 1 Right child index is calculated as: 2 * i + 2 Parent index is calculated as: (i - 1) / 2 (rounded down) For example, if parent node is at index 0 , its left child is at 2(0)+1 = 1 , and its right child is at 2(0)+2 = 2 . If a node is at index 4 , its parent is at (4-1)/2 = 1 . Sift-Up and Sift-Down Operations To preserve the min-heap ordering constraint (that each parent node must be $\le$ both of its child nodes), the priority queue implements two index-relocating algorithms: Sift-Up (Inserting) : When adding an element via offer(e) , the value is appended at the end of the array (bottom-right of tree). It is compared to its parent; if smaller, they swap. This process repeats upward until the heap property is satisfied or the element becomes the root. Sift-Down (Extracting) : When pulling the minimum element via poll() , the root (index 0) is returned. The last element in the array is relocated to index 0, and is sifted downward by swapping with its smaller child. This repeats until it has no children or is smaller than both. Interactive Heap Simulator Interact with the binary heap visualizer below. Add elements to trigger Sift-Up swaps, or poll the smallest item to trigger Sift-Down swaps. Notice how nodes in the tree synchronize with slots in the underlying array representation. Heap Capacity Limit 7 Elements PriorityQueue Size 0 Insert 15 Insert 5 Poll (Remove Root) Reset Heap Insert Custom Simulator initialized. Pre-populated heap array: [10, 30, 20, 50, 40]. Max-Heaps using Comparators By default, Java's PriorityQueue sorts elements in their natural ascending order (acting as a min-heap). If you need a max-heap (where poll() retrieves the largest element first), you must initialize it with a custom comparator that reverses the natural ordering: PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder()); Under the hood, the sift-up and sift-down algorithms will compare elements using comparator.compare(x, parent) . If the comparator reverses the check, swaps will happen when children are larger than parents, turning the structure into a max-heap. Time Complexities peek() : O(1) . The highest priority item is always at index 0 of the backing array. offer() / poll() : O(log n) . Restoring the heap constraint requires traversing a single branch of the tree, which is bounded by the logarithmic tree height. Heapify constructor ( new PriorityQueue(collection) ) : O(n) . Building a heap bottom-up is a standard algorithm that runs in linear time. Practice — Index Math Verify your understanding of heap array index mapping equations. For a heap node stored at index i in a zero-indexed array, how is the left child's index calculated? 2 * i + 1 2 * i + 2 2 * i - 1 2 * i + 0 Practice — Heapify Complexity Compare the cost of bulk heap construction against individual element additions. What is the time complexity of building a PriorityQueue from an unsorted collection of size n? O(n) O(log n) O(n log) O(n^2) Retrieval Practice Cover the answer. If you iterate through a PriorityQueue using an iterator or a enhanced for-each loop, does it yield elements in sorted ascending order? Reveal No, it does not. The iterator simply scans the backing array sequentially from index 0 to size - 1 . While index 0 is guaranteed to be the minimum, the remaining array indexes are arranged to satisfy parent-child heap constraints, not linear sorted order. To extract elements in sorted order, you must call poll() in a loop until the queue is empty. Primary reading Read the official OpenJDK implementation of PriorityQueue.java source code (focus on siftUp and siftDown methods). What's next Now that you've completed the basic data structures track, you can ask your teacher for a summary comparison cheat sheet covering ArrayList, LinkedList, HashSet, TreeSet, and PriorityQueue. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — for example, ask how PriorityQueue resizes its backing array when it runs out of capacity.

lessons.title: Comparable vs. Comparator
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 11 · Lesson 12 of ? · TreeSet reference Comparable vs. Comparator ~6 minutes · ties to mission The Core Difference In Java, sorting and ordering require clear rules. Java provides two interfaces for this, each with a different intent: Comparable (Natural Ordering) Implemented by the class itself to define its default sorting behavior (e.g., Numbers sorted numerically, Strings sorted alphabetically). Method: public int compareTo(T o) Comparator (Custom/External Ordering) Implemented externally (often as a lambda) to sort objects using alternative rules, or to sort classes you do not own/modify. Method: public int compare(T o1, T o2) The Return Contract Both methods follow a strict mathematical return contract. They return an integer value indicating the order of elements: // For Comparable (compareTo) int result = obj1.compareTo(obj2); // For Comparator (compare) int result = comp.compare(obj1, obj2); Negative Integer: obj1 is smaller/comes before obj2 . Zero (0): obj1 is equal to obj2 . Positive Integer: obj1 is larger/comes after obj2 . Under the Hood: TreeSet & Duplicate Rejection This is where collection internals become critical. Unlike HashSet (which uses hashCode() and equals() ), TreeSet relies entirely on comparisons. When you insert an element into a TreeSet (backed by TreeMap ): Java traverses the Red-Black tree, comparing the new element to the current node. If the comparison returns a negative number, it walks left. If positive, it walks right. If the comparison returns 0 , the TreeSet rejects the new element as a duplicate , and does not modify the set. Warning: Uniqueness Gotcha If your comparison logic returns 0 for two objects, they are duplicates in the eyes of a TreeSet , even if equals() says they are different. A TreeSet can violate the standard Set contract if its comparison is inconsistent with equals() . Let's See It in Code Below is a custom class implementing Comparable for natural ordering, paired with a custom Comparator lambda: import java.util.*; class User implements Comparable<User> { int id; String name; User(int id, String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; } // Natural order: sort by id @Override public int compareTo(User other) { return Integer.compare(this.id, other.id); } } public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { // TreeSet using Natural Order (Comparable) Set<User> byId = new TreeSet<>(); byId.add(new User(10, "Riyaz")); byId.add(new User(5, "Sayyad")); // Reject: duplicate ID (10) even with a different name! byId.add(new User(10, "Alice")); // TreeSet using Custom Order (Comparator) Set<User> byNameLength = new TreeSet<>( (u1, u2) -> Integer.compare(u1.name.length(), u2.name.length()) ); byNameLength.add(new User(1, "Riyaz")); // length 5 byNameLength.add(new User(2, "Sayyad")); // length 6 // Reject: length 5 is a duplicate of "Riyaz"! byNameLength.add(new User(3, "Alice")); } } Practice — duplication checks Test your understanding of TreeSet duplicates: Pick the correct statement regarding TreeSet duplicates: TreeSet rejects duplicates based only on equals(). TreeSet rejects duplicates based on compareTo() == 0. TreeSet rejects duplicates using hashCode() values. TreeSet rejects duplicates using reference equality. Primary reading Read the Comparable Javadoc and the Comparator Javadoc . Focus specifically on the discussion of being "consistent with equals." Stuck on anything? lessons.title: The Collections Utility Class
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 12 · Lesson 13 of ? · Collections Reference The Collections Utility Class ~7 minutes · ties to mission Collection vs. Collections In Java, it is easy to confuse the two names: java.util.Collection is the root interface of the collections hierarchy (implemented by List, Set, Queue). java.util.Collections is a utility class consisting exclusively of static methods that operate on or return collections. It cannot be instantiated. 1. Sorting & Searching Two of the most frequently used methods are for ordering and retrieving elements: Collections.sort(List<T> list) : Sorts elements using the objects' natural order ( Comparable ) or a custom Comparator . Stable Sorting: The sort algorithm is stable (Timsort in modern JDKs). Equal elements are guaranteed to remain in their original relative positions after sorting. Collections.binarySearch(List<?> list, T key) : Performs an optimized logarithmic search. Prerequisite: The list MUST be sorted in ascending order before invoking this method. If it is not sorted, the returned index is undefined and unpredictable. Note on Lists: Runs in O(log n) on RandomAccess lists (ArrayList). However, on sequential-access chains (LinkedList), it traverses nodes step-by-step, degrading to O(n) . 2. General Utility Methods The class contains a wide variety of static helper algorithms for manipulating list and collection states: Method Purpose & Key Behaviors reverse(list) Reverses the order of elements in the specified list. shuffle(list) Randomly permutes elements using a default or custom source of randomness. swap(list, i, j) Swaps the elements at index i and index j in the list. fill(list, obj) Replaces all elements in the list with the specified element obj . copy(dest, src) Copies all elements from src to dest . Dest must be at least as long as src , or IndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown. min(coll) / max(coll) Returns the minimum or maximum element according to natural order or custom comparator. frequency(coll, obj) Returns the number of elements in the collection equal to the specified object. disjoint(c1, c2) Returns true if the two collections have no elements in common. 3. Wrappers: List Control View Gates Three key wrappers intercept calls to control a collection's properties, returning a thin delegating view: unmodifiableList(list) : Intercepts write calls (e.g., add() , remove() ) and throws UnsupportedOperationException . synchronizedList(list) : Wraps all calls inside a synchronized(mutex) block. *Note:* manual synchronization on the mutex is required when using an iterator loop. checkedList(list, Class) : Validates elements added to the list at runtime, preventing generic type evasion and heap pollution. 4. Wrapper View vs. True Immutable Collection It is vital to understand the difference between wrapper views and modern immutable collections (like List.of() ): List<String> backing = new ArrayList<>(); backing.add("Apple"); // 1. Wrapper View (Unmodifiable) List<String> wrapper = Collections.unmodifiableList(backing); // 2. Immutable Collection List<String> immutable = List.copyOf(backing); // Modifying the backing list... backing.add("Banana"); System.out.println(wrapper); // prints [Apple, Banana] (reflects changes!) System.out.println(immutable); // prints [Apple] (truly immutable!) Wrapper View: Reads directly from the underlying mutable backing collection. It is a write-gate, not a data copy. Immutable Collection: Independent data copy. It doesn't rely on a backing collection, rejects null values entirely, and is heavily optimized for space. Practice — unmodifiable collections Test your understanding of views vs copies: Pick the correct statement regarding unmodifiable collections: Unmodifiable collections reflect underlying backing collection changes. Unmodifiable collections copy backing collections during creation step. Unmodifiable collections prevent backing collections from being mutated. Unmodifiable collections support custom sorting via comparator algorithms. Primary reading Read the Collections Javadoc . Focus specifically on the descriptions of the wrapper methods and Timsort guarantees. Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — paste a code snippet or describe what confused you.

lessons.title: Java Iterator Internals
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 13 · Lesson 14 of ? · Iterator Reference Java Iterator Internals: Interview Guide ~8 minutes · ties to mission 1. Why Iterator Was Introduced Prior to Java 1.2, traversing collections was inconsistent. Legacy structures like Vector used Enumeration . Iterator was introduced to achieve two main goals: Standardization: Provides a uniform traversal interface across all collection types (Lists, Sets, Maps), hiding the underlying structural layout (Encapsulation). Safety: Supports safe structural modifications (removal) during iteration and implements fail-fast checks to detect concurrent modifications. 2. Internal Cursor Mechanism Each collection class implements Iterable and defines an internal private class (e.g., ArrayList.Itr or LinkedList.ListItr ) implementing the Iterator interface. They maintain internal pointers to keep track of state: ArrayList Iterator: Tracks int cursor (index of the next element to return) and int lastRet (index of the last element returned; reset to -1 after removal). LinkedList Iterator: Tracks a Node reference nextNode (the next node to visit) and lastReturned (the last node visited; reset to null after removal). 3. Methods Internals (hasNext, next, remove) The standard loop checks and traverses elements sequentially: // hasNext() checks if cursor hasn't reached size limit public boolean hasNext() { return cursor != size; } // next() retrieves the element and increments the cursor public E next() { checkForComodification(); // Mismatch check int i = cursor; if (i >= size) throw new NoSuchElementException(); Object[] elementData = ArrayList.this.elementData; cursor = i + 1; return (E) elementData[lastRet = i]; } 4. The Fail-Fast vs. Safe-Remove Mechanics Why does collection.remove() throw a ConcurrentModificationException while iterator.remove() does not? It comes down to two variables: modCount : Maintained by the collection, counting structural modifications. expectedModCount : Maintained by the iterator, initialized to the collection's modCount at startup. If you call list.remove() , only modCount increments. The next call to iterator.next() notices that modCount != expectedModCount and triggers a fail-fast crash. If you call iterator.remove() , it performs the removal, increments the collection's modCount , and immediately re-synchronizes the iterator's state : public void remove() { if (lastRet < 0) throw new IllegalStateException(); checkForComodification(); try { ArrayList.this.remove(lastRet); cursor = lastRet; lastRet = -1; expectedModCount = modCount; // < -- STATE RE-SYNCED! } catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException ex) { throw new ConcurrentModificationException(); } } 5. Time Complexity Analysis hasNext() and next() : O(1) across both List structures. iterator.remove() : ArrayList: O(n) . Although finding the node is O(1) , deleting it requires shifting array elements via System.arraycopy() . LinkedList: O(1) . The node pointer is held directly by the iterator, meaning relinking the previous and next nodes requires only constant time. 6. Key Interview Questions Q: What happens if you call remove() twice in a row without calling next()? It throws IllegalStateException . After the first call to remove() , the iterator resets lastRet = -1 . The second call checks if (lastRet < 0) and fails immediately because you cannot remove an element that hasn't been retrieved yet. Q: What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iterators? Fail-fast: Throws ConcurrentModificationException on structural modifications during iteration (e.g., ArrayList, HashSet). Fail-safe (Weakly Consistent): Iterates over a clone of the collection or handles concurrent changes smoothly without throwing exceptions (e.g., CopyOnWriteArrayList , ConcurrentHashMap ). 7. Real-World Use Cases Filtering Collections: Removing items matching a predicate during traversal (equivalent to modern collection.removeIf(filter) ). Custom Collections: Implementing the Iterable interface in your custom structures to allow users to leverage the standard foreach loop syntax. Practice — consecutive removal Test your understanding of structural updates: Pick the correct statement regarding iterator removal behavior: Calling remove twice without next throws IllegalStateException. Calling remove twice without next throws ConcurrentModificationException. Calling remove twice without next bypasses fail-fast check verification. Calling remove twice without next shifts elements without cursor updates. Primary reading Read the Iterator Javadoc and analyze the inner Itr class inside the OpenJDK ArrayList Source Code . Stuck on anything? Ask your teacher in Cursor — paste a code snippet or describe what confused you.

lessons.title: Java ListIterator Internals
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 14 · Lesson 15 of ? · ListIterator Reference Java ListIterator Internals: Interview Guide ~8 minutes · ties to mission 1. Why ListIterator Exists The standard Iterator interface is designed to work across all Collections (including Sets and Queues). Because of this, it is limited to forward-only traversal and supports only element deletion. Lists are index-ordered collections. To exploit this indexable structure, Java introduced the specialized ListIterator (which extends Iterator ) to support: Bi-directional traversal (moving backward and forward). Modifying elements during iteration using set() . Inserting elements mid-stream using add() . Querying element index positions without advancing the cursor. 2. Forward and Backward Traversal In addition to next() and hasNext() , ListIterator adds: hasPrevious() : Returns true if there are elements behind the cursor. previous() : Returns the element behind the cursor and moves the cursor one position backward. nextIndex() / previousIndex() : Returns the index of the element that would be returned by a subsequent call to next() or previous() . 3. Visualizing Cursor Positions The core concept to master for interviews is that the cursor always lies in the gaps between elements (before the first, between two, or after the last element): Element: [Element 0] | [Element 1] | [Element 2] Index: 0 | 1 | 2 Cursor: ^ ^ ^ ^ Start Between Between End Index 0 0 and 1 1 and 2 Index 3 For example, if the cursor is at the Start (before index 0): Calling next() returns Element 0 . The cursor shifts right (lies between 0 and 1). Calling previous() returns Element 0 . The cursor shifts left back to the Start. Interview Tip: Iteration Flip If you call previous() immediately after next() , you will retrieve the exact same element you just read! 4. State Modifications: add(), remove(), and set() The behavior of modifications depends on the last traversed element: add(e) : Inserts e immediately before the cursor position. The cursor shifts right so the new element is behind it. Subsequent calls to next() are unaffected, but calling previous() returns this newly added element. Constraint: Calling add() resets the last-returned index tracker ( lastRet = -1 ). You cannot call remove() or set() immediately after adding. remove() : Deletes the last element returned by next() or previous() . Constraint: Can only be called once per call to next() / previous() , and cannot be called immediately after add() . set(e) : Replaces the last element returned by next() or previous() with e . Constraint: Cannot be called immediately after add() or remove() . 5. Internal Implementation (ArrayList vs. LinkedList) ArrayList: ListItr is an inner class extending Itr . It implements previous() by decrementing the internal cursor index: public E previous() { checkForComodification(); int i = cursor - 1; if (i < 0) throw new NoSuchElementException(); Object[] elementData = ArrayList.this.elementData; cursor = i; return (E) elementData[lastRet = i]; } LinkedList: ListItr maintains node references. Since LinkedList is a doubly-linked list, calling previous() is trivial and fast: it simply reads nextNode.prev . 6. Common Interview Questions Q: What happens if you call listIterator.add() followed by listIterator.remove()? It throws IllegalStateException . In the OpenJDK implementation, calling add() clears the state pointer by setting lastRet = -1 . Since remove() requires lastRet >= 0 , it fails immediately to prevent state corruption. Q: What is the difference between Iterator and ListIterator? Iterator is uni-directional, operates on any collection, and supports read-and-delete. ListIterator is bi-directional, restricted to List implementations, supports index queries, and allows insertions/replacements during traversal. Practice — consecutive actions Test your understanding of modification constraints: Pick the correct statement regarding ListIterator add behavior: Calling add resets lastRet to prevent consecutive removal. Calling add shifts elements to allow consecutive removal. Calling add bypasses fail-fast check for consecutive removal. Calling add clears previous index details for consecutive removal. Primary reading Read the ListIterator Javadoc and analyze the inner ListItr class inside the OpenJDK ArrayList Source Code . Stuck on anything? lessons.title: Fail-Fast vs. Fail-Safe Iteration
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 15 · Lesson 16 of ? · Iteration Reference Java Fail-Fast vs. Fail-Safe Iterators: Interview Guide ~8 minutes · ties to mission 1. What is ConcurrentModificationException (CME)? In Java, iterating over a collection while modifying its structure (adding, removing, or clearing elements) is generally unsafe. If the runtime detects an illegal structural modification during traversal, it throws a ConcurrentModificationException . 2. modCount and expectedModCount Internals Standard collections (like ArrayList ) track modifications internally. The fail-fast iterator uses two fields to enforce safety: modCount : An index variable on the collection class. It increments on every add, remove, or clear structure call. expectedModCount : A local cached copy stored inside the Iterator object upon creation. In every call to next() or remove() , the iterator calls checkForComodification() : final void checkForComodification() { if (modCount != expectedModCount) throw new ConcurrentModificationException(); } 3. Why iterator.remove() updates modCount correctly If you call list.remove() during iteration, only modCount changes, causing a subsequent next() call to detect a mismatch and crash. However, calling iterator.remove() is safe because the iterator deletes the element through the collection, increments the collection's modCount , and then synchronizes its cached state: expectedModCount = modCount; // Re-synchronized! 4. Why Fail-Fast is Best-Effort The Javadoc states that fail-fast behavior is best-effort and not guaranteed . Here is why: Visibility Gaps: In a multithreaded context, modCount is not declared volatile or synchronized. A thread mutating the collection might update modCount in its local CPU cache, but that update may not be immediately flushed to main memory. Another iterating thread might read a stale value, missing the modification. Non-Structural Changes: Modifying the state of an object already inside the collection (e.g. list.get(0).setName("Bob") ) does not change list size, so modCount is not incremented and no CME is thrown. 5. Fail-Safe / Weakly Consistent Iterators The term "fail-safe" is a common design pattern name (not a term used in the Javadoc; Java Javadoc refers to them as weakly consistent ). Fail-safe iterators traverse a copy or use direct bucket pointer safety to avoid throwing CME. CopyOnWriteArrayList (Snapshot Iteration) When write operations occur (like add() ), this collection clones the backing array, writes to the clone, and swap-references the volatile array pointer. The iterator holds a reference to the original array snapshot at the time of creation. Since that snapshot is never mutated, the iterator is 100% safe from CME. Trade-off: High write memory overhead (cloning arrays) and stale read views (the iterator will not see additions made after it was created). ConcurrentHashMap (Bucket Traversal) Iterators here do not copy arrays. Instead, they traverse bucket node chains directly using volatile reads. They reflect some, but not all, subsequent map updates and are guaranteed to never throw CME. 6. Key Interview Questions Q: Can a fail-safe iterator reflect list updates after its creation? It depends on the collection. In CopyOnWriteArrayList , no —it iterates over a static array snapshot. In ConcurrentHashMap , yes —it traverses active buckets directly using weakly consistent reads. Q: What is the main structural trade-off between Fail-Fast and Fail-Safe? Fail-fast iterators are memory-efficient (O(1) space) and detect bugs quickly, but crash under concurrency. Fail-safe iterators are concurrent-friendly but incur higher memory overhead and may traverse stale data. Practice — best-effort behavior Test your understanding of visibility checks: Pick the correct statement regarding fail-fast iterator checks: Fail-fast checks are best-effort and not thread-safe. Fail-fast checks are fully guaranteed and thread-safe. Fail-fast checks are copy-on-write and thread-safe. Fail-fast checks are weakly consistent and thread-safe. Primary reading Read the CME Javadoc and analyze the write-paths in the OpenJDK CopyOnWriteArrayList Source Code . Stuck on anything? lessons.title: Stream Fundamentals
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · Next: Intermediate Operations ➡️ Deep Dive: Stream Fundamentals & Pipeline Mechanics ~25 minutes · ties to mission Senior Interview Focus: When top-tier companies (Google, Amazon, Luminate, Atlassian) evaluate Streams expertise, they look past simple map/filter syntax. They expect deep architectural knowledge: pipeline linking via AbstractPipeline , execution triggering via Sink chain evaluation, JVM allocation overheads, JIT escape analysis optimizations, and concurrency safety. 1. Concept Definition & Core Philosophy What is a Stream? A Stream is not a data structure . It is a declarative pipeline that processes a sequence of elements from a source (such as a Collection, an array, a generator function, or an I/O channel) without storing or mutating the underlying data. It acts as an abstraction for internal iteration . Mental Model: The Assembly Line Think of a Stream as a conveyor belt (the pipeline) where parts (elements) flow from a warehouse bin (the source) past several robotic arms (intermediate operations). The robots do not touch the warehouse bin itself; they only modify the parts as they pass by. At the end of the belt, a packer wraps them into a package (the terminal operation). The belt only moves when the packer requests a package—otherwise, the conveyor belt remains stationary. Key Differences: Collections vs. Streams Feature Collection Stream Primary Purpose Storage and access of elements in memory. Computation and transformation of data. State/Memory Holds all elements in memory (eager allocation). Does not store elements; processes them on-the-fly (lazy). Mutability Can be modified (add, remove, clear). Read-only; does not modify the source. Iteration Control External (Client controls loop using for-each / Iterator ). Internal (Framework controls traversal and optimization). Reusability Can be traversed multiple times. Single-use; consumed once terminal operation executes. Infinity Must have a finite, predefined size. Can be mathematically infinite (lazy generators). 2. Why Java Introduced Streams (The Paradigm Shift) Prior to Java 8, data processing was strictly imperative. Developers wrote external iteration logic using nested loops, Iterator loops, and local mutable variables.
