Each op declares flags it preserves, clears, or injects via opFlags bitmask math in AbstractPipeline.combineOpFlags() . Flag Propagation sorted() injects SORTED . distinct() injects DISTINCT . unordered() clears ORDERED — unlocks parallel merge optimizations. Downstream ops read combined flags to skip redundant work (e.g. skip second distinct() if already distinct). 6. Parallel Pipeline Internals (Internals Angle) opEvaluateParallel and Node Trees Sequential path: spliterator pushes elements through wrapped sinks in one thread. Parallel path: each stateful stage may call opEvaluateParallel() , which: Splits spliterator via trySplit() until chunks are small enough. Runs evaluateToNode() on each chunk — produces a Node<T> (internal tree/array structure). Merges sibling nodes via Nodes.concat() or op-specific combiners. This is not the same as Collector combiners — pipeline-level merging happens at stateful barriers; collector combiners run at the terminal collect() step ( Collectors reference ). trySplit Feeding ForkJoin Tasks AbstractTask subclasses (in java.util.stream ) wrap split spliterators as ForkJoinTask work units. Work-stealing schedules them on commonPool() (see Parallel Streams for pool hazards — not repeated here). Ordered vs Unordered Parallel Paths Ordered: node merge must preserve encounter order — may serialize merges, reducing speedup. Unordered: Nodes can flatten without order constraints; UNORDERED collector flags align with this. 7. Source Wrappers & Edge Cases Stream.concat Builds a ConcatSpliterator over two sources. Loses SIZED unless both sides are sized. Closing propagates to both sources. Stream.generate / Stream.iterate Supplier/iterator-backed — typically infinite or unknown size. estimateSize() returns Long.MAX_VALUE . Short-circuiting terminals essential. flatMap Sub-Pipeline Creation users.stream().flatMap(u -> u.getOrders().stream()) For each user, flatMap creates a child pipeline + spliterator, drains it into the parent sink, then discards it. High allocation: AbstractPipeline nodes per element. Production latency spikes often trace here. Closeable Streams and onClose Head pipeline accumulates onClose handlers. BaseStream.close() runs them after terminal completion — useful for I/O-backed spliterators. CME and Structural Modification Collection spliterators snapshot modCount (or equivalent). Structural change during traversal throws ConcurrentModificationException — same family as fail-fast iterators ( Fail-Fast lesson ). 8. JVM & Performance Internals Allocation Profile Pipeline nodes: one AbstractPipeline per intermediate op (small, short-lived). flatMap : child pipelines per element — dominant cost in nested streams. sorted() : full element array + possibly boxed wrappers. Parallel: Node arrays, task objects, combiner temporaries. JIT / Loop Optimizations Fused sink chains inline into a single hot loop — no iterator hasNext/next overhead. SIZED sources let begin(n) pre-allocate exact buffers. peek() may be elided if JVM proves side-effect-free (don't rely on this — peek is for debugging). When Internals Explain Production Latency P99 spike after adding .sorted() on 500k rows — full in-memory sort barrier. GC churn after flatMap over nested collections — millions of short-lived pipeline objects. Thread dump shows ReferencePipeline / AbstractTask — parallel stream work on commonPool. Reading OpenJDK Source Start here: ReferencePipeline.java — map , filter , flatMap op classes AbstractPipeline.java — evaluate , wrapAndCopyInto , flag combination StreamOpFlag.java — flag propagation rules Nodes.java — parallel node builders and concat 9. Module 02 Synthesis & Interview Traps Full Picture BUILD: source → [StatelessOp | StatefulOp]* (AbstractPipeline linked list) RUN: TerminalOp.evaluate() → wrapSink (backward chain) → sequential: wrapAndCopyInto OR parallel: evaluateParallel + Node merge → Collector combiner (if collect) / reduction / forEach Interview Traps "Stream stores elements" — No. It stores pipeline metadata + source reference. Lazy vs deferred timing — Lazy means no traversal until terminal; not "runs later on another thread." sorted() as barrier — Must buffer all elements (or chunk in parallel). O(n log n) memory + CPU. Deadly on infinite streams. Sink chain vs iterator — Push model (source drives) with fused callbacks, not pull next() . Thread dumps — java.util.stream.ReferencePipeline$Head.forEach , AbstractTask.compute = stream execution in flight. Collectors tie-in — Terminal collect wraps a Collector as a TerminalSink ; parallel uses combiner at merge time. Parallel tie-in — Same pipeline classes; different evaluate path. Pool contention is operational, not structural. Short-circuit — cancellationRequested() propagates up; spliterator stops advancing. Works only if terminal supports it. Key Takeaways Streams compile to AbstractPipeline linked lists — built lazily, executed once. Terminal ops compile a Sink chain backward; stateless ops fuse into one traversal. Stateful ops ( sorted , distinct , limit , skip ) are barriers that buffer or count. Spliterator characteristics + StreamOpFlag drive optimizations and parallel behavior. Parallel evaluation uses Node trees and splits — separate from collector combiners. flatMap and sorted are the usual production latency suspects — know the internals, not just the API. 10. 5 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: When does a stream pipeline actually traverse source elements? When terminal operation runs. When intermediate operation runs. When stream object is created. When source collection is built. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (When terminal operation runs.) Intermediate ops only link AbstractPipeline nodes. evaluate() fires on terminal invocation — that's when spliterator traversal begins. Q2: Which operation acts as a stateful execution barrier? sorted intermediate operation. map intermediate operation. filter intermediate operation. peek intermediate operation. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (sorted intermediate operation.) sorted() buffers elements in its sink until end() , then sorts — breaking single-pass fusion. map / filter / peek are stateless. Q3: How is the Sink chain assembled at runtime? Wrapped backward from terminal. Wrapped forward from source. Built as iterator pull chain. Built as collection copy chain. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Wrapped backward from terminal.) PipelineHelper.wrapSink() starts at the terminal sink and wraps each upstream opWrapSink() . Source pushes into the outermost wrapped sink. Q4: What does unordered() clear on the pipeline? ORDERED stream op flag. SIZED stream op flag. DISTINCT stream op flag. SHORT_CIRCUIT op flag. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (ORDERED stream op flag.) unordered() clears StreamOpFlag.ORDERED , allowing parallel merges and collectors to skip encounter-order constraints. Q5: Primary allocation cost of flatMap internally? Child pipeline per element. Terminal sink per element. Source spliterator per element. Combined flags per element. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Child pipeline per element.) Each upstream element spawns a sub-stream (pipeline + spliterator) that is drained into the parent sink — high allocation under large N. 11. Reasoning Exercises Barrier map: For list.stream().filter().map().distinct().sorted().collect() , identify which stages fuse and where barriers force buffering. Thread dump read: Given a stack with ReferencePipeline$Head.forEach and ForkJoinPool$WorkQueue , explain what the JVM is doing. flatMap vs map: Estimate allocation difference for 10k users each with 5 orders — map vs flatMap . Which internal structures multiply?

lessons.title: Thread Fundamentals & Lifecycle
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ⬅️ Prev: Streams Capstone · ➡️ Next: Synchronization & Monitors Deep Dive: Thread Fundamentals & Lifecycle ~25 minutes · ties to mission · Cheat sheet Senior Interview Focus: Interviewers rarely ask you to subclass Thread . They probe whether you know start() vs run() , thread states under load, daemon shutdown rules, why raw thread creation is a production smell, and how this connects to the shared heap you already studied. Parallel streams (Module 02) sit on top of this model — you already used the shared pool; now you own the primitives underneath. Primary sources: Oracle — Defining and Starting a Thread · Oracle — Thread javadoc (SE 23) · Oracle — Processes and Threads 1. Why Threads Exist (Enterprise Framing) A Spring Boot service handling 500 HTTP requests cannot run them one-after-another on a single call stack. Threads let the JVM keep many units of work in progress — waiting on DB I/O, computing, or coordinating — without blocking the whole process. You already saw one abstraction: parallel streams fork work onto ForkJoinPool.commonPool() . That pool is made of threads. This module starts at the primitive those pools manage. 2. Process vs Thread Concept Process Thread What it is OS-isolated program with own address space Unit of execution inside a process Memory Private virtual memory Shares process heap; owns its own stack Failure isolation Crash usually stops the process Uncaught exception kills that thread; JVM may keep running Cost Heavy to create / switch Lighter than a process (platform threads still non-trivial) JVM mental model (ties to Stack vs Heap): one JVM process → one shared Heap + Metaspace → many threads, each with a private call stack (frames, locals, operand stack). Shared mutable heap objects are where races live. ┌──────────── JVM Process ────────────┐ │ Heap (shared objects) │ │ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ │ │ │ Stack │ │ Stack │ │ Stack │ │ │ │ main │ │ worker │ │ http-1 │ │ │ └────────┘ └────────┘ └────────┘ │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘ 3. Concurrency vs Parallelism (Bridge from Streams) Concurrency: Multiple tasks in progress . May time-slice on one core. Classic for I/O-bound request handling. Parallelism: Multiple tasks executing at the same instant on multiple cores. Classic for CPU-bound splits (parallel streams). Interview line: concurrency is about structure (overlapping work); parallelism is about execution (simultaneous cores). You can have concurrency without parallelism (single core + blocking I/O). Parallel streams are a parallelism tool — not a general concurrency framework. 4. Platform Threads vs Virtual Threads (Preview) Per the Thread javadoc : Platform thread: Typically 1:1 with an OS kernel thread. Large stack. Limited resource. Suitable for all task types. Can be daemon or non-daemon. Virtual thread (Java 21+): User-mode thread scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier platform threads. Cheap; designed for blocking I/O at scale. Always daemon. Not for long CPU-bound work. This lesson focuses on platform thread fundamentals — you need them to understand pools, locks, and the JMM. Virtual threads get their own section later; do not invent them as a free speedup for CPU work. 5. Creating Work: Runnable vs Extending Thread Oracle's tutorial prefers separating the task from the execution vehicle . Preferred: implement Runnable (or lambda) Runnable task = () -> System.out.println( "running on " + Thread.currentThread().getName()); Thread t = new Thread(task, "worker-1"); t.start(); // schedules a new thread; returns immediately to caller Legacy: subclass Thread class Worker extends Thread { @Override public void run() { /* work */ } } new Worker().start(); Why Runnable wins: your task class can still extend something else; the same task can run on an Executor , a virtual thread, or a test harness without being locked into the Thread type hierarchy. Production code almost never subclasses Thread . Modern: Thread.Builder (Java 21+) Thread.ofPlatform().name("worker-1").start(task); Thread.ofVirtual().name("vt-1").start(task); 6. The Critical Trap: start() vs run() Call What happens t.start() JVM schedules a new thread. That thread eventually invokes run() . Caller continues concurrently. t.run() Ordinary method call on the current thread. No new thread. No concurrency. Calling run() directly is a classic junior bug and a favorite interview trap. Also: a thread may be started only once . A second start() throws IllegalThreadStateException . 7. Thread Lifecycle (getState()) Thread.State (via t.getState() ) — interview-ready names: NEW ──start()──► RUNNABLE ◄──► BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING │ └── run ends / uncaught ──► TERMINATED NEW: constructed, not started. RUNNABLE: executing or ready to execute (includes waiting for CPU — Java does not expose a separate "RUNNING"). BLOCKED: waiting to enter a synchronized monitor held by another thread. WAITING: waiting indefinitely ( Object.wait() , LockSupport.park() , join() without timeout). TIMED_WAITING: waiting with a timeout ( sleep , wait(timeout) , join(timeout) ). TERMINATED: run finished (normal or via uncaught exception after handler runs). Production note: thread dumps ( jstack , VisualVM) show these states. A pile of BLOCKED threads on one monitor is a lock contention smell. A pile of WAITING on a pool queue may be healthy idle workers. 8. Coordination Basics: join, sleep, interrupt join() worker.join() — current thread waits until worker reaches TERMINATED . Use when the caller needs the worker's result before continuing (or prefer higher-level Future.get() later). sleep() Thread.sleep(ms) — current thread enters TIMED_WAITING . Does not release monitors you hold. Rarely correct for production coordination (prefer locks, latches, conditions). interrupt() Cooperative cancellation. t.interrupt() sets the interrupt status. Blocking methods ( sleep , join , wait , many I/O ops) throw InterruptedException and clear the status. Your code should either restore the interrupt flag ( Thread.currentThread().interrupt() ) or exit cleanly — never swallow and continue as if nothing happened. try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); // restore status return; // stop work } 9. Daemon vs Non-Daemon Non-daemon: keeps the JVM alive. main starts as non-daemon. Worker pools are usually non-daemon unless you deliberately want fire-and-forget. Daemon: JVM can exit when only daemon threads remain. Useful for background helpers (e.g. cache cleaner) that must not block shutdown. Set before start: t.setDaemon(true) . Virtual threads are always daemon. Unstarted non-daemon threads do not block shutdown — only started ones count. 10. Uncaught Exceptions An exception that escapes run() does not crash the JVM by default. It goes to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler (or the thread group's / default handler), then the thread terminates. In a servlet container, a dead worker with a silent handler = mysterious capacity loss. Always log in handlers for long-lived pools. 11. Why Production Rarely Calls new Thread() Spawning unbounded raw threads under load → OOM / native thread exhaustion. No reuse, no queueing policy, no metrics. Senior answer: Prefer an ExecutorService (fixed/cached/work-stealing pool) with bounded queues and rejection policy. Raw Thread is for teaching and rare special cases — not for request paths. Executors are the next major section. You already met one: ForkJoinPool.commonPool() behind parallel streams. 12. Shared State Warning (Foreshadow) Two threads reading/writing the same heap field without coordination → data races. Visibility and atomicity are not guaranteed by "it worked on my machine." Next lessons: synchronized , volatile , the Java Memory Model. Until then: treat shared mutable state as unsafe unless proven otherwise. 13. Revision Notes Process = address space; thread = stack + shared heap. start() schedules; run() is just a method on the current thread. States: NEW → RUNNABLE ↔ BLOCKED/WAITING/TIMED_WAITING → TERMINATED. Prefer Runnable / builders; prefer executors over raw threads in production. Daemon threads do not keep the JVM alive; restore interrupt status on catch. 14. 5 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Calling thread.run() instead of start() does what? Runs task on current thread. Starts new OS kernel thread. Queues task on common pool. Creates daemon virtual thread. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Runs task on current thread.) run() is a normal method invocation. Only start() asks the JVM to schedule a new thread that will then call run() . Q2: Which Thread.State means waiting on a monitor enter? BLOCKED waiting for lock. WAITING waiting for lock. RUNNABLE waiting for lock. NEW waiting for lock. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (BLOCKED waiting for lock.) BLOCKED is specifically for threads waiting to enter a synchronized block/method. WAITING covers wait() / join() / park() without timeout. Q3: Best default way to define concurrent work? Implement Runnable then submit. Extend Thread then override. Extend Thread then sleep. Implement Thread then submit. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Implement Runnable then submit.) Oracle and production practice separate task from thread. Runnable (or Callable ) plugs into executors and builders; subclassing Thread burns your single inheritance slot. Q4: When can the JVM exit despite live threads? Only daemon threads remain. Only non-daemon threads remain. Any NEW threads remain. Any BLOCKED threads remain. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Only daemon threads remain.) Shutdown begins when all started non-daemon threads have terminated. Remaining daemon threads are abandoned. Q5: Why avoid new Thread per HTTP request? Unbounded create risks exhaustion. Thread start always throws error. Runnable cannot run on pools. join always blocks forever. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Unbounded create risks exhaustion.) Each platform thread costs native memory and scheduling. Under spike load, unbounded creation OOMs the process. Use a bounded executor with a queue and rejection policy. 15. Reasoning Exercises Trace: Write a main that starts two threads printing 0..4. Explain why output order is non-deterministic without synchronization. Bug hunt: A teammate writes new Thread(task).run() and says "concurrency is broken." Fix and explain. Lifecycle: Start a thread that sleep(5000) . From main, print getState() before start, after start (briefly), and after join() . Interrupt: Loop in a worker checking Thread.interrupted() . From main, interrupt after 1s and confirm clean exit with flag restored in a catch path. Daemon: Start a daemon thread with an infinite loop. Let main return. Observe JVM exit — contrast with non-daemon.

lessons.title: Synchronization & Monitors
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 2 of 8 · Lesson 3 → · Cheat sheet Deep Dive: Synchronization & Monitors ~28 minutes · ties to mission · builds on Lesson 1 , java.lang.Object Senior Interview Focus: You already know threads share the heap and that BLOCKED means waiting on a monitor. Now own the lock model: what synchronized actually guarantees, why counter++ is not atomic, how wait() differs from sleep() , and when intrinsic locks are the wrong tool. Interviewers love the broken-counter trace and the "which object is the lock?" question. Primary sources: Oracle — Intrinsic Locks and Synchronization · Oracle — Guarded Blocks (wait/notify) · JLS Chapter 17 — Threads and Locks 1. Why Synchronization Exists Module 00 taught you: heap is shared, stack is per-thread. Module 03 Section 01 warned: two threads reading/writing the same field without coordination → data races . A data race is when two threads access the same memory location, at least one is a write, and there is no happens-before relationship between them. The JVM does not promise a sensible result — you may see lost updates, torn reads, or "works on my laptop" flakiness under load. Lost update (classic) class Counter { int count = 0; void increment() { count++; } // NOT atomic — read, add, write } Two threads both read count == 5 , both write 6 . Expected 7, got 6. One increment vanished. Check-then-act (enterprise trap) if (!cache.containsKey(key)) { // Thread A checks — absent cache.put(key, loadFromDb()); // Thread B checks — absent, both load } Even if each line looks safe alone, the compound action is not atomic. Spring singleton services with mutable fields hit this constantly unless designed thread-safe. 2. Critical Section & Mutual Exclusion A critical section is code that touches shared mutable state. Mutual exclusion means at most one thread executes that section at a time for a given lock. Java's built-in mechanism: every object carries an intrinsic lock (monitor lock). synchronized acquires it before entering and releases it on exit — even if an exception escapes. 3. JVM Monitor Model (Interview Level) You met monitors briefly in java.lang.Object : wait() , notify() , Mark Word lock bits. Here is the operational model: Every object has one monitor (intrinsic lock) and one wait set. Entry queue: threads blocked trying to enter synchronized on this monitor → Thread.State.BLOCKED . Wait set: threads that called wait() on this object → WAITING / TIMED_WAITING . Owner: at most one thread holds the lock at a time. Mark Word lock states (preview) The object header's Mark Word tracks lock state. HotSpot optimizes: State Meaning Biased Lock biased toward one thread — uncontended fast path Thin / lightweight Simple stack-based lock via CAS when low contention Fat / inflated Full monitor with native mutex + wait set under heavy contention You do not tune these in application code. Senior value: explain why uncontended synchronized is cheap and why lock convoys under contention hurt throughput — thread dumps show piles of BLOCKED . 4. synchronized Methods vs Blocks Instance method — locks this public synchronized void transfer() { // implicitly: synchronized (this) { ... } } Static method — locks the Class object public static synchronized void resetAll() { // implicitly: synchronized (MyService.class) { ... } } Instance lock and class lock are different monitors . A static synchronized method does not block an instance synchronized method on the same object unless they share the same lock object. Block — explicit lock object private final Object lock = new Object(); void update() { synchronized (lock) { // only threads using THIS lock object block each other } } Interview rule: synchronization protects the lock object you chose — not "the method" or "the class" abstractly. Two blocks on different objects do not exclude each other. 5. Reentrancy A thread that already holds a monitor may acquire it again. Each acquire must be matched by a release (nested synchronized blocks/method calls unwind correctly). public synchronized void outer() { inner(); // same thread re-enters same monitor — legal } public synchronized void inner() { /* ... */ } Without reentrancy, code calling synchronized helpers from synchronized methods would self-deadlock. This is why Java monitors are reentrant . 6. wait / notify / notifyAll From Object — now with concurrency framing: Caller must own the object's monitor → else IllegalMonitorStateException . wait() atomically releases the lock and places the thread in the object's wait set. On notify() / notifyAll() , a waiter moves to re-enter the lock; it does not run until it re-acquires the lock. sleep() does not release monitors — different from wait() . Always wait in a while loop synchronized (lock) { while (!conditionMet()) { lock.wait(); } // work — condition still true after re-acquire } Reasons: spurious wakeups (allowed by spec), another thread may steal the condition between notify and your re-entry, multiple waiters with notifyAll() . Default: prefer notifyAll() unless you have a massive homogeneous pool and proven single-waiter semantics. Producer–consumer sketch class Drop { private String message; private boolean empty = true; public synchronized void put(String msg) { while (!empty) { wait(); } message = msg; empty = false; notifyAll(); } public synchronized String take() { while (empty) { wait(); } String msg = message; empty = true; notifyAll(); return msg; } } Oracle's guarded-block pattern — same lock guards both the condition and the wait/notify calls. 7. IllegalMonitorStateException Thrown when: wait() , notify() , or notifyAll() called without holding that object's monitor. (Related) LockSupport.unpark misuse — different API, same "wrong state" family. Common bug: calling someObject.wait() while holding a different lock than someObject . 8. Atomicity vs Visibility (Preview — S03 Next) Property What it means synchronized gives? Atomicity Action completes as one indivisible step Yes — only one thread in block Visibility Thread B sees Thread A's writes promptly Yes — unlock establishes happens-before for next acquirer synchronized provides both. volatile provides visibility + ordering for single reads/writes, not compound check-then-act. Full JMM rules → Section 03. 9. Classic Bugs & Interview Traps Unsynchronized counter: count++ — fix with synchronized block or AtomicInteger (later). Wrong lock object: two methods synchronize on different objects — no mutual exclusion. String literal lock: synchronized ("LOCK") — interned strings share monitors across the JVM → accidental coupling. Use private final Object lock = new Object() . Lock during I/O: holding monitor while calling DB/HTTP blocks all other threads on that lock — throughput killer. notify without changing condition: waiter wakes, while-loop re-checks, loops forever if state wrong. 10. When synchronized Is Fine vs java.util.concurrent synchronized is fine when: Simple invariants on a few fields Short critical sections, no I/O inside lock Coarse-grained guarding of a small object's state Reach for java.util.concurrent (Sections 04–06) when: Need timed/try locks, fair ordering, read/write split Executor pools, concurrent maps, latches, semaphores High contention — explicit locks + better structures reduce convoys Senior line: start with the simplest correct lock; measure; upgrade when contention or API limits bite. 11. Enterprise Framing Spring singleton beans: one instance, many request threads. Mutable fields (counters, caches without sync) = latent races. Prefer immutable state, concurrent collections, or confine mutation to a single-thread executor. Shared service cache: check-then-act on HashMap is unsafe. ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent (Section 06) or synchronized guard around the whole check+put. Thread-safe by design: minimize shared mutable state; make races structurally impossible before sprinkling synchronized . 12. Revision Notes Data race = concurrent access, at least one write, no synchronization. Every object has a monitor; synchronized acquires/releases it. Instance method → this ; static → Class ; block → object you name. wait releases lock; sleep does not. Always while + prefer notifyAll . synchronized = atomicity + visibility; volatile deep dive is next section. 13. 5 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Instance synchronized method locks which monitor? The instance monitor (this). The class monitor (Class). The thread monitor (Thread). The stack monitor (Stack). View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (The instance monitor (this).) JLS: instance synchronized methods lock the monitor of the object invoked ( this ). Static methods lock the Class object instead. Q2: Calling wait() on a held monitor does what? Releases lock and suspends. Keeps lock and suspends. Releases lock and terminates. Keeps lock and terminates. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Releases lock and suspends.) wait() adds the thread to the wait set and releases the monitor so others can enter. sleep() suspends without releasing locks. Q3: Why guard wait() with a while loop? Guard against spurious wakeup. Guard against thread death. Guard against daemon shutdown. Guard against GC collection. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Guard against spurious wakeup.) Also: other threads may change the condition before you re-acquire. Re-test the predicate every time you wake. Q4: Static synchronized method locks what? The Class object monitor. The instance monitor (this). The Thread object monitor. The Method object monitor. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (The Class object monitor.) Static synchronized methods lock the Class object for the declaring class — not any instance. Q5: Two threads unsynchronized increment—result? Lost updates are possible. Lost updates are impossible. Deadlock is always guaranteed. JVM throws on second write. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Lost updates are possible.) count++ is read-modify-write. Without synchronization or atomics, increments can be lost — no exception, just wrong counts. 14. Reasoning Exercises Race trace: Two threads call increment() 1000 times each on the same unsynchronized counter. Can the final value be below 2000? Explain the lost-update window. Fix the counter: Add the minimal synchronized fix. Would synchronizing on Integer.valueOf(0) be safe? Why not? Lock object: Class has synchronized void a() and synchronized void b() . Thread 1 in a() calls b() . Deadlock or OK? Why? wait/notify bug: Producer calls notify() outside synchronized block. What exception? Fix it. Enterprise: Spring @Service holds HashMap<String, User> cache mutated on every request. Name two failure modes and one structural fix. Questions? Ask your coach — walk through a race trace, thread dump BLOCKED lines, or a guarded-block design together.

lessons.title: volatile & Java Memory Model
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 2 · Lesson 3 of 8 · Lesson 4 → · Cheat sheet Deep Dive: volatile & the Java Memory Model ~30 minutes · ties to mission · builds on Lesson 2 , Stack vs Heap Senior Interview Focus: synchronized gives atomicity + visibility — but coarse locks hurt throughput, and not every shared field needs a monitor. Interviewers probe: why a plain boolean shutdown can loop forever, what volatile actually guarantees (and what it does not ), and why broken double-checked locking was a JDK-era classic. This is the bridge from "locks work" to "why java.util.concurrent exists." Primary sources: Oracle — Memory Consistency Errors · Oracle — Atomic Access · JLS Chapter 17 — Threads and Locks · JSR-133 FAQ (Doug Lea) 1. Why synchronized Alone Isn't Always Enough Lesson 2 taught: synchronized provides mutual exclusion and visibility (unlock happens-before next lock). That is correct — but production code often needs: Visibility without holding a lock — e.g. a shutdown flag read in a hot loop while another thread sets it once. Lower overhead — acquiring a monitor on every read of a status flag serializes threads unnecessarily. One-way publication — writer initializes state once; many readers need to see it without synchronizing every read. Senior framing: use the weakest synchronization that is correct. Over-synchronizing is a latency and deadlock-risk smell. 2. The Hardware Reality (Interview Level) Threads share the heap, but CPUs cache memory locally for speed. Without coordination: Store buffers / caches: Thread A writes flag = true — Thread B may still see false from its cache. Instruction reordering: Compiler and CPU may reorder independent statements if the single-thread result is unchanged — breaking naive multi-thread assumptions. You do not need to model cache lines in interviews. You need one line: without a happens-before edge, the JMM allows stale reads and surprising orderings. "It worked on my machine" is not a memory model. 3. Java Memory Model (JMM) The JMM (formalized by JSR-133, Java 5+) defines which values a read is allowed to observe. It is a contract between your code, the compiler, and the runtime — not a description of one CPU. Programmers reason in happens-before. The JVM may reorder and cache — but cannot break happens-before guarantees. Memory consistency error: different threads have inconsistent views of what should be the same data. Fix: establish happens-before between writer and reader. 4. happens-before Rules (Core Set) If action A happens-before B, then A's effects are visible to B. Key edges for interviews: Rule Meaning Program order Within one thread, earlier statements happen-before later ones Monitor unlock → lock Unlock on monitor M happens-before every subsequent lock on M volatile write → read Write to volatile v happens-before every subsequent read of v Thread.start Everything before start() happens-before actions in the new thread Thread.join All actions in thread T happen-before join() returns Transitivity If A hb B and B hb C, then A hb C The volatile rule is powerful: a read of volatile v sees the latest write to v and (transitively) prior writes that happened-before that write in the writer thread. 5. volatile Semantics volatile on a field means: Reads and writes go through main memory semantics — no stale cached copy indefinitely. Writes establish happens-before with subsequent reads of that variable. Reordering constraints: volatile accesses cannot be reordered with each other; post-JSR-133, normal field accesses around volatiles are also constrained. What volatile does NOT do volatile int count = 0; void increment() { count++; } // STILL BROKEN — read-modify-write volatile makes each individual read/write visible — not compound operations. For atomic counters → AtomicInteger (Section 06) or synchronized . 6. volatile vs synchronized volatile synchronized Atomicity Single read/write only Whole block/method Visibility Yes (write → read hb) Yes (unlock → lock hb) Blocking No Yes — mutual exclusion Best for Status flags, one-shot publish, DCL holder Multi-step invariants, wait/notify 7. long and double Without volatile JLS: reads/writes of long and double are atomic only when declared volatile (or accessed under synchronization). Without that, a read may see a "torn" value — high 32 bits from one write, low 32 from another. Modern 64-bit JVMs often make this safe in practice — but the language contract still matters in interviews and for portability. 8. final Fields & Safe Publication (Preview) If an object's final fields are set in the constructor and the reference is published safely, readers see fully constructed final values without extra synchronization on those fields. Safe publication means the reader's first access to the object happens-after construction completes via one of: Static initializer (class init is JVM-synchronized) Storing ref into volatile field Storing ref under synchronized and releasing lock Thread.start() passing the object to the new thread Unsafe: publishing this from constructor (escape) — another thread may see partially constructed state. 9. Double-Checked Locking (Interview Classic) Broken (pre-JSR-133 / missing volatile) // BROKEN — do not use class BrokenSingleton { private static BrokenSingleton instance; static BrokenSingleton getInstance() { if (instance == null) { synchronized (BrokenSingleton.class) { if (instance == null) { instance = new BrokenSingleton(); // reordering hazard } } } return instance; } } Another thread may see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object (reordered writes). Also: without volatile, the outer null check has no happens-before with the writer. Correct — volatile holder (idiom) class SafeSingleton { private static volatile SafeSingleton instance; static SafeSingleton getInstance() { SafeSingleton local = instance; if (local == null) { synchronized (SafeSingleton.class) { local = instance; if (local == null) { instance = local = new SafeSingleton(); } } } return local; } } volatile on instance publishes the fully constructed object. Production today: prefer enum singleton or holder-class idiom — but know DCL for interviews. Holder class idiom (no volatile needed) class Holder { private static class LazyHolder { static final Holder INSTANCE = new Holder(); } static Holder getInstance() { return LazyHolder.INSTANCE; } } JVM class initialization is synchronized — safe lazy init without explicit locks in application code. 10. Classic Bugs Flag without volatile: worker loop never exits after main sets shutdown = true . Stale config: reload thread writes new settings; request threads read cached values forever. DCL singleton: returns broken half-built instance. volatile counter: still loses increments — wrong tool. // Bug: shutdown may never be seen boolean shutdown = false; void worker() { while (!shutdown) { doWork(); } } void stop() { shutdown = true; } // Fix: volatile boolean shutdown = false; 11. Enterprise Framing Scenario Typical choice Shutdown / running flag volatile boolean One-shot config publish volatile ref to immutable config object Metrics counter under contention LongAdder / AtomicLong (not volatile++) Multi-field invariant update synchronized or atomic snapshot Spring bean field visibility Prefer immutable beans; if mutable, understand @Scope and thread confinement Senior line: volatile = visibility for one variable's write/read chain. Atomics = CAS for compound updates. synchronized = multi-statement invariants + wait/notify. 12. Revision Notes No happens-before → stale reads and reorderings allowed. volatile write → read establishes visibility (and transitively prior writes in writer). volatile does not make count++ atomic. DCL needs volatile holder; holder-class / enum safer in production. long / double need volatile or sync for atomicity guarantee. 13. 5 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: volatile int count; count++ is safe? No — compound op not atomic. Yes — volatile makes all atomic. Yes — if only two threads. No — unless count is final. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (No — compound op not atomic.) count++ is read-modify-write. volatile only guarantees visibility of individual reads/writes, not the whole operation. Q2: Write to volatile v guarantees what? Later read of v sees it. Later read of v may miss. All fields become volatile. All threads stop immediately. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Later read of v sees it.) Volatile write happens-before subsequent volatile read of same variable. Transitivity pulls in prior writes in the writer thread. Q3: Broken DCL singleton lacks what? Volatile on instance field. Final on instance field. Static on instance field. Private on instance field. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Volatile on instance field.) Without volatile , another thread can see a non-null reference to a partially constructed object due to reordering. Q4: long read without volatile may be? Torn across two 32-bit halves. Always atomic on all JVMs. Blocked until monitor held. Promoted to double width. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Torn across two 32-bit halves.) JLS: 64-bit primitives are only guaranteed atomic when volatile or accessed under synchronization. Q5: Shutdown flag never seen — fix? Declare flag as volatile. Declare flag as final. Declare flag as static. Declare flag as transient. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Declare flag as volatile.) Writer thread's shutdown = true needs happens-before with reader's check. volatile establishes that edge without a lock. 14. Reasoning Exercises Visibility trace: Thread A sets x = 5 then volatileReady = true . Thread B loops on volatileReady then prints x . Can B ever print 0? Why or why not? Fix the flag: Worker never stops when shutdown is plain boolean . Minimal fix? Would synchronized on stop() alone suffice without syncing the read loop? DCL interview: Explain to an interviewer why new Singleton() inside DCL is dangerous without volatile — use "partially constructed object." Choose the tool: (a) one-writer shutdown flag, (b) 50 threads incrementing a hit counter, (c) transfer between two accounts. volatile, AtomicInteger, or synchronized for each? Safe publication: Why is static final Holder INSTANCE = new Holder() inside a static nested class safe without volatile on the outer class? Questions? Ask your coach — walk through a happens-before diagram, a broken DCL, or when to pick AtomicInteger over volatile.

lessons.title: Explicit Locks
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 3 · Lesson 4 of 8 · Cheat sheet · Next: Executors → Deep Dive: Explicit Locks ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on Lesson 2 , Lesson 3 Senior Interview Focus: synchronized is the default. Interviewers ask when it is not enough: timed/interruptible acquire, fairness, multiple wait-sets, lock downgrade. They also hunt the trap synchronized never has — forgetting unlock() . This lesson is the java.util.concurrent.locks toolkit, not AQS internals. Primary sources: Oracle — Lock Objects · Lock javadoc · ReentrantLock · Condition · ReadWriteLock · StampedLock · Oracle — Deadlock / Liveness 1. Why Explicit Locks Exist Lesson 2: intrinsic locks are block-structured — acquire and release are tied to a synchronized scope. The JVM always unlocks on exit, even via exception. That safety has a cost: you cannot try-and-give-up, time out, interrupt a thread stuck in lock acquisition, choose FIFO fairness, or split waiters onto two condition queues. java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock exists for those cases. Flexibility means you own unlock. Miss the finally and the lock is gone for the process lifetime of that object. Need Intrinsic lock Explicit Lock Auto unlock on exception Yes Only if you write finally tryLock / timed wait No Yes Interruptible acquire No (block is not interruptible) lockInterruptibly Fairness policy No API Constructor flag Multiple wait-sets One wait set per object Many Condition s per lock Hand-over-hand / unlock in other method Awkward Designed for it Senior default: synchronized until one of those rows is a real requirement. Explicit locks are not "more thread-safe." 2. Lock Interface Contract Core methods: lock() — block until acquired. Reentrant implementations increment hold count if you already own it. unlock() — release one hold. Wrong thread / not held → typically IllegalMonitorStateException . lockInterruptibly() — like lock() but abort with InterruptedException if interrupted while waiting. tryLock() — return immediately; true if acquired. tryLock(timeout, unit) — wait up to a bound; interruptible. newCondition() — bind a condition queue to this lock. Always finally lock.lock(); try { // critical section } finally { lock.unlock(); } For tryLock : unlock only if acquire succeeded. if (lock.tryLock()) { try { // work } finally { lock.unlock(); } } else { // skip / degrade — never unlock } happens-before (same as monitor) From the Lock javadoc: a successful lock has the same memory effects as a JLS Lock action; a successful unlock matches Unlock. So unlock happens-before the next successful lock on the same Lock — same visibility story as Lesson 2/3. Unsuccessful tryLock does not create that edge. Reentrant lock/unlock of an already-held lock also need not publish new memory effects. Never synchronized (lockInstance) on a Lock object. That acquires the intrinsic monitor of the lock object — unrelated to lock.lock() . 3. ReentrantLock Same ownership model as synchronized : one owner thread, reentrant hold count, exclusive mutual exclusion. Extra knobs: fairness, interruptible/timed acquire, Condition s, instrumentation. private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock(); // non-fair (default) private final ReentrantLock fair = new ReentrantLock(true); // FIFO-ish under contention Reentrancy: nested lock() from the owner increments getHoldCount() . Each unlock() decrements; lock frees at zero. isHeldByCurrentThread() : analog of Thread.holdsLock(monitor) — asserts and tests, not a sync protocol. Fair vs non-fair: fair prefers the longest-waiting thread under contention. Throughput is often much worse. Fairness of the lock is not fairness of the scheduler — a thread can still reacquire immediately if others are not yet queued. Barging trap: untimed tryLock() does not honor fairness . If the lock is free, it takes it even when waiters exist. Timed tryLock(0, SECONDS) respects fairness (and is interruptible). synchronized vs ReentrantLock — who wins Pick When synchronized Simple mutual exclusion, wait/notify on one object, you want the compiler/JVM to guarantee unlock. Default in Spring services for tiny critical sections. ReentrantLock Need try/timed/interruptible acquire, fairness, multiple Condition s, or lock held across non-nested scopes (rare — document it). Do not rewrite every synchronized method as ReentrantLock for "performance." Measure. Intrinsic locks are heavily optimized (and Lesson 2's biased/thin/fat story still applies). 4. ReadWriteLock / ReentrantReadWriteLock Pair of locks: shared read (many readers) or exclusive write (one writer, no readers). Write-unlock happens-before a later read-lock on the same RW lock — readers see the writer's updates. private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); Object get() { rw.readLock().lock(); try { return snapshot; } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } } void refresh(Object next) { rw.writeLock().lock(); try { snapshot = next; } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } Wins when reads dominate and the protected data is non-trivial (cache, config snapshot, directory). Hurts when: Write-heavy — exclusive write serializes everyone; extra RW machinery is waste. Tiny reads — lock overhead dominates the work. Frequent upgrades — see deadlock below. Downgrade (write → read) is supported Acquire write, mutate, acquire read while still holding write , then release write. You remain a reader; no other writer sneaks in between. rw.writeLock().lock(); try { mutate(); rw.readLock().lock(); // downgrade: still exclusive until write unlocks } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } try { observe(); // other readers may join; writers still blocked } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); } Upgrade (read → write) deadlocks Write lock waits until all readers release — including you. Holding the read lock and then calling writeLock().lock() waits forever for yourself. Pattern: release read, acquire write, re-check the invariant (another writer may have run). Or use StampedLock.tryConvertToWriteLock (next section) with a retry loop — still not a free upgrade. 5. StampedLock (Interview Level) Java 8 capability lock: write, read, and optimistic read . Acquisition returns a long stamp. Release/convert needs that stamp. Does not implement Lock / ReadWriteLock (views exist: asReadLock() etc.). Optimistic read: tryOptimisticRead() returns a non-zero stamp if no writer currently holds the lock. You copy fields into locals, then validate(stamp) . If validate is true, those reads are a consistent snapshot (happens-before from the last write-unlock). If false, a writer ran — retry or take a real read lock. long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead(); double x = this.x; double y = this.y; if (!sl.validate(stamp)) { stamp = sl.readLock(); try { x = this.x; y = this.y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); } } return Math.hypot(x, y); Prefer over RW lock when reads are very short, writes rare, and you can tolerate retry — e.g. a hot coordinate / versioned snapshot. Do not use as a general Spring-service mutex. Misuse traps (interview gold): Not reentrant. Nested acquire from the same thread deadlocks or fails. Do not call unknown methods while holding a stamp. No ownership. Another thread can unlock your stamp. Unlike ReentrantLock . Skip validate — you may compute on torn / half-updated fields. That is the whole point of the API. Optimistic mode is weak: writers can invalidate at any time. Side-effecting reads inside the optimistic window are forbidden. Out of scope: stamp bit layout, formal proofs, AQS. 6. Condition Lesson 2: one wait set per monitor; wait / notify / notifyAll . Condition splits that into named queues on one Lock . Monitor Condition wait() await() notify() signal() notifyAll() signalAll() Same rules: must hold the lock; await atomically releases it and reacquires before return; always while (spurious wakeup + missed predicate). Signalling without holding the lock: ReentrantLock 's conditions throw IllegalMonitorStateException . Classic win: bounded buffer with notFull and notEmpty . A put that frees a slot signals only consumers; a take that frees space signals only producers. One monitor + notifyAll wakes the wrong waiters and burns CPU. final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock(); final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition(); final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition(); void put(E x) throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (count == items.length) notFull.await(); items[putptr++] = x; if (putptr == items.length) putptr = 0; count++; notEmpty.signal(); } finally { lock.unlock(); } } E take() throws InterruptedException { lock.lock(); try { while (count == 0) notEmpty.await(); E x = items[takeptr++]; if (takeptr == items.length) takeptr = 0; count--; notFull.signal(); return x; } finally { lock.unlock(); } } Production: use ArrayBlockingQueue — this pattern is for interviews and for when you own the invariant. 7. Deadlock & Liveness Oracle liveness: deadlock, starvation, livelock. Explicit locks add tools — they do not delete the physics. Lock ordering: always acquire A then B globally. Nested inversion (thread 1: A then B; thread 2: B then A) is the Alphonse/Gaston deadlock from the tutorial. tryLock + backoff: acquire both or release what you hold and retry with a timeout — the tutorial's Safelock idiom. Use when lock order cannot be global (graph of peers). Interruptible acquire: cancellation path when a lock wait is stuck — still need a policy for who retries. Fair locks reduce lock starvation; they can increase latency. They do not fix livelock (threads keep yielding without progress). 8. Classic Bugs Forgot unlock — exception path, early return, or tryLock success then return without finally . No auto-release. Unlock without holding — IllegalMonitorStateException (including unlocking after failed tryLock ). Locking the wrong object — synchronized (this) while mutations use a ReentrantLock field (two locks, no exclusion). signal without holding the lock — exception (typical) or lost wakeup (if a custom Condition allowed it). RW upgrade deadlock — read held, write requested. StampedLock optimistic read without validate — silent data corruption. Reentrant call into StampedLock — self-deadlock. 9. Enterprise Framing Scenario Typical choice Read-heavy in-memory cache / config refresh ReentrantReadWriteLock (or immutable snapshot + volatile ref from Lesson 3) Starvation-sensitive work queue (fair access) new ReentrantLock(true) — measure; fairness is expensive Metrics / logging "skip if busy" tryLock() — drop the sample rather than stall the request path Rare mutable state on a Spring singleton Private final ReentrantLock (or synchronized on a private final object) — never lock on the bean this that callers can steal Hot read of a tiny struct, rare writes StampedLock optimistic read + validate Simple invariant, one wait-set Stay on synchronized Senior line: explicit lock = extra protocol. Pay for tryLock, fairness, or multiple Conditions — not for looking concurrent. Later sections (not here): executors / pools (S05), concurrent collections / atomics (S06), CompletableFuture / virtual threads, lock-free algorithms, AQS internals. 10. Revision Notes Unlock in finally . Always. tryLock unlocks only on success. Unlock → next lock on same Lock is happens-before (successful ops). Untimed tryLock() barges on a fair lock. RW: many readers or one writer. Downgrade yes; upgrade no (deadlock). StampedLock: validate optimistic reads; not reentrant. Condition.await ≡ wait : hold lock, loop on predicate, two queues beat notifyAll for producer-consumer. 11. 5 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Exception in the critical section, unlock not in finally. Result? Lock stays held after exception. JVM auto-releases like sync do. Hold count resets itself to 0. Fairness flag flips itself on. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Lock stays held after exception.) Explicit locks have no block-structured auto-release. That is the price of tryLock and cross-method locking. Q2: Fair ReentrantLock; another thread is queued. Untimed tryLock() when free? Succeeds — barging is allowed. Fails — must honor the queue. Throws — fairness forbids try. Blocks — until the queue drains. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Succeeds — barging is allowed.) Javadoc: untimed tryLock() takes a free lock even if waiters exist. Timed tryLock(0, SECONDS) honors fairness. Q3: Thread holds RW read lock, then calls writeLock().lock(). Typical result? Self-deadlock waiting for itself. Silent upgrade to write mode. Read lock converts automatically. Write lock is shared with reads. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Self-deadlock waiting for itself.) Write waits for every reader to leave. You are still a reader. Downgrade (write then read) is the supported direction. Q4: StampedLock tryOptimisticRead without validate. Risk? Torn fields used as if consistent. Stamp becomes reentrant safely. Write lock is taken automatically. Happens-before is always granted. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Torn fields used as if consistent.) Optimistic mode is a weak read. Only validate(stamp) == true gives the write-unlock happens-before guarantee. Q5: Condition.await() without holding the ReentrantLock. Typical result? IllegalMonitorStateException thrown. Thread sleeps but keeps the lock. Await upgrades lock to fair mode. Signal runs without any waiter. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (IllegalMonitorStateException thrown.) Same discipline as Object.wait() : hold the associated lock. await then releases it atomically. 12. Reasoning Exercises Pick the lock: (a) request-path metric increment you may drop under load, (b) in-memory catalog searched 10k×/s and rebuilt once a minute, (c) transfer between two accounts with a global lock order, (d) tiny (x,y) point, millions of reads, rare writes. For each: synchronized , ReentrantLock , RW lock, tryLock , or StampedLock ? Fix the buffer: A teammate uses one Condition and signal() after both put and take. Sketch the lost-wakeup / wrong-waker bug. Repair with two Conditions (names + who signals whom). Fair vs non-fair: A latency SLO cares about p99 wait for a lock, not throughput. Which constructor? What do you tell the interviewer about tryLock() on that lock? Downgrade trace: Thread W holds write, acquires read, unlocks write. Thread R then acquires read. Thread W2 tries write. Who proceeds, who waits, and why no writer slipped between W's mutate and W's subsequent read? tryLock timeout design: Two resources, no global order. Write the acquire-both-or-release-held pattern (Oracle Safelock). Where do you sleep/backoff, and why must failed acquires still unlock only the locks you actually got?

lessons.title: Executors & Thread Pools
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 4 · Lesson 5 of 8 · Cheat sheet · Next: Collections → Deep Dive: Executors & Thread Pools ~40 minutes · ties to mission · builds on Lesson 1 (raw threads vs pools), Lesson 4 (locks done) Senior Interview Focus: Lesson 1 said "don't spawn new Thread() per request." This lesson is how production actually runs work: bounded pools, queue backpressure, rejection policies, graceful shutdown, and sizing heuristics. Interviewers love factory-method traps ( newCachedThreadPool , unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue in fixed pools) and "what happens when the queue is full?" Primary sources: Oracle — Executors · Executor · ExecutorService · ThreadPoolExecutor · Executors · ForkJoinPool.commonPool 1. Why Executors Over new Thread() Lesson 1: each platform thread costs native stack memory (~1 MB order of magnitude), kernel scheduling, and JVM bookkeeping. Under HTTP spikes, new Thread(task).start() per request creates an unbounded thread count → context-switch storm, OOM, or thrashing. An executor separates task definition ( Runnable / Callable ) from thread lifecycle . A fixed set of worker threads pulls work from a queue. You get: Reuse — amortize thread creation cost. Bounds — cap concurrency + queue depth → predictable memory and load. Policy — what to do when saturated (reject, block caller, drop). Lifecycle — one place to shutdown instead of hunting stray threads. Senior line: raw threads are fine for demos; executors are how you survive production traffic. 2. Executor → ExecutorService → ThreadPoolExecutor Type Role Executor Minimal: execute(Runnable) — fire-and-forget. No lifecycle API. ExecutorService Extends Executor + submit (returns Future ), invokeAll / invokeAny , shutdown / shutdownNow , awaitTermination . ThreadPoolExecutor Concrete pool: core/max threads, keep-alive, work queue, thread factory, rejection handler. The implementation you configure in production. Submission model (ThreadPoolExecutor): If running threads < corePoolSize → create thread, run task. Else if queue not full → enqueue task. Else if running threads < maximumPoolSize → create thread, run task. Else → RejectedExecutionHandler . submit task │ ├─ threads < core? ──yes──► new worker, run now │ ├─ queue has room? ──yes──► enqueue │ ├─ threads < max? ──yes──► new worker, run now │ └─ else ──► reject policy Key insight: the queue sits between core and max. A bounded queue forces you to grow toward maxPoolSize before rejecting; an unbounded queue may never grow past core — tasks pile up in memory instead. 3. Runnable vs Callable & Future Basics Runnable Callable<V> Returns void Typed result V Checked exception Cannot throw (use unchecked) May throw Exception Submit API execute(r) or submit(r) → Future<?> submit(callable) → Future<V> ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); Future<Integer> fut = pool.submit(() -> { return restClient.fetchCount(); // may throw }); // later on caller thread: try { Integer n = fut.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // blocks until done or timeout } catch (TimeoutException e) { fut.cancel(true); // may interrupt worker if running } catch (ExecutionException e) { Throwable cause = e.getCause(); // real failure from Callable } get() — block until complete; wraps failure in ExecutionException . get(timeout, unit) — bounded wait; TimeoutException if not done. cancel(mayInterruptIfRunning) — if not started, never runs; if running and true , sends interrupt (task must cooperate — Lesson 1). isDone() — true after normal completion, exception, or cancellation. isCancelled() — cancelled before completion. Interview trap: execute() swallows nothing — uncaught exceptions go to the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler . submit() stores the exception; you only see it on get() . Out of scope here: CompletableFuture composition (Module 03 S07). 4. ThreadPoolExecutor Knobs ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor( 4, // corePoolSize 16, // maximumPoolSize 60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS, // keepAlive — idle threads above core die after this new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100), // work queue new ThreadFactory() { /* name threads */ }, new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy() ); Core vs max vs keepAlive corePoolSize — baseline workers kept alive even when idle (unless allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true) ). maximumPoolSize — hard cap on concurrent workers. keepAliveTime — threads above core that are idle longer than this are terminated. Queue choice (shapes behavior) Queue Behavior Typical use LinkedBlockingQueue (unbounded) Never "full" → pool stays at core; tasks accumulate in heap newFixedThreadPool trap — hidden OOM under load ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded) Fixed capacity → pushes pool toward max, then reject Production default when you want backpressure SynchronousQueue Zero capacity — handoff; no storage; submit blocks until a worker takes it newCachedThreadPool — grows threads aggressively PriorityBlockingQueue Ordered by priority — rare; know ordering contract Scheduled / priority workloads ThreadFactory Name threads ( billing-worker-%d ), set daemon flag, uncaught-exception handler, or wrap for MDC/logging context. Debugging thread dumps without names is pain. ThreadFactory named = r -> { Thread t = new Thread(r); t.setName("report-pool-" + t.getId()); t.setUncaughtExceptionHandler((th, ex) -> log.error("pool death", ex)); return t; }; 5. Executors Factory Methods — What They Build + Traps Factory What you get Trap newFixedThreadPool(n) Fixed core=max=n, unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue Queue grows forever — no backpressure, OOM under spike newCachedThreadPool() core=0, max= Integer.MAX_VALUE , SynchronousQueue , 60s keepAlive Unbounded thread creation — fine for short tasks, lethal under sustained load newSingleThreadExecutor() One worker, unbounded queue — serialized execution Hidden queue growth; use when strict ordering matters newScheduledThreadPool(n) Delayed / periodic tasks Still need bounds on delayed work volume newWorkStealingPool() ForkJoinPool -style work stealing Different semantics — deques, not classic TPE queue story Senior line: treat Executors helpers as interview trivia. Production pools are usually explicit ThreadPoolExecutor with bounded queue + named threads + metrics. 6. Rejection Policies — When to Pick Each Triggered when pool is at maxPoolSize and queue is full (or handoff fails for SynchronousQueue ). Policy Behavior When AbortPolicy (default) Throws RejectedExecutionException Fail fast — caller handles retry / 503. APIs that must not silently drop. CallerRunsPolicy Runs task on the submitting thread Natural backpressure — slows producers (e.g. batch ingest). Risk: blocks HTTP thread if misused. DiscardPolicy Silently drops the task Only for loss-tolerant telemetry / sampling — document it. DiscardOldestPolicy Drops head of queue, retries submit Freshness over completeness (latest price tick wins). Custom handler: log + metric + dead-letter queue. Interviewers want you to name the policy and the user-visible outcome (503 vs slow vs lost event). 7. Graceful Shutdown pool.shutdown(); // no new tasks; queued work still runs // optional: pool.awaitTermination(30, SECONDS); List<Runnable> dropped = pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupt workers, drain queue into returned list pool.awaitTermination(30, SECONDS); // wait for workers to finish shutdown() — orderly: stop accepting; finish what's queued. shutdownNow() — aggressive: interrupt running tasks, return unstarted tasks. Tasks must handle interrupt (Lesson 1). awaitTermination — block until idle or timeout. Pair with retry loop in app shutdown hooks. Spring / Tomcat: container calls lifecycle stop on beans and connectors — your @PreDestroy or DisposableBean should shut down custom pools the same way. Leaked pools keep JVM alive or lose in-flight work. 8. ForkJoinPool.commonPool — Parallel Streams Tie-In Module 02: parallelStream() uses ForkJoinPool.commonPool() — shared JVM-wide, sized ~ Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() - 1 (with floor). Work-stealing deque, not the classic TPE queue model. CPU-bound fork/join splits benefit from stealing idle workers. Blocking I/O on common pool starves every other parallel stream and CompletableFuture.supplyAsync default — Lesson 2/Streams framing. Custom ForkJoinPool for isolated parallel work is the fix when you must parallelize CPU locally without polluting common pool. Executors lesson = general task pools; FJP = divide-and-conquer. Both are threads under the hood (Lesson 1). 9. Pool Sizing Heuristics Workload Heuristic Why CPU-bound ~ cores or cores + 1 More threads than cores → context switch, cache thrash, no speedup I/O-bound cores × (1 + wait/compute) — Little's law thinking Threads block on DB/HTTP; while one waits, another can run Mixed microservice Separate pools per dependency class One slow downstream must not exhaust the pool for everything Example: 8 cores, task spends 90% waiting on DB → rough target 8 × (1 + 9) ≈ 80 — start conservative, measure queue depth, p99 latency, and CPU. Tuning is empirical. Bounded always wins over "infinite threads fix I/O." Unbounded growth masks overload until the process dies. 10. Enterprise Framing Layer What runs where Tomcat / Jetty worker threads One thread per in-flight HTTP request (bounded connector thread pool). Your service code runs here — don't block it on unbounded custom work. Spring @Async Submits to a configured TaskExecutor (often ThreadPoolTaskExecutor ). Default if misconfigured can be SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor (new thread per task!) — always define a bean with core/max/queue/rejection. Custom app pools Reports, webhooks, bulk export — dedicated bounded pool + rejection + metrics (queue size, active count, rejected tasks). Backpressure Full queue + Abort → 503 / retry-after. CallerRuns → slows ingress. Message bus → consumer lag. Pick story that matches SLA. Senior line: HTTP thread handles the request; offload slow/fire-and-forget to a named pool you can shut down and observe. 11. Classic Bugs Unbounded fixed pool — newFixedThreadPool under load → million-task queue, GC pause, OOM. Cached pool under sustained load — thousands of threads, scheduler collapse. CallerRuns on HTTP thread — saturation runs work on Tomcat worker → cascading latency. Never shutdown — non-daemon workers prevent clean deploy; thread leak on hot reload. submit exception swallowed — never call get() → silent failure. Blocking on common pool — parallel stream + JDBC inside → global starvation. Shared mutable state without sync — pool doesn't fix races; Lessons 2–4 still apply. Later sections (not here): CompletableFuture (S07), concurrent collections / atomics (S06), virtual threads, deep AQS / work-stealing internals. 12. Revision Notes TPE: core → queue → max → reject. Queue type changes everything. execute vs submit — exception path differs. Future.get / cancel / isDone — blocking and interrupt semantics. Fixed pool trap = unbounded queue. Cached pool trap = unbounded threads. Abort = fail fast; CallerRuns = backpressure; Discard* = lossy. shutdown orderly, shutdownNow interrupt, awaitTermination wait. CPU ≈ cores; I/O ≈ cores × wait ratio; measure in prod. commonPool = shared; no blocking I/O there. 13. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: newFixedThreadPool(8) under heavy load. First failure mode? Unbounded queue grows until OOM. Pool rejects at eight threads. Creates ninth thread immediately. Tasks run on common pool. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Unbounded queue grows until OOM.) Fixed factory uses unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue . Pool stays at 8 workers; tasks accumulate in the queue — no RejectedExecutionException until memory gives out. Q2: Core=4 max=16 bounded queue full all workers busy. Next submit? Rejected per handler policy. Always blocks until queue slot. Always spawns unbounded threads. Runs on ForkJoin common pool. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Rejected per handler policy.) At max threads with full queue, TPE cannot accept work — default AbortPolicy throws. CallerRuns would run on submitter instead. Q3: submit(Callable) throws inside task. When seen? On Future.get as ExecutionException. Immediately on calling thread. Never if pool has two threads. Only after shutdownNow is called. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (On Future.get as ExecutionException.) submit captures failure into the Future . Caller must get() (or isDone + get ) to surface ExecutionException with getCause() . Q4: newCachedThreadPool under sustained blocking I/O. Risk? Unbounded thread count exhaustion. Queue blocks at core size. Only one thread ever runs. Tasks always run in caller. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Unbounded thread count exhaustion.) SynchronousQueue + max= Integer.MAX_VALUE → each blocked submit spawns another thread. Classic production foot-gun. Q5: CallerRunsPolicy when pool saturated. Effect? Submitter thread runs the task. Oldest queued task is dropped. RejectedExecutionException is thrown. Task is sent to common pool. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Submitter thread runs the task.) Backpressure: producer slows down. Dangerous if submitter is a Tomcat HTTP worker — latency propagates to clients. Q6: parallelStream with JDBC inside map. Main risk? Starves ForkJoin common pool. Creates daemon threads only. Bypasses happens-before rules. Forces single-thread execution. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Starves ForkJoin common pool.) Blocking I/O on common pool ties up shared workers — other parallel streams and default async stall. Use dedicated executor or sequential/stream off common pool. 14. Reasoning Exercises Design a pool: Bulk PDF export — 30s CPU + 200ms S3 upload per job, peak 200 jobs/min. Propose core, max, queue size, rejection policy. Defend each number. Factory trap: Teammate uses Executors.newFixedThreadPool(50) for incoming webhooks. Draw the failure timeline under 10× traffic spike. Rewrite as explicit ThreadPoolExecutor . Shutdown story: App receives SIGTERM during deploy. Order: stop accepting HTTP, drain in-flight, shutdown custom pool, awaitTermination . What if a task ignores interrupt after shutdownNow ? Future contract: Three submit calls; you need all results or fail the batch in 5s. Sketch invokeAll vs manual get(timeout) + cancel siblings on first failure. Tomcat + @Async: Controller returns 202 immediately; work runs async. Where can CallerRunsPolicy still block the client? How do you fix it? Sizing: 4 cores, each task 5ms CPU + 95ms HTTP. Rough pool size? What metric tells you you're too high? Too low? Questions? Ask your coach — executors + rejection under load is a favorite Senior Backend drill.

lessons.title: Concurrent Collections & Atomics
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 5 · Lesson 6 of 8 · Cheat sheet · Next: CompletableFuture → Deep Dive: Concurrent Collections & Atomics ~38 minutes · ties to mission · builds on L1 – L5 · Fail-Fast lesson Senior Interview Focus: You know locks (L4) and pools (L5). Production shared state usually lives in java.util.concurrent data structures — not Collections.synchronizedMap on a HashMap . Interviewers probe CHM computeIfAbsent , weakly consistent iterators vs CME, when CopyOnWrite wins, and atomics vs synchronized for hot counters. Primary sources: Oracle — Concurrent Collections · ConcurrentHashMap · CopyOnWriteArrayList · BlockingQueue · AtomicInteger · java.util.concurrent.atomic 1. Why Synchronized Wrappers Are Often Wrong Module 01: Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) wraps every method in synchronized (mutex) . Sounds safe. Production problems: Coarse lock — one mutex for the whole map. High read contention serializes everyone (Lesson 4's RW lock exists for a reason). Compound ops not atomic — javadoc warns: you must manually synchronize on the wrapper for check-then-act: // BUG — two threads can both see absent key if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); // Required with synchronized wrapper: synchronized (map) { if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); } Iteration trap — must synchronize during the entire loop. Forget once → data races or CME on some paths. Null keys/values — synchronized wrappers delegate to underlying collection rules; CHM disallows nulls by design (ambiguity under concurrency). Senior line: synchronized wrapper = "I synchronized each method." Interview line: "That's not enough for iteration or check-then-act — use CHM or hold one lock for the whole invariant." 2. ConcurrentHashMap — Interview Internals (Java 8+) History bite: Java 7 used segments — fixed array of sub-maps, each with its own lock. Java 8+ replaced segments with a single bin array (like HashMap) plus per-bin synchronization. Bin — array slot holding a linked list of Node s (key, hash, value, next). Treeify — when a bin grows past 8 nodes (and table ≥ 64), list becomes a red-black tree for O(log n) lookups. Untreeify below 6. Lock granularity — writers typically lock/synchronize on the first node of a bin (or CAS on empty bin). Different bins proceed in parallel. Reads — usually lock-free volatile reads along bucket chains; no global reader lock. Out of scope: full resize/rebalance proofs, AQS, lock-free skip lists. Key APIs (production) // Atomic "get or create" — one thread runs mappingFunction per key cache.computeIfAbsent(userId, id -> loadFromDb(id)); // Atomic update counters.merge(key, 1L, Long::sum); // Bulk — may be more efficient than loop map.forEach((k, v) -> ...); map.reduceValues(1L, Long::sum); computeIfAbsent — fixes the check-then-act race from Lesson 2 without external lock. Mapping function must be fast and must not recursively modify the same map on the same thread (deadlock risk). putIfAbsent / replace — single-entry atomic ops. size() and iteration semantics Operation Under concurrency size() / isEmpty() Approximate — snapshot-ish count; fine for metrics, wrong for strict control-flow gates Iterator / forEach / entrySet() Weakly consistent — never throws CME; may or may not see entries added after iteration started; won't reflect removals already passed containsKey / get Point reads with happens-before from concurrent writes (volatile/CAS paths) Tie to Lesson 16 : CHM iterators are weakly consistent — not a snapshot copy like CopyOnWrite, not fail-fast like HashMap . They reflect some concurrent updates. 3. CopyOnWriteArrayList Backing array is volatile . Read — no lock, direct array index. Write ( add , set , remove ) — copy entire array, mutate copy, publish new reference. Wins: read-heavy, rare writes — listener lists, config subscribers, iteration-heavy snapshots where stale reads are OK. Costs: O(n) copy per write; iterator holds snapshot from creation — won't see later adds; high write rate = GC churn + memory. Iterator: snapshot at birth — no CME ever; won't see concurrent writes after iterator created. // Spring-style listener list pattern private final List<EventListener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); void fire(Event e) { for (EventListener l : listeners) // safe without lock l.onEvent(e); } Wrong tool: frequently mutating work queue — use BlockingQueue (L5). 4. BlockingQueue Family — Producer-Consumer Lesson 5 introduced queues as executor work buffers. Here: the coordination API — block instead of spin or busy-wait. Implementation Capacity Notes ArrayBlockingQueue Bounded (fixed array) One lock (or dual-lock variant) — predictable memory; fair optional constructor LinkedBlockingQueue Bounded or unbounded Linked nodes — higher overhead; unbounded = heap growth risk (L5 trap) SynchronousQueue Zero Handoff — producer blocks until consumer takes; newCachedThreadPool PriorityBlockingQueue Unbounded heap Ordering by priority — know comparator stability DelayQueue Unbounded Elements available after delay — scheduling patterns BlockingQueue<Task> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100); // producer — blocks when full (backpressure) q.put(task); // consumer — blocks when empty Task t = q.take(); // timed variants: offer(e, timeout), poll(timeout) Lesson 4's manual Condition buffer is what these classes implement for you. Production: prefer the queue unless you own a special invariant. 5. Atomics — Visibility Without a Full Lock Lesson 3: volatile gives visibility, not read-modify-write atomicity. i++ on volatile is still a race. java.util.concurrent.atomic wraps a volatile field with CAS operations. Class Use AtomicInteger / AtomicLong Counters, sequence IDs, stats AtomicReference<V> Atomic swap of object reference (immutable snapshot pattern) AtomicIntegerArray etc. Striped atomic slots without boxing LongAdder (bonus) High-contention counting — striping reduces CAS failures AtomicInteger requests = new AtomicInteger(); requests.incrementAndGet(); // atomic ++ requests.addAndGet(5); boolean ok = requests.compareAndSet(expect, update); // CAS int current = requests.get(); // volatile read CAS overview (interview level) Compare-And-Set: atomically "if current == expect, set to update; else fail." CPU instruction (e.g. x86 CMPXCHG ). On failure, retry loop — optimistic concurrency. // conceptual CAS loop (AtomicInteger does this internally) void increment() { for (;;) { int current = value; // volatile read int next = current + 1; if (compareAndSet(current, next)) return; // success — publish happens-before // else retry — another thread won } } ABA problem (interview mention): value goes A→B→A; CAS sees A and thinks nothing changed. AtomicStampedReference exists — deep dive out of scope. Not a substitute for invariants spanning multiple fields — use locks or immutable snapshots. Hot counter under extreme contention — consider LongAdder over hammering one AtomicLong . 6. Tie-Back: Fail-Fast vs Weakly Consistent HashMap + sync wrapper ConcurrentHashMap CopyOnWriteArrayList Concurrent iteration CME or race if unsync'd Weakly consistent, no CME Snapshot, no CME Sees concurrent adds Unsafe Maybe (weakly) No (snapshot) Check-then-act Manual sync block computeIfAbsent N/A for map pattern Lesson 16: fail-fast is best-effort — even modCount can miss cross-thread writes. Concurrent collections choose a defined weaker contract instead of pretending. 7. Enterprise Framing Scenario Pick In-memory cache (per-key load once) ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent + bounded size policy / Caffeine for TTL Request/metrics counters LongAdder or AtomicLong — not synchronized on every hit Spring singleton with mutable map field ConcurrentHashMap or immutable copy-on-write snapshots — not raw HashMap Event listener registry CopyOnWriteArrayList if rare register/unregister, frequent dispatch Work handoff between pool threads ArrayBlockingQueue — bounded backpressure (L5) CHM vs synchronized HashMap CHM when concurrent readers + writers, atomic compound ops, or iterator without global lock. Sync map only if truly low contention and you wrap compounds correctly. Senior line: pick the structure that makes the invariant atomic — not "thread-safe" label on a wrapper. 8. Classic Bugs check-then-act on synchronizedMap without synchronizing on wrapper — duplicate loads, lost updates. CHM computeIfAbsent slow/blocking loader — holds bin lock; blocks other ops on that bin; recursive same-map call deadlocks. Trusting CHM.size() == 0 for strict logic under live writers — approximate. CopyOnWrite for hot writes — quadratic copying, memory blow-up. i++ on volatile or plain int — not atomic; use AtomicInteger or synchronize. Atomics on multiple related fields — CAS each field separately ≠ atomic invariant across fields. Iterating synchronizedMap without synchronized(map) — javadoc violation, races. Later sections (not here): CompletableFuture (S07), virtual threads (S08), deep AQS, lock-free skip lists, AtomicStampedReference deep dive. 9. Revision Notes Sync wrapper = per-method lock; compounds + iteration need external sync. CHM Java 8+: bins + treeify; per-bin locking; parallel writes different bins. computeIfAbsent / merge — atomic compound ops. Weakly consistent iteration — no CME; may see some concurrent updates. CopyOnWrite — snapshot reads; expensive writes; stale iterator. BlockingQueue — put / take coordinate producers/consumers. Atomics — CAS retry; visibility + atomic RMW; not multi-field invariants. 10. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: synchronizedMap — containsKey then put if absent. Safe? No — compound needs outer sync. Yes — each method is synchronized. Yes — if map is final field. Yes — on single-thread only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (No — compound needs outer sync.) Two synchronized calls are not one atomic operation. Another thread can insert between them. Use one synchronized(map) block or ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent . Q2: CHM iterator during concurrent puts. Typical behavior? Weakly consistent; no CME thrown. Fail-fast CME on first change. Deadlock until writers finish. Snapshot of entire map frozen. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Weakly consistent; no CME thrown.) CHM iterators never throw CME. They may reflect some updates after creation — unlike CopyOnWrite snapshot, unlike HashMap fail-fast. Q3: CopyOnWriteArrayList — frequent add/remove. Main risk? O(n) copy per write cost.
