Iterator throws CME always. Reads block on global mutex. Null keys are disallowed only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (O(n) copy per write cost.) Every mutating op copies the backing array. Write-heavy workloads burn CPU and memory — wrong structure. Q4: volatile int count; count++ from many threads. Result? Lost updates — not atomic RMW. Fully atomic without any lock. Visibility only — count stays 0. CME on every increment call. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Lost updates — not atomic RMW.) volatile publishes writes but ++ is read-modify-write. Use AtomicInteger or synchronize. Q5: ArrayBlockingQueue full — put() on producer. Effect? Producer blocks until space. Queue throws CME immediately. Oldest element is dropped. Item goes to common pool. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Producer blocks until space.) put blocks — natural backpressure. Contrast offer (false if full) or unbounded queue (never blocks on capacity). Q6: computeIfAbsent mappingFunction does slow DB call. Risk? Blocks other ops on that bin. Iterator throws CME on load. Map rejects null keys only. CAS fails and skips the load. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Blocks other ops on that bin.) Loader runs under bin lock for that key's bucket. Slow I/O stalls concurrent access to keys in the same bin. Load outside then putIfAbsent , or use a dedicated cache library. 11. Reasoning Exercises Pick the structure: (a) per-user session cache with lazy DB load, (b) 50M/sec metric increment, (c) webhook listener list (10 listeners, 1 add/day, 100k fires/sec), (d) order buffer between ingest and worker pool. CHM, CopyOnWrite, Atomic/LongAdder, or BlockingQueue? Fix the cache bug: synchronizedMap + if (!cache.containsKey(k)) cache.put(k, load(k)) . Two failure modes under load. Rewrite with CHM; explain what computeIfAbsent guarantees. Iterator semantics: Thread A iterates CHM. Thread B adds keys. Thread C removes keys. What can A see? Contrast with CopyOnWrite list iteration started before B adds 100 elements. CAS retry: Three threads incrementAndGet on one AtomicInteger from 0. Final value? Could it be 1 or 2? Why not? Producer-consumer sizing: 4 consumers, mean service 200ms, Poisson arrivals 100/sec. Bound ArrayBlockingQueue at 50 — what happens under spike when put blocks? Tie to L5 CallerRuns vs blocking producer thread. Spring bean: Singleton service holds HashMap<String, Config> mutated on admin API and read on every request. Production-safe redesign in one paragraph. Questions? Ask your coach — CHM + atomics show up in almost every Senior Backend loop.

lessons.title: CompletableFuture
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 6 · Lesson 7 of 8 · Cheat sheet · Next: Virtual Threads → Deep Dive: CompletableFuture ~40 minutes · ties to mission · builds on L5 Executors/Future , L6 Collections Senior Interview Focus: Lesson 5 gave you Future — submit, block on get() , done. Production microservices need compose parallel downstream calls, handle failures in-line, and enforce timeouts without callback hell. CompletableFuture is the JDK's answer. Interviewers probe thenCompose vs thenApply , join + CompletionException , and blocking I/O on commonPool . Primary sources: Oracle — Futures · CompletableFuture javadoc · CompletionStage · JEP 266 — More Concurrency Updates 1. Future Pain → Why CompletableFuture Exists Lesson 5 ExecutorService.submit returns Future<T> : Blocking only — get() parks the caller until done. Chaining means nested get() calls or manual polling. No composition — "when A finishes, call B" needs your own callbacks or extra threads. Exception handling awkward — failure surfaces as ExecutionException on get() ; no pipeline hook. No combine — merging two independent futures requires a third thread or blocking both. // Future hell — blocks twice, serial even if B could start after A Future<User> userFut = pool.submit(() -> userClient.get(id)); Future<Orders> ordersFut = pool.submit(() -> orderClient.list(userFut.get().id())); // blocks! Orders o = ordersFut.get(); // blocks again CompletableFuture<T> implements Future<T> and CompletionStage<T> — a promise you can chain, combine, and complete manually. Java 8+. 2. Creating Async Work — supplyAsync / runAsync ExecutorService ioPool = ...; // bounded, named — Lesson 5 CompletableFuture<String> data = CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() -> httpClient.fetch(url), ioPool); CompletableFuture<Void> sideEffect = CompletableFuture .runAsync(() -> auditLog.record(event), ioPool); Factory Returns Task type supplyAsync(Supplier) CompletableFuture<U> Produces value runAsync(Runnable) CompletableFuture<Void> Fire-and-forget side effect Critical production rule: one-arg overloads use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() (Lesson 5). Never put blocking I/O there — starves parallel streams and every other default-async CF site. Senior line: always pass a dedicated Executor for I/O-bound async. Name it. Bound it. Monitor it. 3. Chaining — Transform & Flatten Method Input Output CF type Use thenApply(fn) T → U CompletableFuture<U> Map result (sync stage on completion thread) thenAccept(consumer) T → void CompletableFuture<Void> Consume result, no new value thenRun(action) ignores T CompletableFuture<Void> Run after complete, no access to value thenCompose(fn) T → CompletableFuture<U> CompletableFuture<U> Flatten nested async (next call depends on first) thenCombine(other, fn) both T, U CompletableFuture<V> Merge two independent futures when both done CompletableFuture<OrderSummary> pipeline = CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() -> userClient.get(userId), ioPool) .thenCompose(user -> orderClient.listAsync(user.id())) // NOT thenApply .thenApply(orders -> summarize(orders)); // Parallel fan-in — both start immediately CompletableFuture<User> userF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> loadUser(id), ioPool); CompletableFuture<Credit> creditF = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> loadCredit(id), ioPool); CompletableFuture<Dashboard> dash = userF.thenCombine(creditF, Dashboard::new); thenApply vs thenCompose (interview gold): thenApply(user -> orderClient.listAsync(user.id())) → CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Orders>> — nested hell. thenCompose(user -> orderClient.listAsync(user.id())) → CompletableFuture<Orders> — flat pipeline. Async variants: thenApplyAsync , thenComposeAsync , etc. run the stage on an executor (default: commonPool). Sync thenApply runs on the thread that completed the previous stage — fast map OK; blocking I/O is not. 4. Error Paths — exceptionally / handle / whenComplete Method When it runs Transforms result? exceptionally(fn) Only on failure Yes — recovery value (or rethrow) handle(fn) Always — gets (result, throwable) Yes — one of them is non-null whenComplete(action) Always — side effect No — returns same outcome downstream CompletableFuture<Price> priced = CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() -> pricingService.quote(sku), ioPool) .exceptionally(ex -> Price.fallback()) // only on failure .handle((price, ex) -> ex != null ? Price.zero() : price) // always .whenComplete((p, ex) -> metrics.record(ex)); // logging/metrics exceptionally — fallback / default; if recovery throws, downstream fails. handle — unified success+failure handler; good for "return Either-like result." whenComplete — like finally for observability; exceptions still propagate unless earlier stage handled them. Failed stage skips normal thenApply callbacks — they jump to exceptionally / handle or fail the chain. 5. Fan-Out / First-Wins — allOf / anyOf CompletableFuture<User> u = ...; CompletableFuture<Orders> o = ...; CompletableFuture<Prefs> p = ...; CompletableFuture<Void> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(u, o, p); all.thenRun(() -> { // all three complete (maybe exceptionally) — check each .isCompletedExceptionally() buildPage(u.join(), o.join(), p.join()); }); CompletableFuture<Object> first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(replica1, replica2, replica3); // first to complete wins — others keep running unless you cancel allOf — waits for all ; result is Void ; inspect individuals for values/errors. anyOf — first completion wins; type erasure to Object ; others may still run — cancel if wasteful. 6. get vs join — CompletionException get() join() Checked exceptions InterruptedException , ExecutionException None (unchecked) Failure wrapper ExecutionException with getCause() CompletionException with getCause() Typical use Legacy / boundary where checked OK Stream-style pipelines, lambdas try { User u = future.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { Throwable root = e.getCause(); // real RestClientException etc. } Inside thenApply , an uncaught exception completes the CF exceptionally — downstream join unwraps via CompletionException . 7. Cancellation & Timeouts (Java 9+) future.cancel(true); // mayInterruptIfRunning — task must cooperate (Lesson 1) // Java 9+ — fail if not done in time future.orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // Java 9+ — supply fallback value on timeout (does not throw TimeoutException) future.completeOnTimeout(Price.fallback(), 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); orTimeout — completes exceptionally with TimeoutException if not done in time. completeOnTimeout — completes normally with fallback — good for cache/stale-while-revalidate patterns. Timeouts apply to the CF's completion deadline — chain with thenCompose carefully; each stage can have its own timeout. 8. Pipeline vs Nested Future Hell // BAD — nested, blocks, hard to read Orders o = pool.submit(() -> { User u = userClient.get(id); // blocking return orderClient.list(u.id()); // blocking }).get(); // GOOD — declarative pipeline, non-blocking composition CompletableFuture<Orders> o = CompletableFuture .supplyAsync(() -> userClient.get(id), ioPool) .thenCompose(u -> orderClient.listAsync(u.id())); // BETTER for parallel deps — don't serialize independent calls var userF = supplyAsync(() -> userClient.get(id), ioPool); var creditF = supplyAsync(() -> creditClient.get(id), ioPool); return userF.thenCombine(creditF, this::merge); Senior pattern: fan-out parallel I/O at the top, fan-in with thenCombine / allOf , single error handler at the end. Blocking belongs on the pool thread, not Tomcat worker (Lesson 5). 9. Enterprise Framing Scenario Pattern Parallel downstream calls Start all CFs immediately; allOf + join or thenCombine . Don't call get() on first before starting second. Spring @Async returning CF Controller can return CompletableFuture<Response> — frees servlet thread while work runs on async executor. Must configure a real pool bean — not default per-task thread. Timeout + fallback completeOnTimeout(fallback, ...) or orTimeout + exceptionally . Match SLA: degrade vs fail. Aggregating microservice BFF Bounded ioExecutor ; per-dependency CF; handle per call for partial failure; CHM for request-scoped cache (L6). Not WebFlux CF composes async within threads — fine for blocking clients wrapped in supplyAsync . Reactive streams (Reactor) are a different model — out of scope. Senior line: CompletableFuture is orchestration glue — not a magic fix for blocking I/O without a bounded executor and timeout story. 10. Classic Bugs Blocking I/O on commonPool — default supplyAsync starves JVM-wide parallelism. thenApply instead of thenCompose — nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<...>> . Blocking get() inside thenApply — stalls completion thread; deadlock risk with fixed pool. Serializing independent calls — starting B only after A's get() wastes latency. Ignoring exceptionally — silent failure until terminal join . allOf without checking exceptional completion — join throws even if allOf itself "succeeded." anyOf without cancelling losers — wasted downstream load. Heavy work in sync thenApply on commonPool completion thread — use thenApplyAsync(..., pool) . Later sections (not here): virtual threads (S08), Reactor/WebFlux deep dive, ForkJoinPool work-stealing internals. 11. Revision Notes Future = block + no compose. CF = chain + combine. supplyAsync / runAsync — always pass executor for I/O. thenCompose flattens; thenApply maps. thenCombine / allOf = parallel deps; anyOf = first wins. join → CompletionException ; unwrap getCause() . orTimeout fails; completeOnTimeout degrades. Don't block commonPool. Don't block Tomcat thread on get() . 12. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: thenApply vs thenCompose when next step is async? thenCompose — flattens nested CF. thenApply — flattens nested CF. thenRun — flattens nested CF. thenAccept — flattens nested CF. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (thenCompose — flattens nested CF.) thenApply wrapping a CF gives CF<CF<T>> . thenCompose is monadic flatMap — the interview distinction. Q2: supplyAsync(() -> jdbc.query()) one-arg overload. Risk? Blocks ForkJoin common pool. Runs only on main thread. Throws RejectedExecution always. Creates unbounded platform threads. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Blocks ForkJoin common pool.) Default executor is commonPool() . JDBC blocks — starves parallel streams and other default-async CF work. Q3: future.join() when stage failed. Thrown type? CompletionException wrapping cause. ExecutionException wrapping cause. InterruptedException wrapping cause. RejectedExecutionException cause. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (CompletionException wrapping cause.) join is unchecked. Real failure is e.getCause() . get() uses checked ExecutionException . Q4: exceptionally vs handle on success path? handle runs; exceptionally skips. exceptionally runs; handle skips. Both always transform result. Neither runs on success path. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (handle runs; exceptionally skips.) exceptionally only on failure. handle always — gets (result, ex) with one null. Q5: allOf(f1, f2, f3) all complete. f2 failed. allOf result? Completes normally; f2 join throws. allOf itself completes exceptionally. allOf cancels f1 and f3 always. allOf blocks until f2 retries. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Completes normally; f2 join throws.) allOf completes when all stages finish (including exceptionally). Check isCompletedExceptionally() per future before join . Q6: completeOnTimeout(fallback, 2, SECONDS) fires. Outcome? Completes normally with fallback. Completes exceptionally with timeout. Cancels without any completion. Blocks caller for two seconds. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Completes normally with fallback.) completeOnTimeout is graceful degradation. orTimeout completes exceptionally with TimeoutException . 13. Reasoning Exercises Rewrite Future hell: Three sequential blocking HTTP calls today via submit().get() . Sketch CF pipeline with one thenCompose chain + bounded ioExecutor . Parallel BFF: Dashboard needs User, Orders, Recommendations (independent). Start all three without waiting. Combine with allOf . One service down — design partial page with handle per call. Timeout policy: Pricing SLA 500ms; catalog SLA 2s. Where attach orTimeout vs completeOnTimeout ? What does the client see? Thread budget: Tomcat 200 threads, ioExecutor core 50 max 100. Controller does cf.get() on servlet thread. Under load what breaks first? thenApply trap: thenApply(u -> repo.findAsync(u.id())) — return type? Fix. What breaks at join if unfixed? anyOf replicas: Three read replicas, anyOf first response. How cancel the other two? What if slow replica returns stale data after fast one? Questions? Ask your coach — CF composition shows up in every microservices interview.

lessons.title: Virtual Threads
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 7 · Lesson 8 of 8 · Cheat sheet · ➡️ Capstone Exercise Deep Dive: Virtual Threads ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on L1 Platform Threads , L5 Executors , L7 CompletableFuture · Java 21+ Senior Interview Focus: Lessons 5–7 taught pools and async pipelines to avoid blocking platform threads. Virtual threads flip the model: blocking is OK again for I/O — millions of lightweight threads, few OS carriers. Interviewers probe pinning ( synchronized , native), when pools still win, and "just enable Spring virtual threads" traps. Primary sources: JEP 444 — Virtual Threads · Thread.ofVirtual() · newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor · Oracle — Virtual Threads · JEP 453 — Structured Concurrency (Preview) 1. Platform vs Virtual Threads Platform thread Virtual thread What 1:1 wrapper around OS thread JVM-managed lightweight thread Cost ~1 MB stack, kernel scheduling Small JVM stack frame; cheap create/destroy Scale Thousands = pain Millions feasible (I/O wait, not CPU spin) Blocking I/O Expensive — holds OS thread Cheap — unmount, carrier free for others API Thread , pools (L5) Same Thread API — Thread.isVirtual() Lesson 1 mental model still holds: shared heap, per-thread stack. Virtual threads are Thread objects — not a new concurrency primitive like CompletableFuture (L7). Code using Thread , Runnable , blocking JDBC/HTTP largely works unchanged. 2. Carriers — Why Blocking Got Cheap Virtual threads run on a small pool of carrier platform threads (default: ForkJoinPool with parallelism ≈ CPU cores). When a virtual thread hits a blocking operation the JVM knows about (socket read, LockSupport.park , etc.), it unmounts from the carrier — carrier picks another virtual thread. Carrier (platform) Virtual threads ┌──────────────┐ VT-1 ──► JDBC read ──► unmount (carrier free) │ core #3 │ ──► VT-2 ──► running └──────────────┘ VT-3 ──► HTTP wait ──► unmount ... millions waiting, few carriers working Why Lesson 5 pools existed: platform thread + blocking I/O = thread tied up. Virtual threads decouple "task in flight" from "OS thread occupied." You can write straightforward blocking code at massive concurrency — the JVM multiplexes carriers. Out of scope: scheduler implementation, carrier pool AQS rewrite. 3. Creating Virtual Threads (Java 21+) // One-off Thread vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("worker-", 0).start(runnable); // Per-task executor — idiomatic for request-per-task servers ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); executor.submit(() -> handleRequest(req)); // new VT per task // Builder ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofVirtual().name("api-", 0).factory(); newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() — no queue, no pool size knob; each task = new virtual thread. Perfect for "one request, one thread" Tomcat-style code without 200 platform workers. Not a replacement for bounded CPU worker pools — see Section 6. CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, virtualExecutor) — valid; still prefer explicit executor over commonPool for I/O (L7). 4. Mounting, Unmounting & Pinning Traps Unmount: virtual thread releases carrier during blocking I/O or park . Mount: carrier resumes virtual thread when I/O completes. Pinning: virtual thread cannot unmount — carrier held for entire critical section. Throughput drops toward platform-thread behavior for pinned work. Cause Why pinned Interview fix synchronized block/method Carrier pinned for monitor enter/held Prefer ReentrantLock (L4) — does not pin Native code / JNI JVM can't unmount in native Minimize native on hot path; audit drivers Some legacy libraries Internal synchronized or native Profile; isolate; bounded platform pool for that call JDK monitoring: jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.pinning events (JFR) or -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full logs pin stack traces. Senior move: run load test, check for pin warnings before flipping prod. Senior line: virtual threads + heavy synchronized in your code or a dependency = silent carrier starvation. 5. When Virtual Threads Win vs When Pools Still Matter Workload Pick Why HTTP/RPC handler blocking on DB, cache, downstream APIs Virtual threads Millions of blocked waits; carriers stay busy CPU-bound compute (crypto, compression, big JSON parse) Bounded platform pool (~ cores) More threads ≠ faster; adds scheduling overhead Mixed service VT for request path; small fixed pool for CPU stages Don't run 10k parallel SHA-256 on VT Fire-and-forget with backpressure Bounded queue + platform or semaphore-limited VT newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor has no queue cap — unbounded task acceptance can OOM heap Lesson 5 sizing still applies to CPU work. Virtual threads solve thread count for blocking , not CPU parallelism . 6. Structured Concurrency — Interview Preview Problem: fan-out tasks (L7 allOf ) without scope — child outlives parent, lost failures, hard cancellation. Idea: tasks share a structured scope — if parent fails or deadline hits, all children cancel; if one child fails, scope fails together. Like nested try-with-resources for concurrency. // Preview API shape (Java 21+ preview — check your JDK) try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) { Subtask<User> user = scope.fork(() -> loadUser(id)); Subtask<Orders> orders = scope.fork(() -> loadOrders(id)); scope.join(); // wait for all scope.throwIfFailed(); // propagate first failure return build(user.get(), orders.get()); } // scope closes — unfinished children cancelled Interview: explain why — failure propagation, cancellation tree, no orphan threads. CompletableFuture.allOf doesn't cancel siblings on one failure unless you wire it. Full API variants ( ShutdownOnSuccess , deadlines) — encyclopedia out of scope. 7. Compatibility — ThreadLocal, Interrupt, Thread Dumps Feature Virtual thread notes ThreadLocal / InheritableThreadLocal Works — but millions of VTs × fat ThreadLocals = heap disaster. Prefer scoped values ( ScopedValue , Java 21+) for request context in new code. Interruption (L1) Same contract — interrupt() , InterruptedException , cooperative cancel still required. Thread dumps jcmd Thread.print / IDE — virtual threads listed separately; shows parked/mounted state. Essential for prod debugging. Thread.isVirtual() Distinguish in logs/metrics. Identity Don't pool virtual threads — create per task; pooling VTs defeats the purpose. 8. Enterprise — Tomcat & Spring Boot Layer Virtual thread mode Spring Boot 3.2+ spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true — Tomcat/Jetty handle requests on virtual threads. Blocking controller code scales without reactive rewrite. Tomcat Request thread = virtual; blocking servlet API OK. Watch pinning in filters, JDBC drivers, legacy synchronized singletons. Custom executors Replace newCachedThreadPool for I/O with newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor — but keep bounded pools for CPU jobs and for libraries that pin. @Async Point TaskExecutor at virtual executor — not SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor (platform per task). Don't assume free lunch Connection pools (DB, HTTP client) still bounded — 10k VTs hammering DB with pool of 20 = queue/timeouts. VT fixes thread count, not downstream capacity. Senior line: enable virtual threads + audit pinning, ThreadLocal, pool limits, and synchronized blocks — not just flip YAML. 9. How This Closes Module 03 L1 — thread model, interrupt, lifecycle L2–L4 — safe shared mutable state L5 — bounded pools, rejection, shutdown L6 — concurrent collections, atomics L7 — async composition without blocking callers L8 — massive blocking concurrency with simple code — when VT fits, when legacy pools still rule Capstone mock (when you're ready) mixes all of the above under production framing. 10. Classic Bugs Pinning under load — synchronized cache or driver → carriers exhausted, latency spikes. Unbounded newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor + no backpressure — millions of tasks accepted → OOM (L5 lesson still applies to task admission). CPU work on every request via VT — no speedup; worse cache behavior. ThreadLocal context on every VT — memory bloat; migrate to ScopedValue where possible. Assuming reactive needed — VT + blocking JDBC is valid; Reactor not required for concurrency scale. Ignoring connection pool limits — thread count ≠ DB capacity. Out of scope: Loom scheduler internals, full Structured Concurrency API catalog, Module 04 GC. 11. Revision Notes VT = cheap Thread ; carriers = few platform threads. Blocking I/O unmounts; synchronized / native pins. newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() — per task, no pool cap. I/O-bound → VT; CPU-bound → bounded platform pool. Structured concurrency — scoped fan-out, fail/cancel together. ThreadLocal at scale hurts; thread dumps show VTs. Spring spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true — audit deps first. 12. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Main reason virtual threads help I/O services? Unmount on block — few carriers. Replace synchronized with volatile. Remove need for connection pools. Run faster than CPU on one core. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Unmount on block — few carriers.) Blocking I/O no longer holds an OS thread. Carriers multiplex many virtual threads. CPU-bound work doesn't magically speed up. Q2: synchronized block inside hot virtual thread path. Risk? Pinning — carrier held blocked. Virtual thread cannot enter sync. Immediate IllegalMonitorState. Auto upgrade to platform thread. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Pinning — carrier held blocked.) Monitor enter pins the carrier for the critical section. Prefer ReentrantLock or shrink synchronized scope. Q3: CPU-heavy image resize farm — best default? Bounded platform pool ~ cores. newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor. Unbounded cached platform pool. parallelStream on commonPool only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Bounded platform pool ~ cores.) CPU-bound work needs cores, not millions of threads. VT adds overhead without throughput gain. Q4: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor under spike. OOM risk? Yes — no queue cap on tasks. No — JVM caps at core count. No — virtual threads use no heap. Yes — but only on Java 17 builds. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Yes — no queue cap on tasks.) Each submitted task can spawn a VT. Admission control (semaphore, queue, rate limit) still required — L5 backpressure lesson. Q5: join() on failed StructuredTaskScope child. Parent scope? Fails together — shutdown policy. Ignores child failure always. Retries child on new carrier. Converts child to platform thread. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Fails together — shutdown policy.) ShutdownOnFailure propagates first failure; scope closes and cancels siblings — structured concurrency's point vs raw allOf . Q6: Spring virtual threads enabled. DB pool still 20. Effect? VTs compete — pool still bottlenecks. Pool auto-scales with VT count. JDBC becomes non-blocking always. Tomcat rejects all HTTP requests. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (VTs compete — pool still bottlenecks.) Virtual threads fix thread overhead, not downstream limits. 10k concurrent requests still queue on 20 connections. 13. Reasoning Exercises Migration audit: Spring Boot app, 200 platform Tomcat threads, blocking JDBC. List 4 checks before spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true . Pin hunt: Latency spikes after VT migration. How use jdk.tracePinnedThreads or JFR? Name two code patterns you'd fix first. Pool vs VT: Service does 5ms CPU validation then 200ms HTTP call per request. Virtual thread per request or fixed pool of 50? Defend. Structured vs CF: Load user + orders + credit in parallel; any failure → 503, cancel others. Sketch StructuredTaskScope vs allOf + manual cancel. ThreadLocal trap: Request ID in ThreadLocal , 100k concurrent VTs. What breaks? What's the Java 21+ alternative? Capstone preview: Name one topic from each of L1–L7 you'd combine in a Senior concurrency mock with VT as the deployment angle. Questions? Ask your coach — Module 03 complete after notes. Capstone mock when you're ready.

lessons.title: Capstone Exercise
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ⬅️ Prev: Virtual Threads · ➡️ Next: JVM Runtime Architecture Concurrency & Threads Capstone Exercise Capstone exercise • Module 03 • 16 scenarios • JUnit 5 • Java 21+ recommended • Stub • Solved reference How to use: Copy the single Java file into IntelliJ or java-interview-lab . Add JUnit Jupiter 5. Implement each TODO — tests encode the Senior Backend answer. Run all tests until green. Review tied lessons for any red test. Setup Create a new Java class (default package is fine). Paste ConcurrencyCapstoneExercise.java . Let IntelliJ add JUnit 5 (Alt+Enter on @Test ). Implement stubs one by one; run tests after each. Exercises 15–16 need Java 21+ (virtual threads). Scenario Index # Topic Lesson Expected (from tests) 01 Lost update → AtomicInteger S01 S06 10_000 02 volatile guarantees (conceptual) S03 "visibility not atomicity" 03 Check-then-act race on HashMap S02 loader runs > 1 04 CHM.computeIfAbsent single load S06 1 loader call 05 tryLock skip under contention S04 -1 when busy 06 AbortPolicy rejection S05 RejectedExecutionException 07 ArrayBlockingQueue handoff S05 S06 sum 55 (1..10) 08 thenCompose flat pipeline S07 ["o1","o2"] 09 exceptionally fallback S07 0 10 allOf fan-in sum S07 60 11 join + CompletionException S07 "downstream" 12 orTimeout fails S07 TimeoutException cause 13 shutdown + awaitTermination S05 finishes in 2s 14 run() vs start() trap S01 runs on caller thread 15 Thread.ofVirtual().isVirtual() S08 true 16 Pinning construct ID S08 S04 "synchronized" Quick Review — In-Browser Drills No IDE needed. Answers in <details> . Drill A: newFixedThreadPool(8) under spike — first failure? Unbounded queue grows until OOM. Pool rejects at eight threads. Creates ninth thread immediately. Tasks run on common pool. Answer A — S05 : unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue . Drill B: volatile int + count++ from 100 threads? Lost updates — not atomic RMW. Fully atomic without any lock. Visibility only — count stays 0. CME on every increment call. Answer A — S03 + S06 . Drill C: VT + hot synchronized block on JDBC? Pinning — carrier held blocked. Virtual thread cannot enter sync. Immediate IllegalMonitorState. Auto upgrade to platform thread. Answer A — S08 : use ReentrantLock or shrink scope. Drill D: thenApply when next step returns CF? Use thenCompose — flattens nested CF. Use thenApply — flattens nested CF. Use thenRun — flattens nested CF. Use thenAccept — flattens nested CF. Answer A — S07 : flatMap vs map. Production Framing Checklist After all tests green, explain aloud (mock interview): Why Ex 03 fails but Ex 04 passes — compound operation vs atomic map API. When Ex 05 tryLock beats blocking lock() on a request path. What Ex 06 means for your HTTP 503 story under saturation. Why Ex 08 needs thenCompose — what breaks with thenApply . Spring virtual threads on + DB pool 20 — what still bottlenecks ( S08 ). Copy-Paste Source Copy entire file Download stub Download solved Loading ConcurrencyCapstoneExercise.java…

lessons.title: JVM Runtime Architecture & Memory Areas
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ⬅️ Prev: Concurrency Capstone · Lesson 1 of 8 · Lesson 2 → · Cheat sheet JVM Runtime Architecture & Memory Areas ~30 minutes · ties to mission · builds on Stack vs Heap , Class in Metaspace , Threads Share Heap Senior Interview Focus: Interviewers expect you to map a running Spring Boot pod to concrete JVM structures — not recite textbook diagrams. Can you explain what docker stats / cgroup memory includes vs what -Xmx caps? Where do class definitions live vs object instances? Why is a heap OOM fix different from Metaspace or direct-buffer OOM? This lesson stitches together what you already learned in OOP and Concurrency into one production mental model. Primary sources: Oracle — java launcher (SE 21) · JVM Spec — Runtime Data Areas · Oracle — GC Ergonomics (memory pools) 1. JDK vs JRE vs JVM — What Actually Runs in Prod Component What it is Prod relevance JVM The virtual machine: bytecode interpreter + JIT + GC + thread scheduler + memory manager This is the process. One JVM instance per typical Java service container. JRE JVM + core class libraries ( rt.jar era; now modular jmods on the module path) Historical term. Modern deployments ship a JRE subset or full JDK inside the image. JDK JRE + developer tools ( javac , jlink , jcmd , jmap , etc.) Build stage uses full JDK. Runtime image often uses jlink -trimmed runtime or distroless JRE. Container reality: Kubernetes sees one OS process — usually java -jar app.jar or a shell wrapper around it. That process is the JVM. cgroup memory limit must cover: Java heap ( -Xmx ) Metaspace (class metadata — not in -Xmx ) Thread stacks (platform threads × stack size; virtual threads are much cheaper) Code Cache (JIT-compiled native code) Direct / native memory (NIO direct buffers, Netty, JNI, compression dictionaries) JVM native overhead (GC structures, card tables, etc.) Senior trap: setting -Xmx to 100% of container limit guarantees OOMKill. Leave headroom for off-heap areas — rule of thumb 25–40% below cgroup cap depending on stack count and Netty usage. 2. Process vs JVM vs Application Threads You already drew this in Thread Fundamentals . Zoom out one level: ┌────────────── OS Process (PID 4821) ──────────────┐ │ JVM (HotSpot / OpenJDK) │ │ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Shared: Heap · Metaspace · Code Cache │ │ │ │ Direct/Native (off-heap) │ │ │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │ │ │ Stack │ │ Stack │ │ Stack │ │ Stack │ │ │ │ main │ │ http-1 │ │ pool-3 │ │ GC svc │ │ │ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Layer Count in typical microservice Notes OS process 1 per pod/container (usual case) Crash = pod restart. kill -9 = hard stop, no GC cleanup. JVM instance 1 per process Owns all memory pools below. One GC subsystem, one Metaspace (per class loader tree). Application threads Many (Tomcat workers, pool threads, GC threads, JIT compiler threads) Share heap + Metaspace. Each has private stack. Races = unsynchronized heap writes. Production threads you'll see in a thread dump: http-nio-8080-exec-N — servlet request workers pool-N-thread-M — your ExecutorService ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-N — parallel streams GC Thread#N — garbage collector workers C1/C2 CompilerThreadN — JIT tiers (detail in S07) VM Thread — safepoint coordination (below) All of them share the same heap. That's why HashMap in a singleton Spring bean is everyone's problem. 3. Runtime Memory Areas — The Full Map From Lesson 3 (OOP) you know stack vs heap. Here is the complete HotSpot map senior engineers keep in their head: Area Scope Stores Grows / reclaimed by Heap Shared (all threads) Object instances, arrays -Xms / -Xmx . GC reclaims unreachable objects (S03). Stack (per thread) Private per thread Stack frames, local primitives, reference slots Fixed per thread ( -Xss ). Popped on method return — no GC. Metaspace Shared (class loaders) Class metadata, method bytecode, vtables, static fields Native memory. Grows until class loaders collected (S06). -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize . Code Cache Shared JIT-compiled machine code Native. -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize . Swept when full. Direct / Native memory Shared (process) NIO direct buffers, Netty pooled buffers, JNI allocations Not in heap. Limited by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize (default ≈ -Xmx ). PC Registers Per thread Current bytecode instruction address JVM-managed, tiny — rarely discussed in interviews. Heap generations (preview for S03): Young (Eden + Survivor) + Old. Most objects die young. Long-lived caches, singletons, session state → Old. TLABs live inside Eden. ┌─── Metaspace ───┐ │ class metadata │ │ static fields │ └────────┬────────┘ │ Klass pointer ┌──────────── Heap ──────────┼──────────────────────────┐ │ Young (Eden + S0 + S1) │ Old Generation │ │ ┌ TLAB per thread ─┐ │ long-lived objects │ │ └──────────────────┘ │ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Per thread: Stack frames ──► reference slots point into Heap Shared: Code Cache (JIT) · Direct buffers (off-heap) 4. What Lives Where — Primitives, References, Statics Reconcile Class vs Object with the full map: Thing Where Interview one-liner Local int x = 5 Stack frame (actual value) Value lives in the frame; dies when method returns. Local String s = "hi" Reference on stack → object on heap Variable is a pointer slot; "hi" may be in string pool on heap. Instance field private int age Inside object on heap Even primitives inside objects are heap-resident. static int count Metaspace (with class metadata) One copy per class loader, not per instance. static final List<T> CACHE Static reference in Metaspace → List object on heap Reference slot in Metaspace; the list and its elements are heap objects. Class definition / bytecode Metaspace Loaded once per class loader. java.lang.Class is a heap mirror. Method local array new int[1000] Heap (arrays are objects) Reference may be on stack; array body always heap. Trace exercise public class OrderService { private static final Map<Long, Order> CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); public Order find(long id) { int retries = 3; // (A) Order cached = CACHE.get(id); // (B) if (cached == null) { Order fresh = repository.load(id); // (C) CACHE.put(id, fresh); return fresh; } return cached; } } Reasoning (cover answers, then check): (A) retries — stack (primitive local). (B) cached reference — stack; CACHE static ref — Metaspace; ConcurrentHashMap object + entries — heap. (C) fresh reference — stack; Order instance — heap. 5. TLAB Preview — Why Allocation Is Fast Every new hitting a global Eden lock would bottleneck multi-threaded services. HotSpot gives each thread a Thread-Local Allocation Buffer (TLAB) — a small private slice of Eden. Allocation inside TLAB = bump-the-pointer (move an offset) — no lock, nanoseconds. TLAB full → thread gets a new TLAB or allocates slowly in shared Eden. Very large objects may bypass TLAB and go straight to Old (threshold: -XX:PretenureSizeThreshold ). You already met TLABs in Stream Fundamentals (short-lived pipeline objects). Full mechanics — sizing, waste, tuning — in S02 (Object Allocation) . Interview sound bite: "Most ephemeral objects never contend on a global heap lock because TLABs make allocation mostly thread-local bump-pointer." 6. Safepoints & Stop-The-World Preview The JVM must pause application threads at well-defined moments to: Run GC root scanning and compaction (S03) Deoptimize / recompile hot methods (S07) Dump threads ( jcmd Thread.print , kill -3 ) Revoke biased locks, walk stacks for roots A safepoint is a bytecode location where the thread can safely stop and expose a consistent stack/heap view. Between safepoints, a thread may be mid-method. Stop-The-World (STW): all mutator threads blocked at safepoints while VM work runs. Short STW pauses (milliseconds) are normal; multi-second STW = production incident (S03–S05). Thread dump connection: When you capture a dump, each thread's stack trace is a snapshot at a safepoint. That's why all threads show a coherent state — and why "RUNNABLE" in a dump doesn't mean "on-CPU right now" (it can mean runnable-but-not-yet-scheduled). Thread-1: RUNNABLE at Safepoint at com.app.OrderService.find(OrderService.java:42) ... GC Thread#2: RUNNABLE at GC work... Concurrent collectors (G1, ZGC) reduce but don't always eliminate STW phases. Detail in S03. 7. Enterprise OOM Triage — Three Different Beasts Senior on-call skill: read the exception class and message — fixes are not interchangeable. Error Typical message What ran out Common causes Fix direction Heap OOM Java heap space -Xmx heap Memory leak, unbounded cache, huge collections, loading too much data per request Heap dump / MAT (S08), fix retention, paginate, raise -Xmx only after proving need Metaspace OOM Metaspace / class metadata Class metadata area Classloader leak (hot redeploy, dynamic proxies, Groovy/bytecode gen), too many class loaders Find leaking loader, limit generated classes, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize as guardrail not cure Direct buffer OOM Direct buffer memory Off-heap direct memory Netty, NIO, gRPC, large off-heap buffers without release Pool sizing, leak detection, -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize , fix missing release() Unable to create native thread unable to create native thread OS thread / stack budget Unbounded new Thread() , thread pool misconfig, ulimit Bounded executors, virtual threads for I/O, lower -Xss , raise ulimit StackOverflowError Stack overflow Thread stack depth Infinite recursion, very deep XML/JSON parsing Fix recursion, streaming parser — not a heap problem On-call scenario: Pod OOMKilled by Kubernetes but no Java heap dump. cgroup killed the process because total memory (heap + metaspace + direct + stacks + native) exceeded limit — even if -Xmx looked fine. Check container limit vs -Xmx headroom first. 8. Classic Production Mistakes "We raised -Xmx to fix Metaspace OOM." Wrong pool. Classes kept generating; heap change irrelevant. "Heap is 70% used so we're fine." Ignores direct memory spike during Netty upgrade. Static Map cache without bounds — heap leak disguised as "performance optimization." Assuming primitives are "light" on heap — a new int[50_000_000] is ~200 MB on heap regardless. Thread dump shows BLOCKED everywhere — heap healthy but thread starvation; not a GC lesson (concurrency module). Out of scope (later sections): collector algorithms (S03–S04), full GC tuning flags (S05), classloader delegation (S06), JIT tiers (S07), MAT heap dump walkthrough (S08). 9. Revision Notes Prod container runs one JVM process — not "the JDK." Many threads, one shared heap + Metaspace; stacks are private. Locals/refs on stack; objects on heap; statics in Metaspace (object refs point to heap). TLAB = fast thread-local Eden allocation; detail in S02. Safepoints enable GC, JIT, thread dumps; STW = all threads paused. Heap OOM ≠ Metaspace OOM ≠ direct OOM — read the message, fix the right pool. 10. Reasoning Exercises Microservice pod limit 512 MiB. You set -Xmx512m . Healthy? Answer No. Metaspace, thread stacks, Code Cache, and direct memory also consume cgroup budget. JVM will be OOMKilled. Target ~60–75% of limit for -Xmx unless you have precise off-heap measurements. After redeploying 200 times without restart, Metaspace grows monotonically. Heap stable. Leak? Answer Likely classloader leak — old loaders not collectable because something still references them. Classic hot-reload / agent / dynamic codegen pattern. Not a heap leak. Thread dump shows 400 http-nio-exec threads all RUNNABLE at socketRead0 . Heap 40%. Problem? Answer Not heap. Threads blocked in I/O — downstream slowness or missing timeouts. Fix latency/backpressure; virtual threads may help (M03 L8). GC tuning won't help. static final byte[] BUFFER = new byte[1_000_000] — where does the byte array live? Answer Static reference in Metaspace; byte array object on heap . One array shared by all instances under that class loader. 11. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Docker cgroup OOMKill with -Xmx at 70% of limit. Likely cause? Off-heap exceeded remaining budget. Heap alone always equals cgroup. JVM ignores container limits always. Only Code Cache uses off-heap. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Off-heap exceeded remaining budget.) Metaspace, stacks, direct buffers, and native GC structures sit outside -Xmx . Total process RSS must fit the cgroup. Q2: Where does static reference field store its pointer? Metaspace with class metadata. Inside each instance on heap. On the main thread stack only. Code Cache next to JIT code. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Metaspace with class metadata.) Static fields live with the class definition. The referenced object itself is on the heap. Q3: TLAB primary benefit in multi-threaded service? Avoid global Eden lock on most news. Store static fields per thread. Replace garbage collection entirely. Move all objects to Old gen faster. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Avoid global Eden lock on most news.) TLABs let threads allocate via bump-pointer in a private Eden slice. Full sizing in S02. Q4: Thread dump taken during GC safepoint. What is true? Stacks are consistent snapshot points. Threads mid-bytecode show half frames. Only RUNNABLE threads appear. Heap contents printed inline always. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Stacks are consistent snapshot points.) Safepoints freeze mutators at safe locations so VM can walk stacks. That's why dumps are coherent. Q5: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace. First sensible action? Investigate classloader retention. Double -Xmx heap immediately. Disable garbage collection. Shrink thread stack -Xss only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Investigate classloader retention.) Metaspace stores class metadata. Leaked loaders or unbounded dynamic class generation are the usual suspects — not heap size. Q6: Local int x = 42 inside running method. Location? Current thread stack frame. Heap next to object header. Metaspace with static data. Direct buffer off-heap area. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Current thread stack frame.) Primitive locals live in the stack frame's local variable array. Instance field primitives live inside heap objects. 12. Bridge to Next Lessons S02 — object allocation, TLAB sizing, escape analysis S03–S04 — GC algorithms, STW vs concurrent phases S05 — tuning flags that match your memory map S06 — class loaders and Metaspace lifecycle Concurrency cross-link — shared heap + safepoint dumps explain races and diagnostics you already studied 🏠 Home · ⬅️ Prev: Concurrency Capstone · Lesson 2 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: Heap Regions, TLAB & Object Layout
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 2 of 8 · Lesson 3 → · Cheat sheet Heap Regions, TLAB & Object Layout ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on S01 Runtime Architecture , Klass Word , Allocation Lifecycle , Mark Word Senior Interview Focus: Can you explain why a REST handler allocating 10,000 short-lived DTOs per second is usually fine, but a 2 GB static cache is a different GC problem? Can you sketch an object's bytes on the heap — header, fields, padding — and say when compressed oops apply? This lesson connects generational theory to the physical layout you already met in OOP. Primary sources: Oracle — GC Ergonomics · OpenJDK — Compressed Oops · Aleksey Shipilëv — Objects Inside-Out 1. Generational Heap Layout HotSpot splits the Java heap into generations based on an empirical observation: most objects die young. Collecting only the young region is fast; scanning the entire heap every time would not scale. ┌─────────────────────────────── Java Heap (-Xmx) ───────────────────────────────┐ │ Young Generation │ Old Generation (Tenured) │ │ ┌──────── Eden ────────┐ ┌─S0─┐ ┌─S1─┐ │ long-lived objects, promoted │ │ │ new allocations │ │ │ │ │ │ caches, singletons, pools │ │ └──────────────────────┘ └────┘ └────┘ │ │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Region Role Typical ratio (ergonomic defaults) Eden All new objects start here (via TLAB — below) Largest slice of Young Survivor S0 / S1 Hold objects that survived at least one Young GC; only one active at a time during copy Small (often ~10% of Young each) Old (Tenured) Objects that survived enough Young collections or were pre-tenured Grows until -Xmx cap Young GC (Minor collection): scans Eden + active Survivor, copies live objects. STW but typically short. Detail in S03. Old GC (Major / Mixed): scans Old generation. Slower, less frequent. Long-lived data dominates pause risk here. 2. Object Journey — Eden → Survivor → Old Allocation: new OrderDto() lands in Eden (usually inside caller thread's TLAB). Request ends: local references gone → object unreachable → dies in Eden. Next Young GC reclaims it — never copied. Survives one Young GC: copied from Eden (or from the inactive Survivor) into the other Survivor space. GC age in Mark Word incremented. Survives repeatedly: bounced between S0 and S1. Each survival bumps age. Promotion: when age reaches -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold (default 15, collector may lower dynamically) or Survivor is full, object moves to Old. Pre-tenuring: very large objects may skip Young entirely and go straight to Old ( -XX:PretenureSizeThreshold — often ~50% of Young on some collectors). Request lifecycle (typical REST handler): new DTO, new List, parse JSON ──► Eden handler returns, refs dropped ──► eligible Young GC ──► reclaimed (never promoted) Singleton cache loaded at startup ──► Eden first survives many Young GCs ──► S0 ↔ S1 age threshold hit ──► Old (stays until unreachable) This is the bridge from Object Lifecycle : allocation is step 2; generational movement is what happens before step 5 (reclamation). 3. TLAB — Fast, Lock-Free new In S01 you saw TLAB preview. Here is the mechanism: Each application thread gets a private Thread-Local Allocation Buffer — a contiguous chunk carved from Eden. Allocation inside TLAB = increment an offset pointer ( bump-the-pointer ). No lock. Nanoseconds. TLAB exhausted → thread requests a new TLAB from Eden (brief synchronization) or falls back to shared slow path. Objects larger than TLAB remaining space (or huge objects) may allocate outside TLAB / pre-tenure. Senior sound bite: "Multi-threaded services stay fast because most new never contends on a global heap lock — each thread bumps its own TLAB in Eden." Concept Detail Why thread-safe without lock Only one thread writes into its TLAB slice; other threads have separate slices. TLAB waste Last object in a TLAB may leave unusable slack; refilled on next allocation burst. Tuning flags -XX:+UseTLAB (default on), -XX:TLABSize , -XX:ResizeTLAB — rarely touched in prod; know they exist. 4. Object Layout Deep Dive You met headers in Class vs Object and java.lang.Object . On-heap layout (HotSpot, 64-bit, compressed oops on — typical prod): ┌──────────────── Object in Heap ────────────────┐ │ Mark Word (8 bytes) │ │ Klass pointer (4 bytes compressed) │ │ instance fields (primitives + ref slots) │ │ padding (align to 8-byte boundary) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ 4.1 Mark Word (8 bytes on 64-bit) One word, multiplexed — meaning changes with object state: State Mark Word holds (simplified) Normal / unlocked GC age (4 bits), identity hashcode (lazy-computed, shifted), unused bits Biased lock Thread ID of biased owner — fast path for uncontended synchronized Thin lock Lock record pointer — lightweight contention Fat lock Pointer to monitor structure — heavy contention GC mark During collection, used for forwarding / mark bits GC age — survival count used for promotion decisions. Identity hashcode — computed once on first hashCode() without override, then cached in Mark Word if space allows. 4.2 Klass pointer Points to class metadata in Metaspace (vtable, field layout, type info). Enables getClass() , instanceof , virtual dispatch. With compressed class pointers , 4 bytes instead of 8. 4.3 Instance fields & padding Fields laid out per class definition (reordering possible for packing). JVM pads object size to 8-byte alignment on 64-bit — affects "empty object = 16 bytes" interview answer. 4.4 Empty object size (interview) Typical 64-bit HotSpot with compressed oops + compressed class pointers: Mark (8) + Klass (4) + padding (4) = 16 bytes for a plain empty instance. Without compression: often 16 bytes header alone or more with alignment rules — always say "depends on JVM flags and JDK version." 5. Compressed Oops & Compressed Class Pointers 64-bit pointers are 8 bytes. Most heaps are < 32 GB — HotSpot can store 32-bit compressed references that encode offsets into the heap base. -XX:+UseCompressedOops (default when heap ≤ ~32 GB) — 4-byte object references in headers and arrays. -XX:+UseCompressedClassPointers — 4-byte Klass pointers (requires compressed oops on most configs). Heap base — JVM maps a contiguous region; compressed ref + base = real address. > 32 GB heap — compressed oops often disabled → larger headers, more memory per object, different tuning tradeoffs. Interview: "Compressed oops let 64-bit JVM use 32-bit refs for heap pointers, cutting object header and array overhead — but typically only while heap stays under the ~32 GB compressed-oops range." 6. Array Layout vs Plain Objects Arrays are objects too — special layout: ┌──────────────── Array Object ──────────────────┐ │ Mark Word │ │ Klass pointer (points to array class metadata)│ │ array length (4 bytes) │ │ elements[0..n] (primitives or ref slots) │ │ padding │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Type Header overhead Per-element cost int[] ~12–16 bytes + alignment 4 bytes per int (no per-element object) Integer[] ~12–16 bytes + alignment 4-byte ref each → separate Integer object on heap (boxing cost) Object[] ~12–16 bytes + alignment 4-byte compressed ref per slot; elements are separate objects Senior trap: new byte[1_000_000] ≈ 1 MB + header — one array object. List<Byte> with boxing = millions of tiny objects → Young GC pressure. 7. False Sharing Preview When two threads update different fields that land in the same CPU cache line (64 bytes typical), cores invalidate each other's caches — throughput collapse. Not a GC issue — hardware + layout issue. @Contended (JVM internal / sun.misc) pads hot counters; LongAdder stripes across cells. Arrays of mutable longs used as per-thread counters packed tightly → classic false sharing. Full perf module (M07) later. Know the term for interviews when discussing concurrent counters next to object headers. 8. Enterprise Framing — Young vs Old Pressure Pattern Generation impact Prod symptom Per-request DTOs, JSON nodes, stream intermediates Eden churn — die young Frequent short Young GC pauses (usually OK); high allocation rate Spring singleton beans, connection pools, session caches Promote to Old Stable Old occupancy; Full GC risk if unbounded Static ConcurrentHashMap cache without eviction Entries + keys in Old Old gen grows until Full GC or OOM — not a "Young GC tuning" fix parallelStream() on large collections Spike of short-lived pipeline objects Eden spike; watch allocation rate + commonPool (M02/M03) Loading entire DB result into List<Entity> Large object graphs in Old if retained Heap pressure, long GC pauses — paginate/stream from DB On-call framing: "High Young GC frequency with low pause times often means healthy short-lived allocation — fix retention in Old, not Eden size, unless allocation rate is genuinely excessive." 9. Classic Mistakes "More Eden = always better." Steals from Old; can increase promotion rate or Full GC risk. Assuming boxing is free — each Integer is a full object (16+ bytes) vs 4 bytes in int[] . Ignoring array header — small arrays cost disproportionate overhead. Disabling compressed oops on 8 GB heap — wastes memory for no benefit. Tuning GC before fixing unbounded Old-gen cache — collector can't fix a leak. Out of scope: full GC algorithms (S03), collector selection (S04), Metaspace/class loading (S06), escape analysis / scalar replacement detail (S07). 10. Revision Notes Young = Eden + S0 + S1; Old = tenured long-lived objects. Most objects die in Eden; survivors copy between Survivors then promote. TLAB = per-thread Eden slice; bump-pointer, lock-free for most new . Object = Mark Word + Klass + fields + padding; Mark holds GC age, hash, lock state. Compressed oops = 4-byte refs when heap ≤ ~32 GB (typical). Arrays add length field; primitive arrays dense, object arrays hold refs. Request DTOs → Young churn; caches/singletons → Old pressure. 11. Reasoning Exercises Service allocates 50 MB/s of short-lived JSON parsing objects. Old gen stable. Problem? Answer Often no structural problem. High Young GC rate expected. Tune only if pause times violate SLO. Reduce allocation (parser reuse, streaming) if CPU spent in GC is too high. -Xmx40g on 64-bit. Compressed oops still on? Answer Likely disabled — above ~32 GB threshold. Object headers and refs grow; factor into capacity planning. Two-field class: long id and boolean flag . Why might object be 24+ bytes not 17? Answer 16-byte header + 8-byte long + 1-byte boolean + padding to 8-byte alignment → 24 or 32 bytes depending on field order and JVM packing. Thread A and B each increment adjacent volatile long counters in one shared object. Low contention but slow. Cause? Answer False sharing — same cache line invalidated across cores. Not a lock issue. Stripe counters ( LongAdder ) or pad fields (M07). 12. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Default first allocation region for new object? Eden via thread TLAB. Old generation directly always. Metaspace next to class data. Survivor S0 before Eden always. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Eden via thread TLAB.) New instances start in Eden unless pre-tenured as humongous/large. TLAB provides fast thread-local bump allocation. Q2: Object survives third Young GC. Likely location? Active Survivor or promoting. Still only in Eden always. Code Cache as native copy. Stack frame of creator thread. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Active Survivor or promoting.) Live objects are copied from Eden/Survivor on each Young GC. After several survivals, promotion to Old is likely. Q3: TLAB main performance benefit? Avoid Eden lock on most news. Store static fields per thread. Skip garbage collection forever. Compress objects at alloc time. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Avoid Eden lock on most news.) Per-thread bump allocation in a private Eden slice removes global synchronization on the hot path. Q4: Mark Word stores which at unlock idle state? GC age and hash metadata. Full vtable method list copy. All instance field values. Bytecode of constructor body. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (GC age and hash metadata.) Normal state uses Mark Word for age, identity hash, and later lock encoding under contention. Q5: -XX:+UseCompressedOops typical limit driver? Heap size near thirty-two GB. Thread count exceeds core count. Metaspace exceeds one gigabyte. Direct memory exceeds Xmx value. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Heap size near thirty-two GB.) Compressed oops encode 32-bit offsets into heap base; above ~32 GB heap they are usually disabled. Q6: int[1_000_000] vs million Integer objects? Array one object — far less overhead. Both use identical heap bytes. Array stores in Metaspace only. Boxed form has no extra headers. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Array one object — far less overhead.) Primitive array: one header + 4M bytes payload. Boxed: ~1M objects each with 16+ byte headers. 13. Bridge to Next Lesson S03 — how Young/Old GC actually runs (copy, mark, STW phases) S04 — G1 vs ZGC vs Parallel — which matches your generational map Cross-link — Mark Word lock states tie to Synchronization & Monitors 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 3 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: Garbage Collection Fundamentals
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 2 · Lesson 3 of 8 · Lesson 4 → · Cheat sheet Garbage Collection Fundamentals ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on GC Roots & References , S02 Generations , Monitors Senior Interview Focus: Interviewers probe whether you understand reachability (not "delete when null"), what a pause actually blocks, and why a cache in a static Map is a GC problem not a "memory leak in C sense." You should explain Minor vs Major GC, reference strengths with when the collector acts, and why p99 latency often matters more than average throughput for APIs. Primary sources: Oracle — Java GC Introduction · Oracle — java.lang.ref · JVM Spec — GC Roots 1. Why GC Exists — Trade-offs Approach Pros Cons Manual (C/C++ free ) Predictable dealloc timing; no collector pauses Use-after-free, double-free, leaks — security + stability risk at scale Automatic (Java GC) Developer focuses on business logic; fewer dangling-pointer bugs Pause times, CPU overhead, non-deterministic reclamation timing Java bets: developer productivity and safety beat perfect determinism. Your job in production is to shape allocation and retention so GC stays within SLO — not to micromanage every free . 2. Reachability from GC Roots GC does not run when you assign null . It runs when memory pressure triggers a collection, then asks: is this object reachable from any GC root via strong references? You covered roots in Object Lifecycle . Production-complete root set: GC Root Example Why it matters Thread stacks Local refs in active stack frames Request-scoped objects alive while handler runs Static fields private static Map<K,V> CACHE Classic accidental retention — lives for JVM lifetime JNI global refs Native code holding Java objects Native libs can pin objects invisible to Java code Synchronized monitor refs Thread blocked in synchronized(obj) JVM keeps monitor object reachable while thread waits ( Lesson 2 ) Class loaders / JVM internals Loaded classes, JMX beans, some thread locals Metaspace + heap cross-links (S06 preview) void handle() { Order o = load(); // o reachable from stack root process(o); } // frame popped → o eligible unless retained elsewhere static List<Order> LOG = new ArrayList<>(); LOG.add(o); // now reachable from static root → never collected Unreachable ≠ immediately freed. Eligible for collection on next GC cycle in that generation. Visibility to other threads is a separate JMM topic — see volatile & JMM ; GC only cares about reference graph integrity at safepoint. 3. Reference Strengths — When the Collector Runs Each Expand oop-0005 with collector timing (not finalize): Strength Collected when Typical use Strong Never while reachable from roots Normal fields, locals, collections Soft ( SoftReference ) After heap is tight — collector clears soft refs before throwing OOM, usually after stronger refs processed Memory-sensitive caches (image thumbnails, parsed docs) — "keep until we need RAM back" Weak ( WeakReference ) Next GC cycle when only weakly reachable — regardless of heap fullness WeakHashMap keys, canonicalization maps, class loader adjacency Phantom ( PhantomReference ) After object finalized/deallocated — ref enqueued; get() always null Post-mortem cleanup via ReferenceQueue + Cleaner (off-heap resource release) Interview ordering: Strong survives longest → Soft cleared under memory pressure → Weak at next GC → Phantom signals "object memory gone, run cleanup action." 4. GC Phase Vocabulary All collectors compose variants of these ideas: Phase What happens Mark Traverse from roots; mark live objects Sweep Reclaim unmarked space; may leave fragmentation Compact Move live objects together; updates references; eliminates fragmentation Copy Copy live objects to fresh region; abandon old region in one go — no sweep fragmentation Copying vs Mark-Sweep-Compact Strategy Where used Trade-off Copying Young generation (Eden → Survivor) Fast when few survivors; needs spare space (from-space / to-space) Mark-Sweep-Compact Old generation (classic) Works in place; compact phase is costly (longer pauses) 5. Stop-The-World vs Concurrent Phases Stop-The-World (STW): all application mutator threads paused at safepoints. GC (or part of it) runs. Your API handlers literally stop making progress. Concurrent: GC threads work while app threads run — with barriers/bookkeeping so app and collector don't corrupt the heap. Still usually has some short STW phases. Pause = wall-clock time your service threads are frozen at safepoints. Metrics: Throughput — % time app runs vs GC (batch jobs care) Latency / p99 — tail pause hits slowest requests (APIs care) Enterprise framing: A 50 ms average pause sounds fine until p99 is 800 ms during Mixed GC — that's user-facing timeout territory. Measure pause distribution, not just mean. 6. Generational Hypothesis (Bridge from S02) Hypothesis: most objects die young; few survive long. Collect Young often — small live set, copying collector, short pause. Collect Old rarely — large graph, expensive mark/compact. Promotion — survivors age in Survivor spaces then move Old ( S02 ). 7. Minor GC vs Major / Full GC Term Typical scope Frequency / pause Minor / Young GC Eden + Survivors Often; usually milliseconds Major GC Old generation Less often; can be hundreds of ms+ Full GC Entire heap + often class metadata cleanup Rare in healthy apps; long STW — incident signal Naming caveat: logs vary by collector (G1 "Young" vs "Mixed" — S04). Fundamentals: know what generation is being collected and whether app threads paused. Healthy API service pattern: Minor GC ████░░░░████░░░░████ frequent, small pauses Major/Mixed GC ░░░░█░░░░░░█░░░ occasional, watch p99 Full GC ░░░░░░░░░░░█░░░░░░░ rare — investigate 8. Safepoints — Why Threads Must Pause From S01 : GC must see a consistent reference graph. If threads moved references mid-copy, the heap corrupts. JVM inserts safepoint polls in bytecode (loops, method returns, etc.). At safepoint, thread stack roots are frozen and scannable. Long counted loops without safepoint poll → "GC stuck waiting for thread" (rare but real in tight native/math loops). Thread dumps, deoptimization, and some lock operations also use safepoints — GC isn't the only reason. 9. Classic Bugs 9.1 Accidental retention Static collections — static List<Event> buffer never cleared; every event pinned until restart. Inner class holding outer — non-static inner holds implicit this$0 → entire outer graph retained. ThreadLocal leak (preview) — pool thread + ThreadLocal without remove() after request → previous request's graph stuck on thread. Brutal with Tomcat worker pools. Listener registries — forgot to unregister callback on shutdown. 9.2 Premature promotion Short-lived objects that survive one or two Young GCs due to timing (not true long-lived data) get promoted to Old. Old fills faster → more Major GC → longer pauses. Cause: allocation burst + unlucky GC timing, Survivor too small, -XX:MaxTenuringThreshold too low. Fix direction: reduce unnecessary retention in request path; tune Survivor/tenuring (S05) after proving with GC logs — not guesswork. 10. Enterprise — p99 Latency vs Throughput Workload GC priority Why REST / gRPC APIs Low pause (p99, p999) STW pause = stalled request; SLA breach on tail Batch ETL / report generation Throughput Total jobs/hour; occasional long pause OK if bounded Real-time pricing / gaming Hard pause ceiling Sub-10 ms pauses may matter — collector choice critical (S04) What seniors monitor: GC pause times (p99), allocation rate, promotion rate, Old gen occupancy trend, Full GC count. Alert on Full GC frequency, not every Minor GC. Out of scope: G1 vs ZGC comparison (S04), flag cookbook (S05), heap dump walkthrough (S08). JMM visibility — concurrency-0003 only. 11. Revision Notes GC reclaims unreachable objects, not "null" objects on demand. Roots: stacks, statics, JNI, monitors, JVM internals. Strong → Soft (memory pressure) → Weak (next GC) → Phantom (post-death queue). Mark / sweep / compact / copy — building blocks of all collectors. STW = app frozen; concurrent reduces but rarely eliminates pauses. Minor = Young; Major/Full = Old / whole heap — watch p99 not just average. Safepoints freeze stacks for consistent root scan. Static maps + ThreadLocal = classic retention; premature promotion fills Old. 12. Reasoning Exercises WeakHashMap used for session cache keyed by user. User logs out, no other refs. When is entry collected? Answer Key held via weak reference. Next GC when key only weakly reachable — entry can be reclaimed. Not instant on logout; on next GC cycle. For immediate eviction, remove explicitly or use TTL cache (Caffeine). Minor GC every second, 5 ms pause. Old gen flat. API p99 stable. Action? Answer Often none. Healthy short-lived allocation pattern from S02. Optimize only if GC CPU % too high or pauses grow. Don't chase Minor GC count alone. Thread pool worker holds ThreadLocal<Map> with request context, never remove() . Symptom? Answer Each reused thread retains prior requests' maps → Old gen grows, effective leak. Fix: finally { threadLocal.remove(); } or scoped context (VT era: prefer explicit propagation). SoftReference cache of 500 MB images. Heap fills. What happens before OOM? Answer GC clears soft references to reclaim memory — cache entries dropped progressively. OOM only if even after clearing soft refs there isn't enough heap for new strong allocations. 13. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Object eligible for GC when? No strong path from any root. Variable assigned null immediately. Method that created it returns only. finalize method has never run yet. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (No strong path from any root.) Reachability defines life. null and method return are common ways to break reachability, but collection happens later on GC cycle. Q2: WeakReference to object. Only weak refs remain. When collected? Next GC cycle regardless of heap. Only when heap is nearly full. Never until JVM shutdown. Immediately on last strong drop. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Next GC cycle regardless of heap.) Weak refs are cleared aggressively at GC. Soft refs wait for memory pressure. Q3: Young GC typically uses which strategy? Copy live objects to Survivor. Compact entire Old generation. Sweep Metaspace class bytes. Flush thread stacks to disk. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Copy live objects to Survivor.) Young gen copying collector exploits few survivors. Old gen uses mark-sweep-compact variants. Q4: Stop-the-world pause means what for API thread? Thread frozen at safepoint. Only GC threads stop running. Network sockets auto-close always. Heap is expanded without lock. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Thread frozen at safepoint.) Mutators pause so roots and heap are consistent. Request latency includes pause time. Q5: static HashMap grows forever in service. GC issue? Accidental retention from static root. WeakReference on every key by default. Objects move to Code Cache area. Minor GC cannot run while map exists. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Accidental retention from static root.) Static field is a GC root. All reachable entries stay alive — looks like leak, is retention. Q6: Backend API SLO on p99 latency. Metric first? GC pause p99 not average only. Young GC count per minute only. Total heap bytes allocated ever. Number of loaded classes only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (GC pause p99 not average only.) Tail pauses drive tail latency. Mean pause hides Mixed/Full GC spikes. 14. Bridge to Next Lesson S04 — G1, ZGC, Parallel — which collector matches your latency/throughput profile S05 — flags that connect to generations and pause goals S08 — when fundamentals say "retention bug," prove it with heap dump 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 2 · Lesson 4 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: Garbage Collectors & Selection
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 3 · Lesson 4 of 8 · Lesson 5 → · Cheat sheet Garbage Collectors & Selection ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on S03 GC Fundamentals , S01 Memory Map Senior Interview Focus: Can you name the default collector on JDK 21, explain when G1 Mixed GC fires, and why you'd pick ZGC over Parallel for a latency-sensitive API — without reciting 40 flags? Can you defend "defaults + measure first" on a new Spring Boot service in Kubernetes? Collectors are a product choice tied to SLO, heap size, and JDK version — not a religion. Primary sources: Oracle — Available Collectors (SE 21) · Oracle — G1 GC · Oracle — ZGC 1. Collector Families — Overview S03 taught mark/copy/STW vocabulary. Each collector implements those phases differently. Collector Goal Typical use JDK 21 status Serial Single-threaded, small footprint Embedded, tiny heaps, client-style apps Available ( -XX:+UseSerialGC ) Parallel (Throughput) Maximize GC throughput — parallel STW workers Batch jobs, ETL, offline compute — long pauses OK Available ( -XX:+UseParallelGC ) CMS Concurrent Old gen (legacy low-latency attempt) Deprecated — know it existed , replaced by G1/ZGC Removed in modern JDKs G1 (Garbage-First) Region-based, predictable pause target Default on server JDK 9+ for most heaps Default collector ZGC Sub-ms to low-ms pauses, scalable heap Latency-sensitive APIs, large heaps, JDK 15+ prod-ready Available ( -XX:+UseZGC ); generational ZGC evolving Shenandoah Concurrent compaction, low pause Similar niche to ZGC; OpenJDK / some vendors Available on supported builds ( -XX:+UseShenandoahGC ) Interview one-liner: "CMS is legacy — if someone says they tune CMS in 2025, ask which JDK they're actually on." 2. G1 — Default Workhorse G1 splits the heap into equal-sized regions (~1–32 MB, ergonomic). No fixed contiguous Young/Old layout — regions are labeled Eden, Survivor, or Old dynamically. 2.1 Key mechanics Young GC: collect all Eden + Survivor regions — copying live objects to new regions. STW, usually short. Concurrent marking: background phase tracks live data across Old regions between Young GCs. Mixed GC: collects some Old regions (highest garbage first — "Garbage-First") along with Young. STW but bounded by pause target. Humongous objects: larger than half a region → allocated in dedicated contiguous humongous regions in Old. Expensive; avoid huge single allocations when possible ( S02 ). G1 region map (simplified): [E][E][E][S][O][O][H][O][E][O]... Eden Sur Old Humongous Young GC → evacuate Eden+Survivor Mixed GC → Young + subset of Old regions (garbage-first) 2.2 Pause target -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 (default 200 ms) — goal, not guarantee. G1 adapts region collection set to try to stay near target. Tighter target → more frequent smaller collections → may reduce throughput. When Mixed GC hurts p99: Old regions with moderate live data → evacuation pauses spike. Fix retention / humongous objects before chasing flags (S05). 3. ZGC & Shenandoah — Low-Latency Collectors Both target pause times independent of heap size (within reason) — critical when heap is 16–64 GB+ and G1 Mixed GC pauses breach SLO. 3.1 ZGC (interview level) Colored pointers — metadata bits in reference encode GC state; concurrent threads use load barriers to see correct object version. Concurrent relocation — moves objects while app runs; short STW phases for root scanning / phase flip, not full heap copy. Pauses often sub-millisecond to a few ms on typical configs. JDK 21+: generational ZGC (improving young-object collection) — check release notes for your exact JDK; awareness matters in interviews. 3.2 Shenandoah (interview level) Concurrent compaction — Brooks forwarding pointers let app threads read objects while they move. Similar positioning: low pause, concurrent Old collection. Availability depends on JDK distribution (common in OpenJDK builds; verify vendor image). Senior trap: "ZGC uses no STW at all" — false. STW exists but is tiny; don't claim zero pauses. 4. Parallel GC — Throughput First Young: parallel copying STW. Old: parallel mark-sweep-compact STW. Maximizes application throughput (% time not in GC) on multi-core batch workers. Pauses scale with heap + live set — seconds possible on large Old gen. Pick when: offline jobs, report generation, no interactive SLA, plenty of cores, pauses scheduled off-peak. 5. Selection Matrix Factor Favor Notes Latency SLO (p99 < 100 ms) G1 default; ZGC/Shenandoah if Mixed GC spikes Measure pause distribution first Throughput / batch Parallel GC Accept STW pauses; maximize jobs/hour Heap < 4 GB, simple service G1 defaults usually fine Don't over-engineer collector choice Heap 32 GB+ API Evaluate ZGC G1 Mixed GC pause can grow with heap Container limit 512 MiB–2 GiB G1 + sensible -Xmx headroom ZGC has overhead at tiny heaps — verify benchmarks JDK version JDK 17 LTS / 21 LTS CMS gone; ZGC production-ready 15+; know your vendor build Humongous allocation pattern Fix allocation; then G1 or ZGC Large byte arrays bypass Eden benefits 6. When NOT to Tune Senior discipline beats flag shopping: New service, no prod data — use JDK defaults (G1 on 21). Ship. No GC logs or metrics — tuning blind is guessing. Retention bug present — collector won't fix static Map leak ( S03 ). Pause problem not proven — profile p99; maybe it's DB not GC. Copy-paste flags from blog — heap size, allocation rate, and JDK version differ. Correct order: measure → fix code/retention → set heap/container ratio → then collector/flags if SLO still breached. 7. JDK 21+ Defaults & Migration Notes Default collector: G1 ( -XX:+UseG1GC implicit on server-class machines). CMS: removed — migrate stories to G1 or ZGC. Parallel: opt-in for throughput workloads; was default pre-Java 9. ZGC: -XX:+UseZGC — strong for large low-latency heaps; generational mode improving young-gen efficiency (check JDK 21 release notes). Container awareness: JDK 10+ respects cgroup memory/CPU for default heap ergonomics — still validate -Xmx vs limit manually. Migration from Java 8: expect different GC log format (Unified JVM Logging — S05); G1 not Parallel; review pause profiles after upgrade. 8. Enterprise — Spring Boot on Kubernetes 8.1 Heap vs container memory # Example — 1 GiB pod limit JAVA_OPTS="-Xms512m -Xmx512m" # heap only # Leave ~256–400 MiB for Metaspace, threads, direct, native, Code Cache Rule: -Xmx ≈ 50–75% of cgroup limit for typical Spring + Netty services — validate with docker stats / cgroup metrics, not theory alone. 8.2 GC logging in prod (awareness — parsing in S05) Enable structured GC logs from day one on new services: -Xlog:gc*,gc+age=trace,safepoint:file=/var/log/gc.log:utctime,level,pid,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20M Correlate GC pause timestamps with APM p99 spikes. Alert on Full GC frequency, not every Young GC. Ship logs to centralized observability (ELK, Datadog, etc.) — flags only in S05. 8.3 Spring Boot specifics Actuator + Micrometer: JVM memory gauges, GC pause metrics (if binder configured). Virtual threads (Java 21): allocation pattern shifts — still G1 default; monitor Young GC rate. Don't set exotic GC flags in application.properties — JVM opts belong in container env / entrypoint. Out of scope: exhaustive flag catalog (S05), line-by-line log parsing (S05), classloader leaks (S06), async-profiler (S08). 9. Revision Notes Serial — tiny; Parallel — throughput; CMS — legacy dead. G1 — region-based default; Young + Mixed GC; humongous regions; pause goal . ZGC / Shenandoah — concurrent low pause; colored pointers / forwarding (concept level). Pick collector from SLO + heap + JDK — measure before tuning. K8s: -Xmx < container limit; GC logs from day one. JDK 21 default = G1; ZGC opt-in for latency at scale. 10. Reasoning Exercises Batch nightly job, 8 GB heap, 4 s GC pause acceptable at 2 AM. Collector? Answer Parallel GC — maximize throughput; pauses off-peak acceptable. G1/ZGC overhead not justified unless pause causes job overrun. API p99 120 ms SLO, 24 GB heap, G1 Mixed GC pauses 300 ms. Next step? Answer Measure allocation + retention first. If code clean, trial ZGC on JDK 21. Don't only tighten MaxGCPauseMillis — it's a goal not a cap. 512 MiB K8s pod, -Xmx480m . OOMKilled. GC issue? Answer Probably not GC algorithm — off-heap exceeded cgroup ( S01 ). Lower -Xmx to ~60% of limit; check direct memory / thread stacks. Candidate says "we use CMS for low latency." Red flag? Answer Yes if on JDK 17+. CMS removed. Story may be stale or mislabeled — likely G1 or ZGC in practice. Probe JDK version and actual flags. 11. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Default GC on JDK 21 server JVM? G1 Garbage-First collector. Parallel throughput collector. Concurrent Mark Sweep only. Serial single-thread collector. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (G1 Garbage-First collector.) G1 is default since Java 9 on server-class machines. Parallel and ZGC are opt-in. Q2: G1 Mixed GC collects which regions? Young plus some Old regions. Only Eden on every cycle. Metaspace class metadata bytes. Entire heap every single time. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Young plus some Old regions.) Mixed GC reclaims garbage-heavy Old regions alongside Young evacuation — bounded by pause target. Q3: MaxGCPauseMillis on G1 guarantees what? Soft pause target not hard cap. Zero stop-the-world ever again. Heap cannot grow past value. Young gen size fixed in bytes. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Soft pause target not hard cap.) G1 uses the value to guide collection set sizing. Spikes still possible under pressure. Q4: ZGC primary interview-level mechanism? Colored pointers concurrent relocate.
