Only serial mark-sweep Old gen. Disables all safepoint pauses. Stores objects in Metaspace only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Colored pointers concurrent relocate.) ZGC uses pointer metadata and load barriers for concurrent relocation with short STW phase changes. Q5: Best first step before changing collector? Measure GC pauses and retention. Copy random flags from blog post. Disable GC with experimental flag. Set Xmx equal container limit. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Measure GC pauses and retention.) Defaults are fine until data proves otherwise. Fix leaks and allocation before collector swaps. Q6: Humongous object in G1 means? Larger than half a G1 region. Any object in Eden TLAB slice. Static field in Metaspace block. Thread stack frame over one MB. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Larger than half a G1 region.) Humongous objects get dedicated Old regions — costly path; avoid if possible. 12. Bridge to Next Lesson S05 — flag cookbook + GC log reading for the collector you chose S03 retention bugs — fix before ZGC will save you S08 — when logs show long pauses + growing Old, heap dump proves why 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 3 · Lesson 5 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: JVM Flags, GC Logging & Tuning
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 4 · Lesson 5 of 8 · Lesson 6 → · Cheat sheet JVM Flags, GC Logging & Tuning ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on S04 Collector Choice , S01 OOM Map , Stack vs Heap Senior Interview Focus: Can you read a unified GC log line and extract pause time, cause, and heap before/after? Can you explain why prod sets -Xms = -Xmx and why a 32 GB bare-metal heap config kills a 2 GB pod? Flags are levers — interviewers want judgment: measure first, tune second, fix retention before either. Primary sources: Oracle — java command (SE 21) · Unified JVM Logging · Oracle — G1 Tuning 1. Heap Sizing — -Xms / -Xmx Flag Meaning Prod note -Xms Initial heap size JVM may grow heap from here up to -Xmx -Xmx Maximum heap size Hard cap for object heap — not total process memory Why equal -Xms = -Xmx in production Avoids repeated heap resize cycles as load ramps — resize can trigger extra GC and OS allocation churn. Predictable memory footprint for capacity planning and K8s resource requests. Eliminates "heap still growing" surprises during traffic spike. Dev laptops may use smaller -Xms to save RAM. Prod APIs: set both to the same validated value. Container: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage JDK 10+ reads cgroup memory limit and can derive heap ergonomically: -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=75.0 Percentage of container-detected RAM — not host RAM. Still leaves room for Metaspace, stacks, direct memory, native GC structures ( S01 ). Don't set 100%. 50–75% common for Spring + Netty; validate with metrics. Explicit -Xmx overrides percentage-based defaults when both set — know precedence on your JDK. 12-factor trap: copying -Xmx32g from bare-metal into a 2 GiB K8s pod → instant OOMKill. Size for the container . 2. Metaspace — -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize Class metadata lives off-heap in Metaspace — not counted in -Xmx . By default Metaspace grows until OS limit — unbounded growth can OOMKill the process. -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m — hard cap; fail fast with OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace instead of silent cgroup kill. When it blows up: Spring fat classpath, Hibernate enhancement, bytecode agents (APM, Mockito inline), dynamic proxies, Groovy/scripting, hot redeploy without restart. Fix: classloader leak investigation (S06), not bigger -Xmx . 3. GC Logging — Unified JVM Logging ( -Xlog ) Java 9+ replaced legacy -XX:+PrintGCDetails with unified logging. Enable from day one: -Xlog:gc*,gc+heap=debug,gc+age=trace,safepoint:file=/var/log/gc.log:utctime,level,pid,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20M 3.1 What to extract from a log line Example G1 Young GC (simplified — format varies slightly by JDK): [2026-09-15T10:23:01.456+0000][info][gc] GC(142) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 142M->48M(512M) 12.345ms Field Meaning GC(142) GC cycle number — correlate across log Pause Young (Normal) / Mixed Cause / type — Young vs Mixed vs Full 142M->48M(512M) Heap before → after (capacity) — live set dropped 142→48 MB of 512 MB cap 12.345ms Pause time — STW duration for this event 3.2 Reading for incidents Pause time trending up + heap after GC rising → retention / Old gen filling ( S03 ). Frequent Full GC with tiny reclaim → leak or heap undersized for live set. Humongous allocations — look for humongous tags in detailed G1 logs. Correlate GC timestamp with APM trace p99 — prove GC caused latency spike. 4. Key G1 Knobs — What They Do (Not Gospel Recipes) You chose G1 in S04 . Interviewers ask what these mean — not "always set X": Flag / concept What it does Tuning caution -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis Soft pause goal G1 adapts toward (default 200) Lower = more frequent GC, may hurt throughput; not a hard cap -XX:G1HeapRegionSize Size of each G1 region (1–32 MB, power of 2) Larger regions → fewer regions but bigger humongous threshold IHOP ( InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent ) Old gen occupancy % that starts concurrent marking cycle Too low → marking overhead; too high → Mixed GC rushed under pressure -XX:G1MixedGCCountTarget Spread Old region reclaim across N Mixed GCs Smoother pauses vs longer reclaim tail -XX:ParallelGCThreads / ConcGCThreads STW worker count / concurrent marker threads Match CPU limits in K8s — don't assume all host cores Senior rule: change one knob at a time under representative load . Document before/after pause p99 and throughput. 5. When Tuning Helps vs Hurts Tuning helps Tuning hurts / wastes time Proven GC pauses breach SLO after code is clean Retention leak still present — flags mask symptoms Heap consistently at cap with healthy reclaim pattern Copy-paste flags from different heap size / workload Load test reproduces prod allocation rate Tuning on idle dev laptop Collector swap (G1 → ZGC) with metrics baseline 20 flags changed at once — impossible to attribute Correct sequence: enable GC logs → load test → fix retention/allocation → set heap/container ratio → adjust pause goal or collector → individual G1 knobs last. 6. OOM Types — Map to Fix Expand S01 triage table for on-call: Error Pool First fix direction Java heap space -Xmx heap Heap dump, find dominator tree, paginate, bound caches; raise -Xmx only if live set is legitimate Metaspace Class metadata Classloader leak, agents, dynamic codegen; MaxMetaspaceSize as guardrail unable to create native thread OS thread budget Bounded pools, VT for I/O, lower -Xss , raise ulimit Direct buffer memory Off-heap NIO Netty pool sizing, MaxDirectMemorySize , fix missing release GC overhead limit exceeded GC spending >98% time with <2% reclaim Heap too small for live set or severe leak — not "tune IHOP" 7. OutOfMemoryError vs StackOverflowError From Stack vs Heap : OutOfMemoryError — a memory pool exhausted (heap, Metaspace, direct, native threads). JVM may continue if only one thread failed allocation — often process unhealthy soon after. StackOverflowError — thread's stack exceeded depth limit (infinite recursion, deep XML/JSON). Not heap. Fix algorithm / use iterative parser. Flag: -Xss increases stack per thread — multiplies across thread count. void recurse() { recurse(); } // StackOverflowError — stack frames, not heap List<byte[]> leak = new ArrayList<>(); while (true) leak.add(new byte[10_000_000]); // OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space 8. Enterprise — 12-Factor JVM in Docker Config in environment — JAVA_OPTS / JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in K8s manifest, not baked into JAR. Stateless processes — heap doesn't assume local disk; logs to stdout/file with rotation sidecar. Port binding — one JVM per container; resources match resources.limits.memory . Disposability — fast startup; don't need 10 min heap warm-up if -Xms = -Xmx . Dev/prod parity — same major JDK, same collector family, similar heap ratio (not same absolute GB). Starter template (2 GiB pod, Spring API) ENV JAVA_OPTS="\ -XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0 \ -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50.0 \ -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \ -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \ -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heapdump.hprof \ -Xlog:gc*:file=/tmp/gc.log:utctime,level,tags:filecount=3,filesize=10M" Adjust percentages after observing RSS in staging. Add -XX:+UseZGC only after G1 data proves need ( S04 ). Out of scope: custom GC implementation, JFR full course (S08), Spring Actuator metrics catalog (M05). 9. Revision Notes Prod: -Xms = -Xmx for stable footprint. Containers: MaxRAMPercentage — never 100%; validate off-heap headroom. MaxMetaspaceSize — guardrail for class metadata; fix loader leaks. GC logs: pause time, cause, before→after heap. G1 knobs: pause goal, region size, IHOP — understand before changing. Tune under load; fix retention first. OOM message tells which pool; StackOverflow = stack not heap. 10. Reasoning Exercises GC log: Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 890M->885M(1024M) 4200ms . Interpretation? Answer Full GC reclaimed only 5 MB in 4.2 s — live set ~885 MB near 1 GB cap. Likely leak or legitimately huge live set. Heap dump before raising -Xmx . -Xmx raised 4→8 GB. Metaspace OOM continues. Next? Answer Wrong pool. Investigate class loading / agents / classloader retention. Set MaxMetaspaceSize to fail fast while debugging. Dev sets MaxGCPauseMillis=50 on batch job. Throughput drops 30%. Why? Answer Aggressive pause goal → more frequent, smaller collections → more GC CPU overhead. Batch may prefer Parallel GC or default 200 ms goal. 2 GiB pod, MaxRAMPercentage=90 , OOMKilled no Java OOM. Cause? Answer Heap ~1.8 GiB leaves almost nothing for Metaspace, threads, direct, native. cgroup kills process. Lower to ~50–60%. 11. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Why set -Xms equal -Xmx in prod? Avoid heap resize churn at ramp. Disable garbage collection fully. Force Metaspace into heap area. Required for compressed oops only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Avoid heap resize churn at ramp.) Fixed heap size gives predictable memory and avoids growth-triggered GC during load increase. Q2: MaxRAMPercentage applies to what? Container-detected memory limit. Host physical RAM always only. Metaspace size cap exclusively. Per-thread stack size bytes. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Container-detected memory limit.) JDK reads cgroup limit to derive ergonomic heap sizing in containers. Q3: GC log 200M->80M(512M) 15ms means? Heap shrank live set in pause. Metaspace was fully cleared. Stack overflow was recovered. Thread count dropped by half. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Heap shrank live set in pause.) Before→after heap usage of 512M capacity; 15ms STW pause for that GC event. Q4: IHOP on G1 controls what? When concurrent marking starts. Thread stack depth maximum. TLAB size per thread bytes. Direct buffer pool cap limit. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (When concurrent marking starts.) Initiating Heap Occupancy Percent triggers concurrent mark based on Old gen fill level. Q5: StackOverflowError indicates failure in? Thread call stack depth. Java heap object allocation. Metaspace class metadata. Direct byte buffer off-heap. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Thread call stack depth.) Stack overflow is per-thread stack — recursion or deep parsing. Not heap OOM. Q6: First step before aggressive GC flag tuning? Load test with GC logs enabled. Set Xmx to host RAM size. Disable all safepoint polls. Switch to Serial GC always. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Load test with GC logs enabled.) Measure pause distribution and retention under representative load before changing knobs. 12. Bridge to Next Lesson S06 — class loaders & Metaspace leaks behind Metaspace OOM S08 — heap dumps, MAT, JFR when logs prove retention S04 — collector swap only after logs + load test baseline 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 4 · Lesson 6 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: Class Loading, Metaspace & Classloader Leaks
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 5 · Lesson 6 of 8 · Lesson 7 → · Cheat sheet Class Loading, Metaspace & Classloader Leaks ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on S01 Metaspace , static & clinit , Init Order , S05 MaxMetaspaceSize Senior Interview Focus: Can you walk through class loading phases and say exactly when <clinit> runs? Can you explain why redeploying a WAR 200 times without restart blows Metaspace — and why raising -Xmx won't help? Know delegation, when SPI breaks it, and the three classic classloader leak patterns (ThreadLocal, JDBC drivers, redeploy). Primary sources: JVM Spec — Loading, Linking, Initialization · Oracle — ClassLoader · Oracle — Class Loaders 1. Class Loading Phases Before any new Foo() , the JVM must load class Foo . Three high-level phases: Phase What happens Interview note Loading Find bytecode (.class / JAR), define Klass structure in Metaspace, create java.lang.Class mirror on heap Binary name → bytes → metadata Linking Verify bytecode safety · Prepare static fields (defaults, no user code) · Resolve symbolic refs (may be lazy) Verification is not "run your static block" yet Initialization Execute <clinit> — static field assignments + static blocks in source order First active use triggers this (below) Parent class initialized before child. Interfaces initialized when a class implementing them is initialized (rules have edge cases — parent-first is the safe interview answer). 2. When <clinit> Runs — Tie to Static Blocks From static lesson : static blocks compile into one <clinit> method. Runs once per class per defining class loader . Triggers initialization (first active use): new MyClass() — instance creation Access static field declared in class (not inherited without override confusion) Invoke static method declared in class Class.forName("com.app.Config") — with initialization (default) Reflection on class for first time in certain operations Does NOT trigger child init alone: Creating array new MyClass[10] — loads MyClass but does not run <clinit> Accessing static field that is compile-time constant ( static final primitive or String literal) — may be inlined without loading class public class Config { static { System.out.println("clinit"); } // runs once on first active use } // First call prints "clinit": Config.getUrl(); // Array — no clinit: Config[] arr = new Config[10]; Failed <clinit> → ExceptionInInitializerError ; later use → NoClassDefFoundError . 3. Classloader Hierarchy & Delegation Bootstrap (null in Java API) — rt/java.base, core JDK classes ↑ Platform (Extension) — JDK modules / endorsed libs ↑ Application (System) — your classpath / -cp / JAR ↑ Custom loaders — Tomcat Webapp, Spring nested JAR, OSGi bundle Delegation model (default): child asks parent to load first. Parent can't → child tries. Ensures java.lang.String always comes from bootstrap — security + single definition. Loader Loads Bootstrap java.* , core modules — C++ inside JVM; ClassLoader.getParent() returns null Platform JDK modules not in bootstrap (historical "extension") Application Your app classpath — ClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader() Custom Per-deploy unit — Tomcat WebappClassLoader , plugin frameworks 4. Breaking Delegation — SPI & Fat JARs Default delegation fails when parent needs classes implemented by child : Service Provider Interface (SPI): ServiceLoader — JDBC drivers, logging backends. Parent API ( java.sql.Driver ) in bootstrap; implementation in app JAR. META-INF/services/ registration. Spring Boot fat JAR: nested JARs use custom LaunchedURLClassLoader — parent-last or modified delegation so app libs don't clash with embedded container. Deep internals → M05; interview: "Boot doesn't use plain AppClassLoader on flat classpath." OSGi / JPMS (awareness): module boundaries and explicit exports break naive single hierarchy — know name for interview breadth. 5. Class.forName vs ClassLoader.loadClass API Initialization? Typical use Class.forName("com.foo.Bar") Yes — runs <clinit> JDBC Class.forName(driver) — register driver static block Class.forName(name, false, loader) No if second arg false Load without triggering static init loader.loadClass("com.foo.Bar") No — link only, defer init Frameworks that want control over init timing Interview trap: "loadClass and forName are the same" — false. forName initializes by default; loadClass does not. 6. Metaspace vs PermGen (Pre-Java 8) PermGen (Java 7−) Metaspace (Java 8+) Location Fixed region inside JVM heap Native memory — not in -Xmx Growth Fixed max — -XX:MaxPermSize Grows with loaded classes; -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize cap OOM message PermGen space Metaspace Interview story "Hot redeploy + class versions = PermGen OOM" Same leak pattern — different pool name Metaspace fixed the "tiny fixed PermGen" problem but did not fix classloader leaks . Unlimited growth → cgroup OOMKill if no MaxMetaspaceSize . 7. Classloader Leaks — Classic Patterns A classloader is collectible only when no strong references to it exist and all its loaded classes are unreachable. Leaks pin the entire loader graph + all its classes in Metaspace. 7.1 Redeploy without restart Tomcat / app server creates new WebappClassLoader per deploy. Old loader should die. If something still references old loader → old classes never unloaded → Metaspace stair-steps up each deploy. 7.2 ThreadLocal + loaded class // Request filter sets ThreadLocal holding UserContext from webapp classloader threadLocal.set(new UserContext()); // Pool thread reused — never threadLocal.remove() // Thread holds ref → ThreadLocalMap → Value → Class from OLD loader Brutal in servlet thread pools. Fix: finally { threadLocal.remove(); } . Virtual threads: same discipline ( M03 L8 ). 7.3 JDBC driver registration Legacy pattern: driver JAR static block registers with DriverManager (held by bootstrap/system refs). Redeploy loads new driver class; old driver + loader pinned. Modern: JDBC 4+ SPI ( META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver ) + DriverManager.deregisterDriver on shutdown; use connection pool that manages lifecycle. 7.4 Other common pins Custom shutdown hooks referencing webapp classes Static singletons in container scope referencing old context Thread started by old deployment still running APM / Hibernate bytecode agents holding transformed class refs 8. When Can a ClassLoader Be GC'd? No strong references to the ClassLoader instance No strong references to any Class objects it defined No threads have stack frames executing methods from those classes All instances of loaded classes unreachable Metaspace for that loader's metadata reclaimed when loader is collected — not before. This is why one stray ThreadLocal can retain megabytes of class metadata . 9. Enterprise Patterns Scenario Classloading impact Practice Spring Boot fat JAR Custom loader, nested JARs, many classes at startup Accept one-time Metaspace footprint; avoid duplicate agent instrumentation Dev hot-reload (Spring DevTools, JRebel) Reloads classes / loaders frequently Dev-only; restart periodically; never compare dev Metaspace to prod Prod Stable loader tree No redeploy-without-restart on long-lived pods — roll new pod instead (K8s) Hibernate / bytecode enhancement Runtime-generated subclasses (proxies) More classes in Metaspace; monitor MaxMetaspaceSize APM agents (Datadog, New Relic) Instrument every loaded class Agent overhead + Metaspace; align agent version with JDK K8s framing: immutable deployments → new pod = fresh JVM = clean loaders. Metaspace leaks from redeploy are a **app-server-on-long-lived-JVM** smell more than stateless K8s — but ThreadLocal + pool threads still bite everywhere. Out of scope: bytecode verification algorithms, ASM/Javassist, deep LaunchedURLClassLoader (M05), JPMS encyclopedia. 10. Revision Notes Load → link (verify, prepare, resolve) → init ( <clinit> ). Init on first active use; arrays don't run clinit. Bootstrap → Platform → Application; parent delegation default. SPI / fat JAR break naive delegation. forName initializes; loadClass does not. PermGen story = Metaspace story with different pool name. Leaks: redeploy, ThreadLocal, JDBC drivers, long-lived threads. Loader GC'd only when zero strong refs to loader + its classes. 11. Reasoning Exercises Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") in static app init. Side effect? Answer Runs driver <clinit> — registers with DriverManager . Needed for legacy explicit load; JDBC 4+ SPI often makes this unnecessary. 200 Tomcat redeploys, Metaspace 2 GB, heap stable. Cause? Answer Classloader leak — old WebappClassLoader instances pinned. Find ThreadLocal, threads, DriverManager, shutdown hooks. Restart JVM or fix leak; -Xmx irrelevant. new Config[100] — does Config clinit run? Answer No. Array creation loads class for element type but does not initialize it. No static blocks execute. Child class first accessed. Parent clinit order? Answer Parent <clinit> runs first , then child. Superclass static state ready before subclass static init. 12. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Static block runs in which loading phase? Initialization after linking. Loading before bytes read. Verify step of linking only. Every new object constructor. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Initialization after linking.) Static blocks compile to <clinit> executed during class initialization, not during load or verify alone. Q2: Default classloader delegation order? Parent asked to load first. Child always loads before parent. Bootstrap loads application classes. No hierarchy on JDK twenty-one. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Parent asked to load first.) Child delegates up so core JDK classes have single bootstrap definition. Q3: loadClass vs forName default difference? forName runs clinit by default. loadClass always runs clinit first. Both skip initialization always. forName only works for arrays. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (forName runs clinit by default.) ClassLoader.loadClass resolves without initializing. Class.forName(name) initializes unless initialize flag is false. Q4: Java eight plus class metadata lives in? Metaspace native memory area. Fixed PermGen inside heap. Eden young generation only. Per-thread stack frames only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Metaspace native memory area.) PermGen removed in Java 8. Metaspace is off-heap; capped with MaxMetaspaceSize . Q5: Classic redeploy Metaspace leak cause? Old classloader still referenced. Heap Xmx set far too low. Too many Eden TLAB slices. Compressed oops disabled only. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Old classloader still referenced.) Pinned loader retains all its class metadata. ThreadLocal and JDBC registration are frequent culprits. Q6: new Foo[50] triggers Foo clinit? No — array creation skips init. Yes — same as new Foo(). Only if Foo has static block. Only on JDK eight and older. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (No — array creation skips init.) Array creation loads the element class but does not run static initialization. 13. Bridge to Next Lessons S07 — JIT, escape analysis (more generated code / compile artifacts) S08 — heap dump won't show Metaspace class leak; use class histogram / native memory tracking M05 — Spring Boot classloader and nested JAR loading detail 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 5 · Lesson 7 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: JIT Compilation & Runtime Optimizations
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 6 · Lesson 7 of 8 · Lesson 8 → · Cheat sheet JIT Compilation & Runtime Optimizations ~35 minutes · ties to mission · builds on final & JIT hints , Escape Analysis , Stream JIT fusion , TLAB Senior Interview Focus: Can you explain why the first 10k requests after deploy are slower than hour-two traffic? Can you describe tiered compilation, what OSR is, and why polymorphic call sites cause deoptimization? Know escape analysis at interview depth — not C2 IR graphs. Primary sources: Oracle — JVM Compilers · OpenJDK — Tiered Compilation · JMH — Java Microbenchmark Harness 1. Interpreter → C1 → C2 — Why Warmup Matters Bytecode starts in the interpreter — correct, flexible, slow. HotSpot profiles execution and compiles hot code to native machine code via JIT compilers: Tier Compiler Trade-off Interpreter None Startup fast; steady-state slow C1 ("client") Quick compile, light optimizations Fast compile time; decent speed C2 ("server") Slow compile, aggressive optimizations Best peak throughput/latency after warmup Tiered compilation (default on server JVM): method starts interpreted → C1 compiles quickly → if still hot, promoted to C2 with deeper analysis. You pay compile CPU upfront for faster hot loops later. Prod reality: cold JVM after deploy = interpreter + first C1/C2 compiles. p99 drops after warmup. Serverless scale-from-zero amplifies this. 2. Hot Methods, Thresholds & OSR Hot method: invocation counter crosses threshold → scheduled for compilation. Compilation threshold: ergonomics flags like -XX:CompileThreshold / tiered thresholds — JVM adapts; don't memorize numbers, know concept . OSR (On-Stack Replacement): long-running loop still in interpreter mid-method → JVM compiles loop body and replaces active stack frame without waiting for method exit. Critical for hot loops inside rarely-called methods. Normal compile: method exits interpreter → C2 native code next entry OSR: long loop running in interpreter → compile loop → swap frame in-place 3. Key Optimizations (Interview Level) 3.1 Inlining Replace callee with callee body at call site — eliminates call overhead, enables further opts. HotSpot inlines small hot methods aggressively. You saw the effect in Stream Internals : fused pipeline can become one tight loop. 3.2 Devirtualization Virtual call animal.speak() normally uses vtable dispatch. If profiler sees one implementation (monomorphic) or stable dominant type, JIT may inline direct call — huge win. Tie final methods/classes : final methods cannot be overridden → compiler/JIT knows target at compile time for those callsites. 3.3 Dead code elimination & constant folding Unreachable branches removed. static final compile-time constants inlined at use site. 3.4 Loop unrolling Duplicate loop body iterations to reduce branch overhead — classic C2 transform on counted loops. 3.5 Lock elision (preview) If JIT proves lock never contends (escape analysis + biased locking history), synchronized block may be stripped in compiled code. Not a license to skip synchronization — proof can fail → deopt. 4. Deoptimization — When Speculation Fails JIT optimizes based on observed runtime behavior . Assumptions baked into compiled code: Call site always hits Dog — then Cat appears → deoptimization Field never changed — then reflection or another thread mutates → deopt Lock elision invalid — contention appears → revert to locking Deoptimization: discard optimized native code, return affected threads to interpreter (or recompile with new profile). Causes latency spike — "perf cliff" when workload changes. Pattern JIT assumption Failure trigger Monomorphic callsite Single receiver type 2+ types at same callsite (megamorphic) Inlined virtual method Stable target New subclass loaded / different receiver Scalar-replaced object Object doesn't escape Reference stored to heap / returned 5. Escape Analysis & Scalar Replacement From Stack vs Heap : not all objects need heap allocation. Escape analysis: JIT analyzes if object reference leaves method/thread scope: No escape — object only used locally, not returned, not stored in field, not passed to unknown code Scalar replacement — object fields become local variables (registers/stack slots); new Point(x,y) may never hit heap/TLAB at all Stack allocation (term often used) — fields live in frame, not as heap object shell int sumOfPairs(List<Pair> data) { int total = 0; for (Pair p : data) { Point local = new Point(p.x, p.y); // may not allocate on heap if JIT proves no escape total += local.x + local.y; } return total; } Limits: large objects, escaping refs, debug flags off, unpredictable aliasing — allocation may still happen. Don't write "micro-benchmark clever" code expecting escape; measure. 6. JIT Logs — Awareness Only Unified logging can surface compilation events (exact tags vary by JDK): -Xlog:jit+compilation=info Legacy (older material still in interviews): -XX:+PrintCompilation You'll see method signatures, compile level (e.g. 3 = C2), and OSR markers. Full flag cookbook not goal — know logs exist for "is this method compiled yet?" 7. Enterprise — Cold Start & Benchmarking 7.1 Cold start (K8s / serverless) New pod: class loading + interpreter + JIT compile storm + Spring context init First N requests pay warmup tax — autoscaling policies must account for this Mitigations: readiness probes that warm critical paths, AOT/native image (GraalVM — mention only), keeping min replicas > 0 7.2 Benchmark after warmup — JMH nod Never trust a single main() loop timing: JMH — warms up JIT, forks JVMs, avoids dead-code elimination traps Measure after warmup iterations; report percentiles Microbenchmark ≠ production — allocation rate, GC, and concurrency differ 7.3 What seniors watch Latency drop after deploy plateau (warmup curve) Deoptimization spikes when traffic pattern changes (new code path, new types) Code Cache fill — too many compiled methods → sweeps/recompiles ( S01 ) GraalVM / Native Image: ahead-of-time compile trades peak JIT optimality for instant startup — different trade-off space; not default HotSpot path. Out of scope: C2 IR graphs, assembly reading, Module 07 perf engineering depth, GraalVM as primary lesson. 8. Revision Notes Interpreter → C1 → C2 tiered; warmup required for peak perf. OSR compiles hot loops inside long methods. Inlining + devirtualization = big wins on monomorphic calls. Deopt when profile assumptions break (polymorphism). Escape analysis → scalar replacement may skip heap alloc. Cold start hurts serverless/K8s scale-from-zero. Benchmark with JMH after warmup — not naive loops. 9. Reasoning Exercises Deploy new version. p99 200 ms first 5 min, then 40 ms steady. GC normal. Explain? Answer JIT warmup — hot paths moving interpreter → C1 → C2. Also possible class data cache warming. Not necessarily a bug. Interface method with 5 implementations called randomly at one callsite. Inlining? Answer Megamorphic — JIT unlikely to inline all targets. Virtual dispatch remains. Deopt if earlier monomorphic assumption breaks. final class method called from known type. Devirtualization easier? Answer Yes. No subclasses → stable target. JIT can inline aggressively (oop-0015). Lambda in hot stream pipeline never escapes intermediate objects. Heap allocation? Answer JIT may fuse + escape-analyze — fewer heap objects than naive reading ( streams-0006 ). Not guaranteed; measure under load. 10. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: Why first requests after deploy slower? Interpreter plus JIT not warmed. GC disabled until ten minutes. Heap fixed at one megabyte. Metaspace cleared every request. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Interpreter plus JIT not warmed.) Bytecode runs interpreted until hot methods compile to native code. Tiered compilation takes time. Q2: OSR primarily helps which case? Hot loop inside rare method. Static clinit running once. Class loading verify phase. Metaspace cap exceeded event. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Hot loop inside rare method.) On-Stack Replacement compiles and swaps an active long-running loop without waiting for method return. Q3: Deoptimization triggered when? JIT assumption no longer holds. Any Young GC cycle runs. Thread enters WAITING state. Compressed oops turned off. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (JIT assumption no longer holds.) e.g. monomorphic callsite becomes megamorphic. Optimized code discarded; interpreter or recompile. Q4: Escape analysis enables what? Scalar replace non-escaping object. Move static fields to stack. Skip class loading entirely. Disable garbage collection. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Scalar replace non-escaping object.) If object doesn't escape scope, fields may live in registers/locals without heap allocation. Q5: C2 vs C1 trade-off? C2 slower compile deeper opts. C1 never compiles any code. C2 only runs in interpreter. C1 replaces garbage collector. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (C2 slower compile deeper opts.) C1 compiles fast with lighter optimizations. C2 spends more compile time for aggressive peak performance. Q6: Reliable microbenchmark practice? JMH with warmup iterations. Single main timing loop only. Measure before any classes load. Disable tiered compilation always. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (JMH with warmup iterations.) JMH accounts for JIT warmup and JVM pitfalls. Naive loops mislead. 11. Bridge to Next Lesson S08 — when JIT/GC tuning can't explain it: heap dumps, JFR, async-profiler M07 — systematic perf engineering beyond interview JIT overview Streams / final — design for monomorphic hot paths; don't fight the optimizer 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 6 · Lesson 8 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: Diagnostics, Profiling & Memory Leaks
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 7 · Lesson 8 of 8 · Cheat sheet · ➡️ Capstone Exercise Diagnostics, Profiling & Memory Leaks ~40 minutes · Module 04 capstone · ties to S01–S07 , Thread Dumps , Pool Exhaustion , Locks Senior Interview Focus: Under incident pressure, can you pick the right tool in 30 seconds? Thread dump for "all threads stuck" — GC logs for pause spikes — heap histogram/dump for growing Old gen. Can you walk an interviewer through latency spike → thread dump + GC log + histogram without opening MAT? Know leak patterns cold; production discipline: reproduce, one change, keep logs. Primary sources: Oracle — jcmd · Oracle — Troubleshooting Guide · Eclipse MAT — Concepts 1. Diagnostic Toolbox Map Tool Command / entry Answers jps jps -l Which Java PIDs are running? Main class / JAR name jcmd jcmd <pid> help Swiss army knife — thread dump, GC heap info, VM flags, JFR start (preferred modern entry) jstat jstat -gc <pid> 1s Live GC pool sizes, GC counts, pause times — lightweight monitoring jstack jstack <pid> or jcmd <pid> Thread.print Thread dump — what every thread is doing, lock states jmap jmap -histo:live <pid> , jmap -dump Heap histogram (class instance counts) or full heap dump file Modern preference: jcmd over legacy tools where equivalent. In K8s: kubectl exec into pod, find PID, run jcmd — or capture via sidecar/agent. 2. Thread Dump Reading You met thread dumps in Thread Fundamentals . Under incident, scan for patterns: State Often means Action BLOCKED Waiting to enter synchronized monitor Find "waiting to lock <0x...>" and who holds that lock ( S02 ) WAITING wait() , park , join — no timeout Trace park target; pool queue empty? TIMED_WAITING Sleep, timed wait, lock timeout Check if stuck in slow I/O or lock tryLock timeout loop RUNNABLE Runnable or in native (socket read, JDBC) Many at socketRead0 → downstream slowness, not CPU "pool-3-thread-1" #42 prio=5 os_prio=0 BLOCKED waiting to lock <0x00000000e1234567> (a com.app.Cache) at com.app.Cache.get(Cache.java:88) ... "http-nio-8080-exec-5" #31 RUNNABLE at java.net.SocketInputStream.socketRead0(Native Method) at org.postgresql.jdbc.PgStream.receive(...) Pool exhaustion ( Executors ): all worker threads BLOCKED or in I/O → queue grows → timeouts. Thread dump shows 200 threads all waiting on same lock or DB. Explicit locks ( L04 ): look for ReentrantLock / AbstractQueuedSynchronizer frames. 3. Heap Dump — When & How 3.1 When to take Old gen climbing, Full GC not reclaiming — Java heap space OOM imminent or occurred Suspected retention leak — heap healthy at restart, grows over hours/days Not first tool for pure CPU spike or thread deadlock — thread dump first 3.2 How (production-safe awareness) # Histogram — lighter, triggers Full GC with :live jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram # Full dump — STW pause, large file jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof # legacy: jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid> Enable on OOM automatically ( S05 ): -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/ 3.3 MAT / dominator tree (concept — not click-by-click) Dominator tree: for each object, which retention path would free the most memory if removed? Top dominators = leak suspects. static HashMap holding millions of entries → dominator is map or static holder class Leak detector report: "Problem suspect" — one big collection retaining 80% heap Compare two dumps (baseline vs leak) — what grew? 4. Common Leak Patterns (S01–S07 Synthesis) Pattern Symptom Find with Static unbounded Map/List Old gen grows; Full GC poor reclaim Histogram: huge HashMap$Node[] or domain objects Unclosed resources FD exhaustion, native memory, connection pool starved Heap + OS lsof ; try-with-resources fix Listener registries Objects never collected after "logout" Dominator: event bus / observer list holding subscribers ThreadLocal Slow Metaspace/heap creep on pool threads Thread dump + heap; missing remove() ( S06 ) Classloader leak Metaspace stair-step; heap may be flat Metaspace OOM; redeploy without restart 5. Native Memory & Direct Buffers Not in heap dump — ByteBuffer.allocateDirect , Netty pooled direct memory: OOM: Direct buffer memory — not fixed by -Xmx Netty PooledByteBufAllocator — leaks if buffers not released Native Memory Tracking (awareness): -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary , jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary RSS > heap + Metaspace → suspect direct/native ( S01 ) 6. CPU vs Allocation Profiling — Flame Graph Mental Model CPU flame graph (async-profiler, JFR CPU events): X-axis = sample proportion (wider = more CPU time) Y-axis = stack depth (bottom = entry, top = hot leaf) Find wide plateau at HashMap.get or regex — optimize that path Allocation profiling : Answers "who allocates most?" — Young GC pressure, TLAB churn Wide bar at new byte[] or JSON parser — reduce allocation rate Different fix than CPU: object reuse, streaming, primitive arrays Interview: CPU profile for "slow" — allocation profile for "GC thrashing but low CPU business logic." 7. JFR — Java Flight Recorder (Awareness) Low-overhead event recorder built into JDK — safe for prod with tuning jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=recording.jfr Events: GC pauses, thread blocks, socket I/O, allocation samples, method hot spots Analyze in JDK Mission Control (JMC) — timeline correlates GC + thread + CPU Continuous profiling alternative to always-on APM — no vendor config lesson here 8. Production Discipline Reproduce under load — staging with prod-like traffic; thread dump alone on idle JVM misleads One change at a time — flag, code fix, pool size — measure before/after Keep GC logs — enabled from deploy ( S05 ) Capture before restart — restart destroys evidence; dump/thread print first Time-correlate — APM p99 spike timestamp = GC log line = thread dump 9. Enterprise Incident Story Arc Symptom: API p99 3 s (normal 80 ms). Error rate low. Started 14:02. 14:02 APM p99 spike 14:03 Check GC logs → Mixed GC pauses 400ms (not enough for 3s alone) 14:04 jcmd Thread.print → 180/200 tomcat threads RUNNABLE at socketRead0 14:05 Root cause hypothesis: DB replica lag — not JVM tune --- Alt path: 14:02 p99 spike + timeouts 14:03 GC logs → Full GC every 60s, heap 95% after GC 14:04 jmap -histo:live → 4M OrderDto instances 14:05 Static cache field in OrderService — code fix, not -Xmx Signal Tool first Latency + all threads in I/O Thread dump → downstream dependency Latency + long GC pauses in logs GC logs → heap tuning or leak Heap growing over days Histogram → heap dump → dominator tree CPU 100% steady CPU profile / JFR — hot method Metaspace OOM Classloader leak path ( S06 ) Pool task rejected Thread dump + pool metrics ( L05 ) Out of scope: full MAT tutorial, async-profiler install, APM vendor setup, Spring Actuator (M05). 10. Module 04 Revision — Full Arc S01 — memory map, OOM types, cgroup headroom S02 — generations, TLAB, object layout S03 — reachability, GC phases, retention S04 — G1/ZGC selection S05 — flags, GC log reading S06 — classloaders, Metaspace leaks S07 — JIT warmup, deopt, escape analysis S08 — diagnostics tie it together under fire 11. Reasoning Exercises All 50 pool threads BLOCKED on same monitor. Queue size 10k. First tool? Answer Thread dump — identify lock holder thread and stack. Fix lock scope or deadlock — not heap dump. Heap 90% after Full GC. Histogram shows 2M char[] . Next? Answer Heap dump + dominator tree — find what retains char arrays (often giant JSON strings or caches). RSS 3 GB, -Xmx1g , heap dump 1 GB. Gap? Answer Off-heap: Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, Code Cache. Check VM.native_memory and direct buffer OOM history. CPU 95%, GC logs quiet. Young GC normal. Tool? Answer CPU profiler / JFR CPU samples — hot method loop, not GC tuning. 12. 6 Senior-Level MCQs Option lengths matched to prevent visual hints. Q1: First tool for suspected deadlock? Thread dump via jstack or jcmd. Full heap dump with jmap only. Disable garbage collection flags. Restart pod before any capture. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Thread dump via jstack or jcmd.) Thread dump shows BLOCKED threads, locks waited on, and holders. Heap dump doesn't show lock graph clearly. Q2: Dominator tree in MAT primarily shows? Objects retaining most heap memory. JIT compilation tier per method. Metaspace classloader hierarchy only. Thread stack depth histogram. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Objects retaining most heap memory.) Dominator analysis finds retention paths — top dominators are leak suspects. Q3: jstat -gc best for? Live GC pool and pause stats. Bytecode verify per class file. Decompiling hot methods only. Editing Spring bean definitions. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Live GC pool and pause stats.) jstat samples GC counters over time — lightweight compared to full dump. Q4: Direct buffer OOM fixed by raising Xmx? No — separate off-heap pool. Yes — Xmx covers all memory. Yes — if UseZGC enabled only. No — only StackOverflow applies. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (No — separate off-heap pool.) Direct memory is outside heap. Fix release/pooling or MaxDirectMemorySize. Q5: CPU flame graph wide bar means? High proportion of CPU samples. Thread is in WAITING state. Object escaped to heap always. Class failed verification step. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (High proportion of CPU samples.) Width = time in that stack frame and children — hot CPU path. Q6: Production incident best discipline? Capture dumps then one fix at time. Change ten flags and redeploy. Skip logs and restart first always. Profile only on developer laptop. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Capture dumps then one fix at time.) Preserve evidence; reproduce under load; single variable changes with GC logs retained. 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 7 · Cheat sheet · ➡️ Capstone Exercise

lessons.title: Capstone Exercise
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ⬅️ Prev: Diagnostics & Memory Leaks · ➡️ Next: Why Spring JVM & Memory Management Capstone Exercise Capstone exercise • Module 04 • 16 scenarios • In-browser + optional JUnit • Stub How to use: Work through all 16 in-browser scenarios first (no IDE). Optional: copy JvmCapstoneExercise.java into IntelliJ, add JUnit 5, implement TODO s until green — stubs mirror diagnostic drills. Tie every miss back to jvm-0001 – 0008 . Scenario Index # Topic Lesson Type 01 Metaspace vs heap OOM message S01 S05 MCQ 02 GC log: Full GC tiny reclaim S05 S08 Reasoning 03 Promotion / Old gen pressure S02 S03 MCQ 04 Classloader leak symptom S06 Reasoning 05 Thread dump: pool BLOCKED S08 M03 L05 MCQ 06 Direct buffer OOM fix S01 S08 MCQ 07 -Xmx = container limit S01 S05 Reasoning 08 G1 vs ZGC pick S04 MCQ 09 TLAB purpose S02 MCQ 10 Empty object size (compressed oops) S02 MCQ 11 JIT warmup after deploy S07 Reasoning 12 Static map leak — first tool S03 S08 MCQ 13 ThreadLocal on pool thread S06 S08 Reasoning 14 forName vs loadClass S06 MCQ 15 Latency + socketRead0 — tool? S08 MCQ 16 Mixed GC pause SLO breach S04 S05 Reasoning 16 Troubleshooting Scenarios Cover answers before opening <details> . Option lengths matched. S01 — Pod OOM: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace . First fix direction? Investigate classloader retention. Double -Xmx heap immediately. Switch to Serial GC only. Shrink Eden with -Xmn flag. Answer A — S06 : Metaspace ≠ heap. Class metadata / loader leak. S05 — GC log: Pause Full (Allocation Failure) 950M->948M(1024M) 3800ms . Meaning? 950M->948M(1024M) 3800ms First action before raising -Xmx ? Answer Live set ~948 MB / 1 GB — Full GC reclaimed ~2 MB in 3.8 s. Retention leak or legit huge live set — heap dump + dominator tree ( S08 ). Not collector tune first. S02/S03 — Short-lived DTOs survive accidental ref in singleton cache. Symptom? Premature promotion fills Old gen. StackOverflow on every request. Metaspace cleared each Young GC. TLAB disabled on all threads. Answer A — Objects should die young but stay reachable → promote → Old grows → longer Mixed/Full GC ( S03 ). S06 — Tomcat: 150 redeploys, heap flat, Metaspace stair-steps. Cause? Answer Classloader leak — old WebappClassLoader pinned (ThreadLocal, JDBC driver, shutdown hook). Fix retention; restart JVM. -Xmx irrelevant. S08 — Thread dump: 48/50 pool threads BLOCKED on same monitor. Queue 8k tasks. First tool already used. Next? Find lock holder stack in same dump. Full heap dump before reading dump. Raise -Xmx to clear queue faster. Enable -XX:+UseZGC immediately. Answer A — Thread dump already taken. Find waiting to lock and who holds monitor ( M03 S02 ). Not heap. S01 — Netty service: Direct buffer memory OOM. Fix? Release buffers; tune direct pool. Double -Xmx heap to 16 GB. MaxMetaspaceSize to 512m only. -Xss 2m on all threads. Answer A — Off-heap direct pool ( S08 ). MaxDirectMemorySize guardrail; fix missing release() . S05 — 2 GiB K8s limit. Dev sets -Xmx2048m . OOMKilled, no Java heap OOM. Why? Answer Heap = entire cgroup — no room for Metaspace, stacks, direct, Code Cache, native GC ( S01 ). Use ~50% MaxRAMPercentage or -Xmx1024m max. S04 — Nightly ETL, 8 GB heap, 4 s pause OK at 2 AM. Collector? Parallel GC for throughput. ZGC for sub-ms pauses. Serial GC for all cores. G1 with MaxGCPauseMillis=10. Answer A — Batch throughput; pauses off-peak acceptable. ZGC/G1 tight pause goals waste CPU. S02 — TLAB primary benefit in multi-threaded service? Avoid global Eden lock on most news. Store static fields per thread. Replace garbage collection fully. Compress all objects at alloc time. Answer A — Per-thread bump allocation in Eden slice. S02 — Empty object bytes (64-bit, compressed oops typical)? Sixteen bytes including header. Zero bytes until first field set. Four bytes reference only. Thirty-two bytes always exact. Answer A — Mark 8 + Klass 4 + padding 4 ≈ 16 bytes typical. S07 — p99 180 ms first 8 min post-deploy; 35 ms steady. GC logs clean. Cause? Answer JIT warmup — interpreter → C1 → C2 tiered compile. Also class/cache warming. Not leak if plateau healthy. Confirm with -Xlog:jit+compilation if needed. S08 — Old gen 92% after Full GC. Histogram: 3M OrderDto . First tool sequence? Heap dump → dominator tree. Thread dump only, skip heap. Restart pod, skip capture. Lower MaxGCPauseMillis to 50. Answer A — Retention proof: dump + MAT dominator — find static Map or cache holder ( S03 ). S06/S08 — Filter sets ThreadLocal per request, never remove() . Pool threads. Slow Metaspace/heap creep. Fix? Answer try { ... } finally { threadLocal.remove(); } — pool thread retains prior request graph. Classic loader/heap leak pattern. S06 — Which triggers <clinit> by default? Class.forName with default args. ClassLoader.loadClass only. new Foo[100] array creation. jmap -histo live snapshot. Answer A — forName initializes; loadClass does not; arrays skip clinit. S08 — p99 spike. GC pauses normal. 190/200 threads RUNNABLE at socketRead0 . Category? Downstream I/O latency. Heap leak — raise Xmx. Metaspace class leak only. JIT deoptimization storm. Answer A — Threads waiting on DB/socket — fix dependency/timeouts, not GC. Incident arc from S08 . S04/S05 — API 24 GB heap, G1 Mixed GC pauses 350 ms, p99 SLO 150 ms. Code clean. Next eval? Answer Trial ZGC on JDK 21 with baseline metrics — after GC logs prove Mixed GC is culprit. Don't only tighten MaxGCPauseMillis (soft goal). Measure one change ( S04 ). Mock Interview Checklist After all 16 green (browser + optional JUnit), explain aloud: OOM message → which pool → which fix (S01 table). GC log line → before/after/cause/pause ms (S05). Thread dump vs heap dump decision tree (S08). Why Metaspace stair-step ≠ heap leak (S06). Container -Xmx headroom rule (S05). JIT warmup vs leak on deploy latency (S07). Optional JUnit Stub 12 coded drills mirroring scenarios above — OOM pool id, GC math, tool pick, ThreadLocal fix, bounded cache. Copy entire file Download stub Loading JvmCapstoneExercise.java…

lessons.title: Why Spring: IoC, DI, Layers & Manual Wiring
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ⬅️ Prev: JVM Capstone · Lesson 1 of 9 · Lesson 2 → · Cheat sheet Why Spring: IoC, DI, Layers & Manual Wiring ~30 minutes · Module 05 Lesson 1 of 9 · builds on Polymorphism , Abstraction , final , JVM process model Senior Interview Focus: Can you explain Spring without listing annotations? Interviewers want: why object graphs explode, what inversion of control actually inverts, why constructor injection beats field injection, what a bean is (and is not), and how layers + DIP keep a payment service testable. This lesson is the “why.” Lifecycle, scan, auto-config, and proxies come later — do not hide behind them yet. Primary sources: Spring Framework — IoC Container · Spring Framework — Dependency Injection · Spring Boot — Structuring Your Code 1. Why new Graphs Rot Must know (interview): Hard-coded construction couples who uses a type to how it is built . Tests, environments, and feature flags all fight that coupling. CheckoutService └─ new StripeClient(apiKey) └─ new HttpClient() └─ new RetryPolicy() └─ new MetricsSink() // now every test needs Stripe + HTTP Pain that shows up in production codebases: Change blast radius — swap Stripe for Razorpay and every new CheckoutService() site changes. Hidden graph — constructors grow; nobody sees the full tree until a NPE in prod. Untestable — cannot inject a fake gateway without bytecode tricks or static mocks. Env chaos — local vs K8s URLs, secrets, pool sizes baked into constructors. Common misconception: “Spring exists so we type less.” No. Spring exists so composition of the object graph is a first-class, inspectable concern — not scattered new . 2. Manual Wiring First (No Spring) Write the composition root by hand. This is still valid Java. Spring later automates this same graph . public final class App { public static void main(String[] args) { UserRepository repo = new JdbcUserRepository(dataSource); UserService service = new UserService(repo); UserController controller = new UserController(service); // start HTTP server, pass controller } } Mental model: One place owns construction. Dependencies flow inward through constructors. The rest of the app never calls new on collaborators. Manual wiring scales until: 80 beans, 3 profiles, 12 optional features. Then you reinvent a container (poorly). That is Spring’s job. 3. IoC — Simple Mental Model Inversion of Control = you stop being the one who decides when and how objects are created. The framework calls you. Without IoC (you drive): main() → new A() → new B() → new C() → a.run() With IoC (framework drives): framework starts → creates C, B, A → injects → calls your methods (HTTP handler, @Scheduled, CommandLineRunner) The “control” that inverted is object lifetime + call graph assembly , not business logic. Your charge() method still belongs to you. Hollywood principle: “Don’t call us — we’ll call you.” Servlet container did this decades before Spring. Spring applied it to plain Java objects . 4. Dependency Injection — How Collaborators Arrive DI is one technique of IoC: the object does not look up collaborators; they are passed in . Style Shape Senior judgment Constructor Foo(Bar bar) + private final Bar bar Default. Required deps, immutable, fully initialized, unit-test with new Foo(mock) . Setter setBar(Bar bar) Optional / reconfigurable. Object can exist half-wired. Use sparingly. Field @Autowired Bar bar; Works. Hides deps. Hard to test without Spring Test. Reflection. Avoid in application code. Spring team guidance (Framework reference): constructors for mandatory deps; setters for optional. Constructor-injected beans are returned only after all required collaborators exist — no “use before init.” You already met this in final : constructor injection + final fields is the Boot 3 house style. Single constructor: @Autowired is optional (Spring 4.3+). Interview trap: “Field injection is fine because Boot uses it in samples.” Samples optimize for brevity. Production services optimize for testability and required-deps-at-compile-time. Nice to know: Boot 3.2 / Framework 6.1 stopped guessing parameter names from bytecode. Compile with -parameters (Maven/Gradle plugins do this) or constructor binding / @Qualifier names break in surprising ways. 5. Who Creates What WITHOUT Spring Application code │ new + wire ▼ Object graph WITH Spring Application code ──asks──► IoC container (ApplicationContext) │ creates + wires beans ▼ Object graph Your main still exists — it starts the container ( SpringApplication.run ). After that, you ask or you get called . You do not assemble 80 constructors yourself. 6. What a Bean Is A bean is an object whose lifecycle and wiring the Spring container manages. It has a name, a type, a scope, and (usually) dependencies recorded in a BeanDefinition . Is a bean: UserService , DataSource , ObjectMapper if registered. Usually not a bean: JPA entities, request DTOs, Money value objects, loop-local ArrayList . Must know: Spring does not intercept every new . A DTO you construct in a controller is a plain heap object — see Stack vs Heap . Only registered types enter the container. 7. Layers & Dependency Direction HTTP │ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ Controller │ translation: HTTP ↔ application commands └──────┬──────┘ │ depends on ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ Service │ use-cases, transactions (S06), orchestration └──────┬──────┘ │ depends on ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ Repository │ persistence port (interface) └──────┬──────┘ │ implemented by ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ Database │ JDBC / JPA (Module 06) └─────────────┘ Arrows mean compile-time dependency . Upper layers depend on abstractions (interfaces), not on JDBC driver classes. That is DIP in one diagram — you met the idea in Abstraction . Production relevance: A controller that talks JDBC skips the service layer → no single transaction boundary, no place for authz, untestable HTTP+SQL mash. Seniors defend the layer, not the annotation. 8. DIP — Tiny Payment Gateway public interface PaymentGateway { Receipt charge(Money amount, String customerId); } public final class CheckoutService { private final PaymentGateway gateway; public CheckoutService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; } public OrderId checkout(Cart cart) { gateway.charge(cart.total(), cart.customerId()); return OrderId.newId(); } } public final class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { /* HTTP to Stripe */ } public final class FakeGateway implements PaymentGateway { /* tests */ } High-level CheckoutService does not import Stripe. Infra implements the interface. Swap in tests with new CheckoutService(new FakeGateway()) — zero Spring required for that unit test. 9. Before / After Spring (Same Graph) After (stereotype sketch — scanning detail is S03): @RestController public class UserController { private final UserService service; public UserController(UserService service) { this.service = service; } } @Service public class UserService { private final UserRepository repo; public UserService(UserRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; } } @Repository public class JdbcUserRepository implements UserRepository { private final DataSource ds; public JdbcUserRepository(DataSource ds) { this.ds = ds; } } Container finds types, creates JdbcUserRepository , then UserService , then UserController — same order you wrote by hand. Annotations are metadata , not magic. 10. Why Spring Is More Than Boilerplate If DI were the whole story, a 40-line composition root would suffice. Spring also provides: Capability Mechanism (named) When you need it Lifecycle Bean factory + init/destroy callbacks Warm caches, close pools — S02 Configuration Environment , profiles, properties dev vs prod without recompile — S03–S04 AOP JDK / CGLIB proxies wrapping beans tx, security, metrics without polluting domain — S06 Transactions PlatformTransactionManager + proxy advice commit/rollback around a service method — S06 Testing Test slices, mock beans, Testcontainers later Slice tests without full server Extensibility Auto-config + conditions + starters Add JDBC → get DataSource unless you defined one — S05 Boot specifically: embedded Tomcat (S07), actuator (S08), opinionated classpath. Framework IoC still sits underneath. 11. IoC Container vs DI — Precise Distinction Term What it is What it is not IoC Who controls creation, wiring, and when your code runs Not “using Spring annotations” IoC container BeanFactory / ApplicationContext holding beans Not the HTTP server DI Passing collaborators in (constructor/setter/field) Not a synonym for IoC You can do DI with zero Spring (manual wiring). You can have IoC without constructor DI (Service Locator / getBean lookups — generally worse). Spring’s default story: container + constructor DI . Common misconception: “DI = IoC.” DI is how dependencies arrive. IoC is who owns the call/create graph . 12. Misconceptions Spring creates every object. False. Only beans. new OrderRequest(json) is yours. new is forbidden. False. Forbidden: new of a collaborator that should be a bean inside another bean (you skip the proxy — S06). Allowed: value objects, builders, test fakes, JDK types. Stereotypes change DI. @Service vs @Component — same container registration for core DI. Specializations are documentation + exception translation later. Spring replaces OOP. False. Polymorphism and interfaces are the injection points. 13. What Happens When Spring Boot Starts? — Preview Only java -jar app.jar │ ▼ SpringApplication.run │ ├─ 1. Environment (properties, profiles, env vars) → S04 ├─ 2. ApplicationContext created → S02 ├─ 3. Bean definitions (scan + @Bean + auto-config) → S03, S05 ├─ 4. Instantiate + inject + init callbacks → S02 ├─ 5. Embedded web server starts (Tomcat by default) → S07 └─ 6. Ready — Actuator, traffic → S08 Do not memorize this as a 40-step list yet. Remember: environment → definitions → instances → server . Detail in later sections. Production Relevance Incident: “works locally, missing bean in prod” — usually scan base package or profile/condition (S03–S05), not “Spring broken.” Review smell: @Autowired on 12 fields, no constructor — untestable and circular-deps-prone (S02). K8s: one JVM process ( S01 JVM ) hosting one ApplicationContext (typical). Beans live on the heap like any objects. Interview Articulation “Spring’s IoC container owns the object graph. We declare types and constructor dependencies; the context instantiates and injects them. DI is the passing-in of collaborators — we prefer constructors so deps are required, final, and mockable without starting Spring. A bean is a container-managed object, not every Java object. Layers keep HTTP, use-cases, and persistence from collapsing into one class.” Interview Traps Equating IoC with DI. Saying field injection is “the Spring way.” Claiming controllers must new services. Promising auto-config details you have not learned (S05). Senior Interview Questions (open) Why is a 200-class app painful if every class constructs its own collaborators? Walk a three-layer graph using only new . What did you just invent? Define IoC in one sentence without the word “annotation.” Constructor vs field injection — three concrete reasons for constructor. What is a Spring bean? Give two objects that should not be beans. Draw Controller → Service → Repository. Which way do source dependencies point? How does DIP show up in a payment integration? Is new ArrayList<>() inside a @Service a smell? Why or why not? Revision Notes Composition root: one owner of new for collaborators. IoC = framework owns create/call graph. DI = pass deps in. Constructor + final = required, testable, initialized. Bean = container-managed. DTOs/entities usually not. Depend on interfaces; infra implements. Boot start preview: env → context → definitions → instances → Tomcat. Interview One-Liners “DI is a technique; the IoC container is the runtime that applies it.” “If I can new it in a unit test with fakes, constructor injection paid off.” “ new of a collaborator inside a bean skips the container — and later the transaction proxy.” “Layers are dependency direction, not folder names.” Senior MCQs Cover answers before opening. Option lengths matched. Q1: IoC primarily inverts which responsibility? Who creates and wires application objects. Who writes SQL inside repository classes. Who allocates heap vs stack for locals. Who compiles Java sources in Maven. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Who creates and wires application objects.) IoC is about object graph assembly and call timing, not SQL, JVM memory, or the compiler. Q2: Preferred injection style for a required UserRepository? Constructor plus a final field. Public setter called after traffic. Field autowire with no constructor. Static lookup from a global map. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Constructor plus a final field.) Spring team guidance: mandatory deps via constructor. Immutable, testable, fully initialized. Q3: Which object is typically a Spring bean? A singleton UserService in the context. A JSON request DTO per HTTP call. A JPA entity loaded from a row. A loop-local ArrayList of IDs. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (A singleton UserService in the context.) DTOs, entities, and local collections are ordinary heap objects, not container-managed beans. Q4: DI versus IoC — accurate statement? DI is one way to implement IoC wiring. DI and IoC are identical terms always. IoC means field injection only in Boot. DI requires Tomcat to exist first. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (DI is one way to implement IoC wiring.) You can DI by hand with no container. Tomcat is the servlet container (S07), not the definition of DI. Q5: Correct compile-time dependency direction? Service depends on PaymentGateway interface. Service imports Stripe SDK classes only. Repository depends on RestController types. Entity depends on DispatcherServlet class. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Service depends on PaymentGateway interface.) DIP: high-level policy depends on abstractions. Infra (Stripe) implements the port. Q6: new HashMap inside a @Service method? Fine — not a collaborator bean. Illegal — Spring forbids all new. Always a circular dependency bug. Requires @Bean on HashMap always. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Fine — not a collaborator bean.) Local JDK structures are not IoC concerns. Smell is new StripeClient() inside the service. Bridge to Next Lessons S02 — ApplicationContext, scopes, lifecycle callbacks S03 — scan, @Configuration , profiles S05 — auto-config (why beans appear from a dependency) 🏠 Home · ⬅️ Prev: JVM Capstone · Lesson 2 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: ApplicationContext, Scopes & Lifecycle
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 2 of 9 · Lesson 3 → · Cheat sheet ApplicationContext, Bean Scopes & Bean Lifecycle ~35 minutes · Module 05 Lesson 2 of 9 · builds on Why Spring , Object lifecycle Senior Interview Focus: Can you walk a bean from BeanDefinition to ready singleton without stuttering? Singleton vs Java enum singleton? Why injecting a prototype into a singleton does not give a new instance per method? Why constructor cycles fail in modern Spring? This is the container — not annotations yet. Primary sources: BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext · Bean Scopes · Lifecycle Callbacks 1. What ApplicationContext Is Must know: ApplicationContext is the IoC container you actually use. It holds bean definitions, creates beans, injects them, publishes events, and (in web apps) is the parent of request-scoped contexts. Typical Boot: one root AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext (name varies) per JVM process. Beans are heap objects rooted by that context — GC will not collect singletons until the context closes ( GC roots ). 2. BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext BeanFactory ApplicationContext Role Core DI: getBean, definitions BeanFactory + enterprise services Messages No i18n MessageSource Events No ApplicationEventPublisher AOP Manual Integrated post-processors / auto-proxy Eager singletons Typically lazy until getBean Pre-instantiates singletons at refresh (default) You never new a raw DefaultListableBeanFactory in Boot. Context is-a BeanFactory. 3. Container Pipeline Configuration (@Configuration, scan, auto-config) │ ▼ BeanDefinition registry (name, class, scope, deps) │ ▼ Instantiate (constructor / factory method) │ ▼ Populate / DI (fields, setters — after ctor) │ ▼ Initialization (BPP, @PostConstruct, InitializingBean) │ ▼ Ready bean in singleton cache │ ▼ Destruction on context close (@PreDestroy, DisposableBean) Mental model: Definitions first (metadata). Instances second. Refresh() runs this pipeline. Failures here are startup failures — better than 3 a.m. NPEs. 4–7. Lifecycle Step-by-Step new Target() // 1 constructor — only ctor-injected deps exist │ ▼ inject remaining // 2 setter/field DI │ ▼ BeanPostProcessor.before // 3 framework wrappers start (proxy often later) │ ▼ @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet / custom init-method │ ▼ BeanPostProcessor.after // 4 often where AOP proxy replaces bean (S06) │ ▼ bean in use │ context.close() │ ▼ @PreDestroy / destroy() / DisposableBean @Component public class CacheWarmer { private final CatalogRepo repo; public CacheWarmer(CatalogRepo repo) { this.repo = repo; log.info("1 ctor — repo injected, not ready to serve HTTP yet"); } @PostConstruct void warm() { log.info("2 @PostConstruct — safe: all deps set, proxy may wrap after"); repo.preload(); } @PreDestroy void stop() { log.info("3 @PreDestroy — context closing, drain work"); } } jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct / PreDestroy (Jakarta EE, Boot 3). Not a substitute for constructors: ctor still runs first. Trap: calling other beans’ business methods from a constructor — they may not be initialized; you can see NPEs or half-proxies. Warm in @PostConstruct or ApplicationReadyEvent . Nice to know: InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet is the Spring interface equivalent of @PostConstruct . Prefer the annotation for app code. 8. Scopes Scope How many instances When singleton (default) One per context Services, repos, DataSource — 99% of beans prototype New every getBean / injection at injection time Stateful helpers — rare; prefer immutable + args request One per HTTP request Web only — request attributes session One per HTTP session Web — avoid fat session state application One per ServletContext Web — similar to singleton in one war websocket One per WebSocket session Messaging apps Web scopes need a web-aware context. Using request in a CLI Boot app fails at injection. 9. Singleton Mental Model ApplicationContext singleton cache: UserService@7a3 ←── Controller.service ←── OtherBean.userService SAME reference (identity ==) Many injection points, one instance . That instance must be thread-safe for shared mutable state — you studied this in threads and monitors . Stateless services are the easy path. 10. Spring Singleton ≠ Enum Singleton Joshua Bloch enum singleton = one JVM-wide instance of that enum type. Spring singleton = one instance per ApplicationContext . Tests with two contexts → two UserService objects. Parent/child contexts → possibly two. Not enum INSTANCE . 11. Prototype Destruction Container calls destroy callbacks on singletons it cached. Prototypes: after handing you the instance, Spring typically does not track them for @PreDestroy . You own disposal (or use a custom scope / DestructionAwareBeanPostProcessor — nice to know). 12. Singleton Injecting Prototype @Controller (singleton) │ injects once at startup ▼ PrototypeBean instance_A // frozen for the life of the controller Must know: Injection happens once for the singleton. Every method call uses instance_A , not a fresh prototype. To get a new prototype per call: scoped proxy ( @Scope(proxyMode = TARGET_CLASS) ) or ObjectProvider (next). 13. ObjectProvider / Provider @Service public class JobRunner { private final ObjectProvider<PrototypeWorker> workers; public JobRunner(ObjectProvider<PrototypeWorker> workers) { this.workers = workers; } public void run() { PrototypeWorker w = workers.getObject(); // new prototype w.execute(); } } jakarta.inject.Provider is the same idea. Prefer this over storing ApplicationContext and calling getBean (service locator smell). 14. @Lazy Defers singleton creation until first use. Use for expensive beans or to break some cycles. Cost: first request pays init; failures move from startup to traffic. Prefer fixing the cycle. 15. Circular Dependencies A ctor needs B, B ctor needs A → BeanCurrentlyInCreationException (typical) Spring 6 / Boot 3: constructor cycles fail fast . Setter/field injection historically allowed a half-created singleton into the other bean (early reference). That hid design bugs. Interview framing: cycles mean muddled responsibilities — extract C that both depend on, or events, not “enable circular references.” spring.main.allow-circular-references=true exists as an escape hatch. Treat as debt. 16. Ordering @DependsOn("flyway") — this bean after that bean’s init. Ordered / @Order — among list of same type (filters, listeners). Not a general “create A before B” for arbitrary beans — use @DependsOn or natural constructor deps. Production Debugging Startup hang in @PostConstruct that calls remote HTTP — blocks refresh; pod never Ready. Prototype leak: creating prototypes in a loop without discard → heap growth (S08 + JVM dumps). Request-scoped bean injected into singleton without proxy → exception or wrong instance. Interview Articulation “ApplicationContext is the IoC container: it registers BeanDefinitions, instantiates, injects, runs init callbacks, then caches singletons. Default scope is singleton — one instance per context, not a JVM enum singleton. A prototype injected into a singleton is resolved once unless I use ObjectProvider or a scoped proxy. Constructor circular dependencies fail at startup; that’s a design smell, not a flag to flip.” Senior Interview Questions BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext — three extras the context adds. Order of constructor, DI, @PostConstruct, destroy. Why not do I/O in a constructor of a bean? Spring singleton vs enum singleton. Prototype injected into singleton — how many instances after 100 HTTP calls? Does @PreDestroy run on prototypes? Constructor cycle: what exception, what refactor? When is @Lazy justified vs harmful? Revision Notes Context = BeanFactory + events + i18n + eager singletons + AOP integration. Pipeline: definition → new → inject → init → cache → destroy. Singleton: one per context; thread-safety is your problem. Prototype: new at lookup; destroy not managed like singleton. ObjectProvider for fresh prototype; ctor cycles fail. Interview One-Liners “Startup is refresh(); traffic is getBean from an already-warm cache.” “Same singleton reference everywhere is a feature — mutable fields are the bug.” “@PostConstruct is after injection, not after the HTTP server is up — use ApplicationReadyEvent for that.” Senior MCQs Q1: Default Spring bean scope? Singleton — one instance per context. Prototype — new instance per HTTP call. Request — one instance per JVM boot. Session — one instance per classloader. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Singleton — one instance per context.) Q2: Prototype injected into a singleton controller. 50 requests? One prototype unless provider/proxy used. Fifty prototypes created automatically. Zero — prototypes cannot be injected. Fifty plus one enum singleton extra. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (One prototype unless provider/proxy used.) Injection is once at singleton creation. Q3: Constructor circular dependency in Boot 3? Fails at startup — fix the design. Always silently creates two proxies. Resolved by Tomcat thread pool size. Impossible because Java forbids cycles. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Fails at startup — fix the design.) Q4: @PreDestroy on a prototype bean? Usually not invoked by the container. Always runs after every HTTP request. Replaces GC for that object always. Runs only if the class is final. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Usually not invoked by the container.) Q5: ApplicationContext compared to BeanFactory? Adds events, messages, eager singletons, AOP hooks. Removes dependency injection completely. Is only the embedded Tomcat engine. Exists solely for WebFlux event loops. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Adds events, messages, eager singletons, AOP hooks.) Q6: Best fix for a new prototype per job run? ObjectProvider.getObject() at call site. Store ApplicationContext and ignore types. Make the job runner request-scoped always. Use static new inside a static block. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (ObjectProvider.getObject() at call site.) 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 1 · Lesson 3 → · Cheat sheet

lessons.title: @Configuration, Scanning & Profiles
lessons.text: 🏠 Home · ← Lesson 2 · Lesson 3 of 9 · Lesson 4 → · Cheat sheet @Configuration, @Bean, Component Scanning & Profiles ~30 minutes · Module 05 Lesson 3 of 9 · builds on S02 Senior Interview Focus: “Bean not found” is a scan/profile/@Bean-name problem until proven otherwise. Can you explain where Boot scans from, when to use @Bean vs @Component, and why calling another @Bean method from a @Configuration class returns the singleton? Profiles in K8s are how prod accidentally gets H2. Primary sources: Classpath Scanning · Java-based Configuration · Boot Profiles 1. Stereotypes — Same DI, Different Intent Annotation Meaning Core DI difference? @Component Generic scanned bean Baseline @Service Application service None for wiring @Repository Persistence adapter Exception translation via advisor (nice to know) @Controller / @RestController MVC handler Discovered by RequestMappingHandlerMapping (S07) Must know: For constructor injection, @Service vs @Component is documentation. Do not invent magic. 2. Component Scanning Flow @SpringBootApplication │ meta: @ComponentScan (default: this package + below) ▼ ClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner │ finds @Component (and meta-annotated) ▼ BeanDefinition registered (name: decapitalized class, or @Component("id")) │ ▼ S02 pipeline: instantiate → DI → init Mental model: Scan writes definitions . Refresh instantiates. If the class is not a definition, you never get a bean — regardless of how pretty the constructor is. 3. Package Boundaries — #1 “Bean Not Found” com.acme.shop.ShopApplication ← @SpringBootApplication here com.acme.shop.api.HelloController scanned ✓ com.acme.payments.StripeConfig NOT scanned ✗ (sibling of shop) Default scan base = package of the annotated application class and subpackages , not the whole JAR. Fix: move code under the app package, or @ComponentScan("com.acme") / @SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = ...) . Trap: putting main in com.acme and accidentally scanning every library component. Too wide is also a bug (duplicate beans, slow start). 4. @Configuration and @Bean @Configuration public class ClockConfig { @Bean Clock utcClock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); } } You own construction. Useful for types you cannot annotate (JDK, third-party ObjectMapper ). 5. @Component Class vs @Bean Method Use @Component on your class when Use @Bean when You own the source; simple ctor DI Third-party type, explicit construction, multiple variants Stereotype communicates layer Conditional setup (S04) around one factory method 6. @Configuration Method Interception (Interview-Level) Full @Configuration classes are CGLIB-enhanced (unless proxyBeanMethods = false ). Calling utcClock() from another @Bean method in the same class hits the container , not a second new Clock — you get the singleton. @Configuration public class TimeConfig { @Bean Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); } @Bean Ticker ticker() { return new Ticker(clock()); // same Clock bean, not a second instance } } @AutoConfiguration / lite mode uses proxyBeanMethods = false — then clock() really runs again. Boot auto-config classes are lite. App @Configuration defaults to proxied. Do not confuse the two (S05). Nice to know: @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) is faster to start; you must inject beans as method parameters instead of calling sibling methods. 7–8. @Profile @Configuration @Profile("dev") public class DevMailConfig { @Bean MailSender mailSender() { return new LoggingMailSender(); } } Activate: spring.profiles.active=dev (env, CLI, K8s). Multiple profiles: comma-separated. Profile-specific files: application-prod.yml (S04). Production pitfalls: Laptop accidentally prod → hits real Stripe. K8s missing SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE → default profile, missing prod DataSource bean. @Profile("!prod") forgotten — H2 on in prod. 9. Common Mistakes Symptom Cause NoSuchBeanDefinitionException Outside scan, missing @Component/@Bean, wrong profile, condition false (S04) NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException Two @Bean of same type — S04 @Primary/@Qualifier Unexpected bean Scan too wide; name clash ( foo vs method name) Default @Bean name = method name. @Bean("utc") overrides. Duplicate names overwrite or fail depending on context — don’t rely on overwrite. 10. Bridge to S02 This lesson fills the first box: how BeanDefinitions get registered . S02 already covered instantiate → init. S05 adds a third registration source: auto-configuration imports. Production Relevance Most “it works on my machine” Boot tickets: main class in the wrong package after a refactor, or profile not set in the Deployment env. First debug step: log ApplicationContext.getBeanDefinitionNames() or Actuator /beans (S08) — is the definition even there? Interview Articulation “Boot scans the application class package and below for @Component. Third-party types I register with @Bean on a @Configuration class. @Configuration is CGLIB-proxied so @Bean methods return the singleton when they call each other. If a bean is missing, I check scan base, profile, and bean name before I blame autowiring.” Senior Interview Questions Where does @SpringBootApplication scan by default? @Service vs @Component for DI? When must you use @Bean instead of annotating the class? Why does ticker() calling clock() not create two Clocks? proxyBeanMethods = false — what breaks if you call sibling @Bean methods? How do you activate prod in Kubernetes? Two modules, application class in api — where do domain @Services live? Bean name of @Bean Clock utcClock()? Revision Notes Scan = package of main + children. Stereotypes ≈ documentation for DI. @Bean for types you don’t own. Full @Configuration intercepts @Bean calls → singleton. Profiles gate definitions; env must match. Interview One-Liners “If it’s not a BeanDefinition, injection cannot save you.” “Sibling @Bean calls go through the container on a proxied @Configuration.” “Wrong scan package is the boring answer — and usually the right one.” Senior MCQs Q1: Main in com.acme.app. Bean in com.other.svc missing. Why? Default scan does not include sibling packages. @Service is invisible to the container always. Tomcat cannot load classes outside java.lang. Constructor injection forbids other packages. View Answer & Explanation Answer: A (Default scan does not include sibling packages.) Q2: @Service versus @Component for constructor DI?
